words: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue. Work side to side, from the left edge out. This sky is only a small patch: it touches the top edge and the left edge, and it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall.

Most of the paint sits in the top half of the sky through the window. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white for the last few strokes where the sky ends. Then stroke back up over the join while both are wet, so the sky gets a little lighter as it goes down.
Let the sky's lower edge stay soft and uneven, with a little rounded bite of bare canvas in it. Leave all the rest of the canvas white.
If you see a hard line where the two colors meet, add a bit more Warm white at the join and blend again.
Let the sky dry first, or the leaves will smear into it. Wipe the old stiff brush nearly dry with Leaf green, then tap with its tip over the sky through the window, starting at the top edge.

Tap most of it over the left half and top half of the leaves outside the window. Then tap more solidly down a narrow strip at the sky's outer side. That strip's top is about 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side is about 1 in from the left edge. Let it hang down a little past the sky like a drooping clump.
Keep a few pale spots of sky showing between the taps, near the corner and in the rounded bite.
Blobs instead of dots mean the brush is too wet. Wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.
Wait until the Leaf green is dry. Wipe most of the Sunny leaf green off the old stiff brush, then tap lightly on the tops of the leaf clumps, starting at the top of the narrow hanging strip.
Use small, scattered taps only, on the side facing the light. Most of the Leaf green should still show underneath.
When you stop, the leaves look much as before, just touched with a few lighter taps. If a patch goes solid, tap over it with Leaf green to break it up.
Make sure the leaves are dry first. Start at the top edge, just right of the sky through the window, with Deep wall blue. Stroke side to side in an even, creamy coat.

Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and keep stroking side to side, working out toward the right edge of the canvas and down to the bottom edge. Stroke back over the join while both blues are wet, so the deeper blue by the window fades softly into the lighter blue.
Leave the pale sky and the leaves in the window showing. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
When you stop, the whole canvas is blue except the window. The blue wall is 16 in wide and 12 in tall. If you see a hard line where the blues meet, add a little more Wall blue there and blend again.

Let the wall dry first. Start with one simple shape: a tall, wide post of Warm white running from the top edge of the canvas to the bottom edge, between the window and the blue wall. Across the middle of the frame, the paint runs from about 1 in to 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
Then add the smaller pieces running out from the post to the left edge: a thin inner post along the window's edge, a thin crossbar high up across the view, and a wider, slightly slanted bottom ledge.

Keep the sky and leaves showing in the window panes, and keep the patch of blue wall between the ledge and the bottom edge. Soften the joins so the frame reads as smooth, flat cream with straight edges and no shading yet.

Let the cream frame dry first. Start where the wide post meets the top edge, on the side of the post that faces the blue wall, and pull a lavender gray band straight down to the bottom edge of the canvas.

Then add the smaller pieces: a thin band down the inner post where it meets the window, a thin line along the underside of the crossbar, a band along the front face of the bottom ledge, and a long slanted shadow down the post where the ledge meets it.

The light comes from the window at the upper left, so the faces turned toward the window stay cream white. Keep each band narrow. A common mistake is covering too much of the cream. When you stop, the frame reads as cream bars with lavender shadow edges.
Let the blue wall and the white window frame dry first, because the sill's top edge is painted right against them.

Start with one long slanted rectangle for the sill's top. Begin just below the white window frame, so its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge. Let it tilt gently lower as it runs out to the right edge of the canvas. Pull flat strokes side to side along the length of the sill, like wood grain.
Then lay a narrower strip for the sill's front edge along the bottom edge of the canvas. Let a thin line show where it meets the top.

When you stop, the whole sill is one flat Warm wood brown shape, solid out to the left, right and bottom edges of the canvas. Keep its top edge crisp. A common mistake is letting the brown wobble up into the wall.
The flat brown must be fully dry. Dip only the tip of the 3/4 inch flat in Warm wood brown, with no water.

Start at the right edge of the canvas on the sill's top. Skim light strokes side to side along the grain, working left until about 4 3/4 in from the left edge. Then skim broken strokes along the front edge strip.

Leave the sill's top near the left edge of the canvas untouched, because the sunlight falls there. Inside it, skim only the narrow slanted bands of the frame's shadow; one crosses about 1/2 in from the left edge.
Stop when it looks streaky and see-through, with the base brown showing. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the base brown back over part of it.
Let the dry-brushed brown dry first. This sunny patch sits at the left end of the sill's top. The whole patch is about 6 1/2 in wide, and its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.

Start with the biggest piece: a long wedge of Sunny peach that widens as it slants toward the front edge, its far end breaking into a few small bits. Then add a slim slanted strip about 3 3/4 in wide nearer the window, and a small piece at the left edge of the canvas.
Pull each piece along the slant of the light. Leave the brown shadow bands of the frame showing between the pieces, and don't paint across them.
When you stop, three crisp peach pieces fan across the sill like sunlight coming through the window.
Let the sill and the blue wall dry first. The blanket goes on top of both.

Start with one long, low oval for the bed, low across the canvas. Its top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge and its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge. Run it to the right edge of the canvas. Its left end stops about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, just touching the white window frame.
Then add the curved roll along the front, with the folded edge under it. Make the left end two rounded bumps, one above the other, where the roll sits on the fold.
Pull the strokes along the length of the blanket. Smooth the joins so it reads as one flat golden shape, with no wall or wood showing through. Give it a second coat if it looks streaky.
Let the Golden yellow dry so the loops stay crisp.

Start just under the top of the raised back rim. Tap rows of small commas there: press, then lift, so each one points down into the hollow of the bed. Follow the curved edge of the hollow around to the left end. Then scatter loose loops across the hollow itself.

The loops are thickest on the lower half of the front roll and along the fold under it. Down the middle of the blanket, that thick band runs from about 8 3/4 in to 10 1/2 in from the top edge. Pull pairs of commas downward so they lean into little V stitches.
Leave plain gold along the top of the rim and the top of the front roll. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.
Wait until the Dark ochre loops are dry.

Start at the rounded end nearest the window, about 1 1/4 in from the left edge. Tap pale commas thickly over that end, because the light comes from the window at the upper left. Press, then lift, with each one curving around the end of the roll.
Then move right with fewer and smaller loops. Put them on the tops of the roll and the fold, and a few across the hollow and the rim. Most of them sit on the left side of the blanket.
Tap them in between the dark loops, not over them. When you stop, the lit end and the tops should glitter softly, and the right part of the blanket should stay mostly gold and dark.

Let the blanket dry first, because the cat lies right over its top. Start with one big oval for the curled body, its top about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, running all the way to the right edge of the canvas.

Add a circle for the head at the window end of the oval, then two triangle ears: one pointing up, one pointing out toward the window, its tip about 1 in from the left edge. Bring the bottom of the oval down onto the blanket's roll, pulling the strokes around the curl like fur.

Cover everything flat mid gray, about 15 in wide. Stop when it reads as one plain gray cat shape with no shading. A common mistake is leaving yellow slivers where the cat meets the blanket: paint right down into the knit.
Let the Mid gray dry first. Begin at the deep fold where the head meets the body, pulling one curved stroke down from behind the upright ear toward the paws.

Then sweep curved strokes around the round rump at the far end of the cat, and along the tail where it curls in under the body toward the paws, following each curve. Add a few broken dark touches on the back and under the chin.

Leave the top of the back, the head and the two paw shapes Mid gray, and leave a patch on the cat's side for the white later. Stop when the cat looks round: dark fold, rump and tail, mid gray on top. Don't flatten it into one dark blob.
Let the Dark gray dry, or the white will turn gray. Start on the muzzle: a narrow white wedge from between the eyes down to the chin, its left side about 3 1/4 in from the left edge.
Below the chin, paint the two front paws as round white mounds tucked side by side on the blanket, curving each stroke around the paw. Leave a thin gray line between the paws and for the toes.
Then lay the patch on the cat's side, about 2 3/4 in wide, pulling curved strokes up along the body so its upper edge breaks into pointed fingers of fur.
Use 2 to 3 thin coats, drying between them, instead of one thick coat. Stop when the muzzle, paws and side patch read clean white.
Let the white patches dry first, because the stripes run right up to them. Start at the top of the cat's back, near the spine, where the top of the stripes is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.

Press the full width of the angle brush at the spine, then pull each stripe down and around the curve of the body toward the blanket, turning onto the edge so it tapers to a point. Let them bend like hoops around a barrel. Cross the tail with short bands, thick at the top of the tail and thin underneath.

On the head, pull short tapered stripes down from the crown toward the closed eyes, add a few small curves on the cheeks, and run a thin dark edge along both ears. Keep off the white muzzle, chest patch and paws, and leave plenty of gray between the stripes.
When you stop, the stripes wrap the whole cat out to about 1 in from the right edge. A common mistake is stripes of even width: every one should start wide and end in a point.
Let the charcoal ear edges dry before you start. Begin with the ear nearer the window. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.

Touch the round's tip down near the base of the ear, press so the belly spreads, then pull up toward the ear's point and lift so the stroke ends on the tip. Two or three of these fill the inside of the ear. Then do the same in the ear on top of the head, whose left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
Keep the pink inside the triangles and leave a thin gray and charcoal rim showing all around each ear.
When you stop, both ears are rosy inside with a dark rim, and the rest of the cat is untouched. If you get a blob instead of a tapered stroke, use less paint and lift faster.
Let the Charcoal stripes and the Soft pink ears dry first, or the light gray will smear them.

Start along the spine of the sleeping tabby cat, near where the back curves away from the head. Load the fan brush lightly. Set its edge in the gray, flick out the way the fur lies, and lift off so each mark thins at its tip. Work down over the back, round the curled tail, and over the head and cheeks.

Most of the paint goes on the right side of the cat's fur, over the big curled body. Let the flicks cross the edges of the Charcoal stripes, but leave their middles dark. Leave the warm white muzzle, chest patch and paws clean, and keep off the pink inside the ears.
When you stop, the whole gray coat looks soft and furry, with darker gray between the flicks. A common mistake is too much paint, which leaves flat light blobs instead of fur.
Start on the white muzzle, where the two white cheeks meet. That is where the nose sits, with its middle about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.

Load the tip of the brush full with creamy Soft pink. Touch down where the bridge of the nose ends, then press so the belly spreads into a small triangle. Pull down toward the chin and lift so the stroke ends on a point.
One or two presses are enough. The nose is a tiny triangle about 3/4 in wide. Keep the white muzzle showing all around it, and leave the gray face alone.
A common mistake is a round blob instead of a triangle, from too much paint or too slow a lift. Use less paint and lift faster. Once it is dry, you can tidy the edges with a little white.
Let the Soft pink nose and the face dry first. Liner lines spread on wet paint.

Thin the Charcoal with water until it flows like ink. Hold the brush upright with light, steady pressure. Start each closed eye at its inner corner by the white muzzle and pull a gentle curve out toward the ear. Begin a little thick and lighten off so the line tapers.

Add a tiny mouth line at the point of the nose. Next, run a thin dark edge along the outer rim of each ear, from base to tip. Tuck a small dark shadow where the chin meets the body, then add a few short lines on the cheek next to it.
When you stop, the face should read as a calm, sleeping cat. Leave the pink inside the ears showing. If a line skips, add water and reload.
The Charcoal eye lines must be dry before you start, or the white will smear gray.
Thin the Warm white with water and reload often. Start each whisker at the edge of the white muzzle. Pull outward in one light, steady stroke, lightening as you go so it fades to a point.

Fan three or four whiskers out across the cheek toward the curled body. Then fan a few more out over the white paws toward the blanket. Most of them sit in the bottom half of the sleeping face and the right half of it. Let them fork a little and wobble slightly.
Stop while they are few and fine. They should read as thin bright lines over the gray, with the eyes, nose and stripes untouched.

shade-frame.text: Let the cream frame dry first. Start where the wide post meets the top edge, on the side of the post that faces the blue wall, and pull a lavender gray band straight down to the bottom edge of the canvas.

Then add the smaller pieces: a thin band down the inner post where it meets the window, a thin line along the underside of the crossbar, a band along the front face of the bottom ledge, and a long slanted shadow down the post where the ledge meets it.

The light comes from the window at the upper left, so the faces turned toward the window stay cream white. Keep each band narrow. A common mistake is covering too much of the cream. When you stop, the frame reads as cream bars with lavender shadow edges.

block-in-sill.text: Let the blue wall and the white window frame dry first, because the sill's top edge is painted right against them.

Start with one long slanted rectangle for the sill's top. Begin just below the white window frame, so its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge. Let it tilt gently lower as it runs out to the right edge of the canvas. Pull flat strokes side to side along the length of the sill, like wood grain.
Then lay a narrower strip for the sill's front edge along the bottom edge of the canvas. Let a thin line show where it meets the top.

When you stop, the whole sill is one flat Warm wood brown shape, solid out to the left, right and bottom edges of the canvas. Keep its top edge crisp. A common mistake is letting the brown wobble up into the wall.

shade-sill.text: The flat brown must be fully dry. Dip only the tip of the 3/4 inch flat in Warm wood brown, with no water.

Start at the right edge of the canvas on the sill's top. Skim light strokes side to side along the grain, working left toward the sunny end of the sill. Then skim broken strokes along the front edge strip.
Leave the sill's top near the left edge of the canvas untouched, because the sunlight falls there. Across that sunny end, skim only the narrow slanted bands where the frame's shadow falls.
Stop when it looks streaky and see-through, with the base brown showing. If it goes on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the base brown back over part of it.

light-sill.text: Let the dry-brushed brown dry first. This sunny patch sits at the left end of the sill's top. The whole patch is about 6 1/2 in wide, and its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.

Start with the biggest piece: a long wedge of Sunny peach that widens as it slants toward the front edge, its far end breaking into a few small bits. Then add a slim slanted strip about 3 3/4 in wide nearer the window, and a small piece at the left edge of the canvas.
Pull each piece along the slant of the light. Leave the brown shadow bands of the frame showing between the pieces, and don't paint across them.
When you stop, three crisp peach pieces fan across the sill like sunlight coming through the window.

block-in-blanket.text: Let the sill and the blue wall dry first. The blanket goes on top of both.

Start with one long, low oval for the bed, low across the canvas. Its top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge and its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge. Run it to the right edge of the canvas. Its left end stops about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, just touching the white window frame.
Then add the curved roll along the front, with the folded edge under it. Make the end nearest the window two stacked rounded bumps, with the roll resting on the fold.
Pull the strokes along the length of the blanket. Smooth the joins so it reads as one flat golden shape, with no wall or wood showing through. Give it a second coat if it looks streaky.

shade-blanket.text: Let the Golden yellow dry so the loops stay crisp.

Start just under the top of the raised back rim. Tap rows of small commas there: press, then lift, so each one points down into the hollow of the bed. Follow the curved edge of the hollow around to the end nearest the window. Then scatter loose loops across the hollow itself.
Pull pairs of commas downward there so they lean into little V stitches.
Leave plain gold along the top of the rim and the top of the front roll. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.text: Wait until the Dark ochre loops are dry.

Start at the blanket's rounded end nearest the window. Tap pale commas thickly over that end, because the light comes from the window at the upper left. Press, then lift, with each one curving around the end of the roll.
Then move across the blanket with fewer and smaller loops. Put them on the tops of the roll and the fold, and a few across the hollow and the rim. Most of them sit on the left side of the blanket.
Tap them in between the dark loops, not over them. When you stop, the lit end and the tops should glitter softly, and the far end of the blanket should stay mostly gold and dark.

block-in-cat.text: Let the blanket dry first, because the cat lies right over its top. Start with one big oval for the curled body, its top about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, running all the way to the right edge of the canvas.

Add a circle for the head at the window end of the oval, then two triangle ears: one pointing up, and one pointing out toward the window, its tip reaching onto the window frame. Bring the bottom of the oval down onto the blanket's roll, pulling the strokes around the curl like fur.

Cover everything flat mid gray, about 15 in wide. Stop when it reads as one plain gray cat shape with no shading. A common mistake is leaving yellow slivers where the cat meets the blanket: paint right down into the knit.

shade-cat.text: Let the Mid gray dry first. Begin at the deep fold where the head meets the body, pulling one curved stroke down from behind the upright ear toward the paws.

Then sweep curved strokes around the round rump at the far end of the cat, and along the tail where it curls in under the body toward the paws, following each curve. Add a few broken dark touches on the back and under the chin.

Leave the top of the back, the head and the two paw shapes Mid gray, and leave a patch on the cat's side for the white later. Stop when the cat looks round: dark fold, rump and tail, mid gray on top. Don't flatten it into one dark blob.

paint-white-patches.text: Let the Dark gray dry, or the white will turn gray. Start on the muzzle: a narrow white wedge from between the eyes down to the chin, its left side about 3 1/4 in from the left edge.
Where the muzzle ends, paint the two front paws as round white mounds tucked side by side on the blanket, curving each stroke around the paw. Leave a thin gray line between the paws and for the toes.
Then lay the patch on the cat's side, about 2 3/4 in wide, pulling curved strokes up along the body so its upper edge breaks into pointed fingers of fur.
Use 2 to 3 thin coats, drying between them, instead of one thick coat. Stop when the muzzle, paws and side patch read clean white.

paint-stripes.text: Let the white patches dry first, because the stripes run right up to them. Start at the top of the cat's back, near the spine, where the top of the stripes is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge.

Press the full width of the angle brush at the spine, then pull each stripe down and around the curve of the body toward the blanket, turning onto the edge so it tapers to a point. Let them bend like hoops around a barrel. Cross the tail with short bands, thick at the top of the tail and thin underneath.

On the head, pull short tapered stripes down from the crown toward the closed eyes, add a few small curves on the cheeks, and run a thin dark edge along both ears. Keep off the white muzzle, chest patch and paws, and leave plenty of gray between the stripes.
When you stop, the stripes wrap the whole cat out to about 1 in from the right edge. A common mistake is stripes of even width: every one should start wide and end in a point.

paint-ears.text: Let the charcoal ear edges dry before you start. Begin with the ear nearer the window. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.

Touch the round's tip down near the base of the ear, press so the belly spreads, then pull up toward the ear's point and lift so the stroke ends on the tip. Two or three of these fill the ear's hollow. Then do the same in the ear on top of the head, whose left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge.
Keep the pink off the ear edges, so a thin gray and charcoal rim still shows all around each ear.
When you stop, both ears have rosy hollows framed by their dark rims, and the rest of the cat is untouched. If you get a blob instead of a tapered stroke, use less paint and lift faster.

flick-fur.text: Let the Charcoal stripes and the Soft pink ears dry first, or the light gray will smear them.

Start along the spine of the sleeping tabby cat, near where the back curves away from the head. Load the fan brush lightly. Set its edge in the gray, flick out the way the fur lies, and lift off so each mark thins at its tip. Work down over the back, round the curled tail, and over the head and cheeks.

Most of the paint goes on the right side of the cat's fur, over the big curled body. Let the flicks cross the edges of the Charcoal stripes, but leave their middles dark. Leave the warm white muzzle, chest patch and paws clean, and keep off the pink inside the ears.
When you stop, the whole gray coat looks soft and furry, with darker gray between the flicks. A common mistake is too much paint, which leaves flat light blobs instead of fur.

paint-nose.text: Start on the white muzzle, where the two white cheeks meet. That is where the nose sits, with its middle about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.

Load the tip of the brush full with creamy Soft pink. Touch down where the bridge of the nose ends, then press so the belly spreads into a small triangle. Pull down toward the chin and lift so the stroke ends on a point.
One or two presses are enough. The nose is a tiny triangle about 3/4 in wide. Keep the white muzzle showing all around it, and leave the gray face alone.
A common mistake is a round blob instead of a triangle, from too much paint or too slow a lift. Use less paint and lift faster. Once it is dry, you can tidy the edges with a little white.

line-eyes.text: Let the Soft pink nose and the face dry first. Liner lines spread on wet paint.

Thin the Charcoal with water until it flows like ink. Hold the brush upright with light, steady pressure. Start each closed eye at its inner corner by the white muzzle and pull a gentle curve out toward the ear. Begin a little thick and lighten off so the line tapers.

Add a tiny mouth line at the point of the nose. Next, run a thin dark edge along the outer rim of each ear, from base to tip. Tuck a small dark shadow where the chin meets the body, then add a few short lines on the cheek nearest the curled body.
When you stop, the face should read as a calm, sleeping cat. Leave the pink inside the ears showing. If a line skips, add water and reload.

line-whiskers.text: The Charcoal eye lines must be dry before you start, or the white will smear gray.
Thin the Warm white with water and reload often. Start each whisker at the edge of the white muzzle. Pull outward in one light, steady stroke, lightening as you go so it fades to a point.

Fan three or four whiskers out across the cheek toward the curled body. Then fan a few more out over the white paws toward the blanket. Most of them sit in the bottom half of the sleeping face and the right half of it. Let them fork a little and wobble slightly.
Stop while they are few and fine. They should read as thin bright lines over the gray, with the eyes, nose and stripes untouched.

words: This sky covers the whole canvas, all 12 in wide and 16 in tall, reaching all four edges. Start with Sky blue in a thin strip along the top edge of the canvas, stroking side to side right across, edge to edge.

Without rinsing, pick up Cream gold and Pale gold and lay a long gold band below that blue. Then lay a wide band of Sky blue through the middle of the sky. Below it, lay long, wavy streaks of Pale gold and Cream gold, with a little Sky blue between them, and finish with a thin strip of blue along the bottom edge of the canvas.
While it's wet, stroke back over every join so the bands melt into each other. Dab the brightest Pale gold near the sky's upper right corner, where the sun glows.
When you stop, no white canvas shows. If a hard line forms where two colors meet, add more of the lighter color there and blend again.
Wait until the sky is completely dry. Start at the top edge, in the sky's upper left corner, with Warm peach. The first band of streaks runs along the top edge and is about 2 1/2 in tall.
Dip only the tip of the dry brush and skim it sideways from the left edge toward the right edge, slanting each stroke a little. Lift off as the streak thins.

Work down the sky in loose bands. The lowest band starts about 7 3/4 in from the top edge. Peach goes along the top of each streak. Skim Dusky rose along its underside, where the cloud turns from the light.
Leave the blue and gold sky showing between the bands and through every ragged edge. If a streak goes on solid, your brush is too loaded, so wipe it.
Let the Warm peach and Dusky rose streaks dry first. Start on the upper band of clouds, about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, with Pale gold on just the tip of the dry brush.
Skim short sideways strokes along the top of each Warm peach streak, following its slant. Lift off before the streak's end.
These are small gold patches, not whole clouds. Put most of them on the right side of the sunset clouds, where the sun sets. Work down to the lowest streaks, about 12 3/4 in from the top edge.
Keep the Dusky rose undersides and most of the peach showing below the gold. When you stop, each cloud should look lit from above, and no streak should be fully covered.

Let the sky dry fully first, because these mountains go right over it. The far blue mountains run all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Their top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge and their bottom is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Start with Far violet for the farther range: a soft, gently bumpy line of peaks just under the gold of the horizon. Fill it down with long level strokes, pulling left and right.
Then lay Mountain blue for the nearer ridge, overlapping the foot of the violet peaks. Keep the strokes long and level so it slopes gently and its lower edge stays soft and uneven.
When you stop, you have a pale violet range behind a darker slate-blue band, both flat with no warm light. Don't make the peaks sharp zigzags; keep them low and rounded.
Wait until the far blue mountains are dry, or the peach will smear into the blue.

Only dip the tip of the brush in Warm peach, with no water, and wipe off the extra. Skim it lightly along the very tops of the far violet peaks, just where they meet the gold sky, in a few short touches.
Put most of it on the right side of the far blue mountains, nearest the setting sun, and only a tiny touch near the middle. Leave the rest of each range its flat blue.

When you stop, it should read as a faint glow catching a few ridge tops, not a stripe. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and dry-brush a little Far violet back over part of it.
Let the far blue mountains dry before you start, since the lake sits right against them.

The glimpse of lake is a thin sliver at the right edge of the canvas, tucked against the foot of the dark slate-blue ridge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
Start at the right edge with Cream gold and pull level strokes toward the middle of the canvas, letting the strip thin to a point at its far end. Keep it flat and level, like still water.
Leave the slate blue showing right up to its top edge. When you stop, it should read as one small, bright strip of water, not a wide pool.

Let the sky and the far blue mountains dry first. Load Yellow green on the 1 inch flat and start at the left edge just below the far blue mountains, where the top of the hills is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.

Pull long, level strokes left and right, tilting each one so the slopes fall as they cross the canvas. Lay them as separate bands with the sky colour showing between them. Stop where they meet the glimpse of lake and keep the lake clean.

Below the bands, lay one solid band of Yellow green fading into Hill green across the whole canvas. Lower down, use Hill green and let the strokes break up, so gold and peach sky shows in ragged gaps down to the bottom edge.
When you stop, green covers the ground from the mountains to the bottom edge in bands and patches, lighter at the back. Don't fill every gap: the darker green goes there next.
Let the first greens dry. Start with Deep green on the 3/4 inch flat at the left edge, right below the far blue mountains. Lay a dark ridge there that runs down the canvas toward the glimpse of lake.

Then fill the sky-coloured gaps between the green bands with long left-and-right strokes, tilted with each slope. Keep a strip of the lighter green along the top of each band, so the hills roll in dark and light.

Leave the wide light band across the middle of the meadow alone. Below it, from a top about 9 1/2 in from the top edge down to the bottom edge, cover the gold and peach gaps. Leave a few lighter patches near the top of this dark area.
When you stop, no sky shows in the green, and most of this paint sits in the bottom half of the hills and meadow. A common slip is darkening the middle band too. That band stays light.
Let the dark bands dry. Wipe the #6 round until it is nearly dry, with only a little Deep green left on it. Start at the left edge in the highest hill band, just below the far blue mountains.
Tap with the tip along the dark bands, making a little row of round clumps on each one. Follow each slope as it falls. Keep the clumps smaller near the back and a bit bigger in the lowest rows.
The bushes stay on the hills. The lowest clumps end about 7 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and nothing goes into the meadow. Leave the light green strips between the rows showing.
When you stop, scattered rows of dark bushes cross the hills all the way across the canvas. If you get blobs instead of dots, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.
Let the hills and meadow dry first. Start with one big upright oval for the cow's shaggy body. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and its middle is about 5 in from the left edge.

Add the head as a rounded piece at the top of the body, toward the cow's right side, with the fringe as a curved cap over it. Then build the rest in curved pieces down each side, every stroke pulled downward the way the hair hangs.
Cover the whole shape flat with Rust brown. Let the bottom end in ragged points that fade into the meadow, about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Stop when you have one flat brown blob about 9 in tall. A beginner often tries to add hair or a face here; don't. Flat is right.
Let the Rust brown dry to the touch. Start on the cow's left side, high on the back, and pull long curved strokes of Dark umber down the body the way the hair hangs.

Most of the dark goes on the cow's left side, away from the sun. Brush it more lightly into the rest: under the fringe and chin, in a band where the head meets the body, in streaks where the locks will part, and low on the body.
Leave a strip of plain Rust brown down the sunlit edge of the chest, and a few spots of it on top of the head.
When you stop, the cow should look round and hairy, dark on the left side, rust on the lit edge. Don't fill it solid dark.
Let the coat dry first. Begin each horn with a wide piece of Horn tan where it meets the top of the head.

For the first horn, pull a curved piece up and out from the head's upper left, tapering to a sharp point that rises high, its top about 2 3/4 in from the top edge. For the second horn, start at the head's far side and curve a shorter piece up to a point, its right side about 2 1/4 in from the right edge.
Tuck each base into the coat so the fringe can fall over it later. Keep the coat around them as it is.
Stop when you have two flat pale tan horns, wide at the head and pointed at the tips. A common mistake is painting them the same width all along.
Let the Horn tan dry first. Start at the tip of each horn and paint the last part solid Dark umber.

Then pull curved strokes from the tip down along the underside of each horn toward the head, bending with the horn. Let the dark thin out as it goes so it blends into the tan, and add a little more near the base where it meets the coat.
Keep the pale tan showing along the top, outer edge of each horn, the side that catches the sun.
When you stop, each horn reads as round: dark tip, dark underside, pale top. Don't cover the whole horn brown.
Let the Dark umber shadows dry to the touch first. Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns, where the coat's top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge.

Press the full width of the brush at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge and ease off as you pull down, so the lock tapers to a point. On the fringe, pull down over the eyes. On the body, follow its round curve and sweep down toward the ragged bottom of the coat.
Work over the whole cow: head, fringe and body. Leave thin dark brown gaps between the locks so the shadows show through.
When you stop, the whole cow reads as long hanging locks with dark brown between them. A common mistake is ending strokes with a blunt stop. Lift as you pull so every lock ends in a point.
Let the ginger locks dry first, or the Honey gold will smear into them.

Start high on the cow's back near the top of the coat. The first lock's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 6 in from the top edge. Press, then ease onto the edge as you pull down along the hair.
Add only a few more small locks: two or three further down the shoulder, a short one lower on the back, and one on the head, about 8 in from the left edge.
Stop while they are small and scattered, with most of the coat still ginger and dark brown. Don't spread gold everywhere: a few touches are what catch the light.
Let the green meadow base and the cow's coat dry to the touch first. Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, near the left edge, where the biggest dark tufts go.
Load the fan lightly. Set its tip down and flick quickly upward, lifting off as you go so each blade thins and breaks at the top. Give every tuft the same slight lean.

Scatter tufts across the whole meadow, bigger and closer together toward the bottom, smaller and fewer as you rise. The highest sit about 10 in from the top edge. Tuck a few in around the cow's ragged lower edge.
Leave plenty of the green base showing between them. When you stop, the meadow is dotted with dark tufts, not covered. Too much paint gives flat blobs, so wipe the fan often.
Wait until the Deep green tufts are dry, or the Yellow green will turn muddy over them. Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work across from side to side.
With a light load, flick each blade upward from its base and lift off, keeping the same lean as the dark grass. Set the blades between and partly over the Deep green tufts.

Keep them thick in the lower meadow and let them thin out as you go up. The highest are about 6 1/2 in from the bottom edge. Run a few up against the cow's lower edge so the grass stands in front of it.
Let the dark tufts show through everywhere. When you stop, the lower meadow reads as a mix of dark and yellow-green blades. Don't paint the dark grass out.
Let the Yellow green blades dry first. Start at the left edge of the canvas, left of the Highland cow, with a small cluster of gold blades. Its top is about 8 1/2 in from the top edge.
Load the fan lightly and flick upward with the same lean, lifting off so each tip breaks. Put a long patch of blades right of the Highland cow, and scatter more across the bottom of the meadow.
Most of the gold goes on the right side, where the low sun catches the grass. Keep the gold off the cow's coat.
Leave the dark and yellow-green blades showing between the gold ones. When you stop, the meadow is full, with gold as the sunlit tips, not a solid layer.
Let the Honey gold locks and the grass over the cow dry first, or the gold will smear into them.

Start on the top of the fringe and the top of the head, where the low sun catches the hair from behind. The top of this gold is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge. Press the full brush down at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge as you pull down, so it tapers the way the hair hangs.
Work down the sun side of the head, chest and body over the ginger locks, most of it in the right half of the sunlit rim. Add a few strokes along the curve of the back.
Leave dark brown between strokes, and leave the shadow side and the horns alone. Don't cover whole locks: catch their tops and edges.
When you stop, the head, fringe and sun side glow gold. Its bottom is about 3 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
The Horn tan and the dark tips must be dry first, and so must the Pale gold rim at the horn bases.
Start on the taller horn where it leaves the head. Lay the brush along its upper edge and pull a curved stroke up toward the tip, bending with the horn. Its top is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
Do the same on the shorter horn, from its base up along its top edge. Its left side is about 8 in from the left edge.
Keep the cream on the top edge of each horn, where the sun hits. Leave the dark tips and the dark undersides showing. Painting cream over the whole horn would make it look flat.
When you stop, each horn has a pale cream line along its top over the tan, with dark at its tip and underneath.

Let the sunlit rim dry first. You work on the cow's face, where the muzzle pokes out of the fringe. This step's marks sit in an area whose bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge and whose right side is about 4 in from the right edge.

Press a small rounded dab on the cheek, at the shadowed end of the muzzle. Then pull curved strokes along the muzzle's lower edge, from the tip of the nose back toward the throat, bending them with the round. Trace the round tip of the nose with one more thin curve.
Most of this paint goes on the left side of the face, away from the sun. Leave the fringe's locks and the middle of the muzzle in their coat colours.
When you stop, the muzzle reads as a rounded snout outlined in Rosy nose, with no shine, nostrils or mouth. A common mistake is filling the muzzle flat. Keep the paint to its edges.
Let the Rosy nose paint dry first. Start at the top of the nose, at the edge nearest the fringe. This band's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
Pull one curved stroke across the top of the nose, bending over its round like a cap. Let both ends curl down a little where the nostrils will go. Only the top of the nose catches the light.
Leave the Rosy nose showing on the rest of the nose. When you stop, the nose has a thin, pale pink top. A common mistake is painting the whole nose pink, so keep it to a narrow band.
Make sure the Nose pink and Rosy nose are dry, or your lines will spread and feather. Thin the Dark umber with water so it flows, and reload often.

Start with the nostrils. Hold the brush upright and make a short dark curve at each end of the Nose pink top. Then pull a short mouth line across where the muzzle meets the chin, with a little wobble in it.

Next, lay lines side by side and overlapping in the shadow where the chin meets the chest, pulling them down toward the cow's body. Most of this step's paint is on the left side of the face, and its bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge.
Leave the pale pink top and the gold rim showing. When you stop, the cow has nostrils, a mouth and a dark chin, and the painting is finished.

This sky covers the whole canvas, all 12 in wide and 16 in tall, reaching all four edges. Start with Sky blue in a thin strip along the top edge of the canvas, stroking side to side right across, edge to edge.

Without rinsing, pick up Cream gold and Pale gold and lay a long gold band just under the first blue strip. Then lay a wide band of Sky blue through the middle of the sky. Under that middle band, lay long, wavy streaks of Pale gold and Cream gold, with a little Sky blue between them, and finish with a thin strip of blue along the bottom edge of the canvas.
While it's wet, stroke back over every join so the bands melt into each other. Dab the brightest Pale gold near the sky's upper right corner, where the sun glows.
When you stop, no white canvas shows. If a hard line forms where two colors meet, add more of the lighter color there and blend again.
Wait until the sky is completely dry. Start at the top edge, in the sky's upper left corner, with Warm peach. The first band of streaks runs along the top edge and is about 2 1/2 in tall.
Dip only the tip of the dry brush and skim it sideways from the left edge toward the right edge, slanting each stroke a little. Lift off as the streak thins.

Work down the sky in loose bands. The lowest band starts about 7 3/4 in from the top edge. Peach goes along the top of each streak. Skim Dusky rose along its underside, where the cloud turns from the light.
Leave the blue and gold sky showing between the bands and through every ragged edge. If a streak goes on solid, your brush is too loaded, so wipe it.
Let the Warm peach and Dusky rose streaks dry first. Start on the upper band of clouds, about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, with Pale gold on just the tip of the dry brush.
Skim short sideways strokes along the top of each Warm peach streak, following its slant. Lift off before the streak's end.
These are small gold patches, not whole clouds. Put most of them on the right side of the sunset clouds, where the sun sets. Work down to the lowest streaks, about 12 3/4 in from the top edge.

Keep the Dusky rose undersides and most of the Warm peach still showing, with the Pale gold only on the edges that face up. When you stop, each cloud should look lit from above, and no streak should be fully covered.

Let the sky dry fully first, because these mountains go right over it. The far blue mountains run all the way across, from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas. Their top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge and their bottom is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Start with Far violet for the farther range: a soft, gently bumpy line of peaks just under the gold of the horizon. Fill it down with long level strokes, pulling left and right.
Then lay Mountain blue for the nearer ridge, overlapping the foot of the violet peaks. Keep the strokes long and level so it slopes gently and its lower edge stays soft and uneven.
When you stop, you have a pale violet range behind a darker slate-blue band, both flat with no warm light. Don't make the peaks sharp zigzags; keep them low and rounded.
Wait until the far blue mountains are dry, or the peach will smear into the blue.

Only dip the tip of the brush in Warm peach, with no water, and wipe off the extra. Skim it lightly along the very tops of the far violet peaks, just where they meet the gold sky, in a few short touches.
Put most of it on the right side of the far blue mountains, nearest the setting sun, and only a tiny touch near the middle. Leave the rest of each range its flat blue.

When you stop, it should read as a faint glow catching a few ridge tops, not a stripe. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and dry-brush a little Far violet back over part of it.
Let the far blue mountains dry before you start, since the lake sits right against them.

The glimpse of lake is a thin sliver at the right edge of the canvas, tucked against the foot of the dark slate-blue ridge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
Start at the right edge with Cream gold and pull level strokes toward the middle of the canvas, letting the strip thin to a point at its far end. Keep it flat and level, like still water.
Leave the slate blue showing right up to its top edge. When you stop, it should read as one small, bright strip of water, not a wide pool.

Let the sky and the far blue mountains dry first. Load Yellow green on the 1 inch flat and start at the left edge just below the far blue mountains, where the top of the hills is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.

Pull long, level strokes left and right, tilting each one so the slopes fall as they cross the canvas. Lay them as separate bands with the sky colour showing between them. Stop where they meet the glimpse of lake and keep the lake clean.

Where the hill bands end, lay one solid band of Yellow green fading into Hill green across the whole canvas. Lower down, use Hill green and let the strokes break up, so gold and peach sky shows in ragged gaps down to the bottom edge.
When you stop, green covers the ground from the mountains to the bottom edge in bands and patches, lighter at the back. Don't fill every gap: the darker green goes there next.
Let the first greens dry. Start with Deep green on the 3/4 inch flat at the left edge, right below the far blue mountains. Lay a dark ridge there that runs down the canvas toward the glimpse of lake.

Then fill the sky-coloured gaps between the green bands with long left-and-right strokes, tilted with each slope. Keep a strip of the lighter green along the top of each band, so the hills roll in dark and light.

Leave the wide light band across the middle of the meadow alone. Where that light band ends, from a top about 9 1/2 in from the top edge down to the bottom edge, cover the gold and peach gaps. Leave a few lighter patches near the top of this dark area.
When you stop, no sky shows in the green, and most of this paint sits in the bottom half of the hills and meadow. A common slip is darkening the middle band too. That band stays light.
Let the dark bands dry. Wipe the #6 round until it is nearly dry, with only a little Deep green left on it. Start at the left edge in the highest hill band, just below the far blue mountains.
Tap with the tip along the dark bands, making a little row of round clumps on each one. Follow each slope as it falls. Keep the clumps smaller near the back and a bit bigger in the lowest rows.
The bushes stay on the hills. The lowest clumps end about 7 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and nothing goes into the meadow. Leave the light green strips between the rows showing.
When you stop, scattered rows of dark bushes cross the hills all the way across the canvas. If you get blobs instead of dots, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.
Let the hills and meadow dry first. Start with one big upright oval for the cow's shaggy body. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and its middle is about 5 in from the left edge.

Add the head as a rounded piece at the top of the body, toward the cow's right side, with the fringe as a curved cap over it. Then build the rest in curved pieces down each side, every stroke pulled downward the way the hair hangs.
Cover the whole shape flat with Rust brown. Let the bottom end in ragged points that fade into the meadow, about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Stop when you have one flat brown blob about 9 in tall. A beginner often tries to add hair or a face here; don't. Flat is right.
Let the Rust brown dry to the touch. Start on the cow's left side, high on the back, and pull long curved strokes of Dark umber down the body the way the hair hangs.

Most of the dark goes on the cow's left side, away from the sun. Brush it more lightly into the rest: under the fringe and chin, in a band where the head meets the body, in streaks where the locks will part, and low on the body.
Leave a strip of plain Rust brown down the sunlit edge of the chest, and a few spots of it on top of the head.
When you stop, the cow should look round and hairy, dark on the left side, rust on the lit edge. Don't fill it solid dark.
Let the coat dry first. Begin each horn with a wide piece of Horn tan where it meets the top of the head.

For the first horn, pull a curved piece up and out from the head's upper left, tapering to a sharp point that rises high, its top about 2 3/4 in from the top edge. For the second horn, start at the head's far side and curve a shorter piece up to a point, its right side about 2 1/4 in from the right edge.
Tuck each base into the coat so the fringe can fall over it later. Keep the coat around them as it is.
Stop when you have two flat pale tan horns, wide at the head and pointed at the tips. A common mistake is painting them the same width all along.
Let the Horn tan dry first. Start at the tip of each horn and paint the last part solid Dark umber.

Then pull curved strokes from the tip down along the underside of each horn toward the head, bending with the horn. Let the dark thin out as it goes so it blends into the tan, and add a little more near the base where it meets the coat.
Keep the pale tan showing along the top, outer edge of each horn, the side that catches the sun.
When you stop, each horn reads as round: dark tip, dark underside, pale top. Don't cover the whole horn brown.
Let the Dark umber shadows dry to the touch first. Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns, where the coat's top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge.

Press the full width of the brush at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge and ease off as you pull down, so the lock tapers to a point. On the fringe, pull down over the eyes. On the body, follow its round curve and sweep down toward the ragged bottom of the coat.
Work over the whole cow: head, fringe and body. Leave thin dark brown gaps between the locks so the shadows show through.
When you stop, the whole cow reads as long hanging locks with dark brown between them. A common mistake is ending strokes with a blunt stop. Lift as you pull so every lock ends in a point.
Let the ginger locks dry first, or the Honey gold will smear into them.

Start high on the cow's back near the top of the coat. The first lock's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, and its top is about 6 in from the top edge. Press, then ease onto the edge as you pull down along the hair.
Add only a few more small locks: two or three further down the shoulder, a short one lower on the back, and one on the head, about 8 in from the left edge.
Stop while they are small and scattered, with most of the coat still ginger and dark brown. Don't spread gold everywhere: a few touches are what catch the light.
Let the green meadow base and the cow's coat dry to the touch first. Start at the bottom edge of the canvas, near the left edge, where the biggest dark tufts go.
Load the fan lightly. Set its tip down and flick quickly upward, lifting off as you go so each blade thins and breaks at the top. Give every tuft the same slight lean.

Leave plenty of the green base showing between them. When you stop, the meadow is dotted with dark tufts, not covered. Too much paint gives flat blobs, so wipe the fan often.
Wait until the Deep green tufts are dry, or the Yellow green will turn muddy over them. Start at the bottom edge of the canvas and work across from side to side.
With a light load, flick each blade upward from its base and lift off, keeping the same lean as the dark grass. Set the blades between and partly over the Deep green tufts.
Keep them thick in the lower meadow and let them thin out as you go up. The highest are about 9 1/2 in from the top edge. Run a few up against the cow's lower edge so the grass stands in front of it.
Let the dark tufts show through everywhere. When you stop, the lower meadow reads as a mix of dark and yellow-green blades. Don't paint the dark grass out.
Let the Yellow green blades dry first. Start at the left edge of the canvas, left of the Highland cow, with a small cluster of gold blades. Its top is about 8 1/2 in from the top edge.
Load the fan lightly and flick upward with the same lean, lifting off so each tip breaks. Put a long patch of blades right of the Highland cow, and scatter more across the bottom of the meadow.
Most of the gold goes on the right side, where the low sun catches the grass. Keep the gold off the cow's coat.
Leave the dark and yellow-green blades showing between the gold ones. When you stop, the meadow is full, with gold as the sunlit tips, not a solid layer.
Let the Honey gold locks and the grass over the cow dry first, or the gold will smear into them.

Start on the top of the fringe and the top of the head, where the low sun catches the hair from behind. The top of this gold is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge. Press the full brush down at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge as you pull down, so it tapers the way the hair hangs.
Work down the sun side of the head, chest and body over the ginger locks, most of it in the right half of the sunlit rim. Add a few strokes along the curve of the back.
Leave dark brown between strokes, and leave the shadow side and the horns alone. Don't cover whole locks: catch their tops and edges.
When you stop, the head, fringe and sun side glow gold. Its bottom is about 3 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
The Horn tan and the dark tips must be dry first, and so must the Pale gold rim at the horn bases.
Start on the taller horn where it leaves the head. Lay the brush along its upper edge and pull a curved stroke up toward the tip, bending with the horn. Its top is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
Do the same on the shorter horn, from its base up along its top edge. Its left side is about 8 in from the left edge.
Keep the cream on the top edge of each horn, where the sun hits. Leave the dark tips and the dark undersides showing. Painting cream over the whole horn would make it look flat.
When you stop, each horn has a pale cream line along its top over the tan, with dark at its tip and underneath.

Let the sunlit rim dry first. You work on the cow's face, where the muzzle pokes out of the fringe. This step's marks sit in an area whose bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge and whose right side is about 4 in from the right edge.

Most of this paint goes on the left side of the face, away from the sun. Leave the fringe's locks and the middle of the muzzle in their coat colours.
When you stop, the muzzle reads as a rounded snout outlined in Rosy nose, with no shine, nostrils or mouth. A common mistake is filling the muzzle flat. Keep the paint to its edges.
Let the Rosy nose paint dry first. Start at the top of the nose, at the edge nearest the fringe. This band's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
Pull one curved stroke across the top of the nose, bending over its round like a cap. Let both ends curl down a little where the nostrils will go. Only the top of the nose catches the light.
Leave the Rosy nose showing on the rest of the nose. When you stop, the nose has a thin, pale pink top. A common mistake is painting the whole nose pink, so keep it to a narrow band.
Make sure the Nose pink and Rosy nose are dry, or your lines will spread and feather. Thin the Dark umber with water so it flows, and reload often.

Start with the nostrils. Hold the brush upright and make a short dark curve at each end of the Nose pink top. Then pull a short mouth line across where the muzzle meets the chin, with a little wobble in it.

Next, lay lines side by side and overlapping in the shadow where the chin meets the chest, pulling them down toward the cow's body. Most of this step's paint is on the left side of the face, and its bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge.
Leave the pale pink top and the gold rim showing. When you stop, the cow has nostrils, a mouth and a dark chin, and the painting is finished.

Under that middle band, lay long, wavy streaks of Pale gold and Cream gold, with a little Sky blue between them, and finish with a thin strip of blue along the bottom edge of the canvas.
While it's wet, stroke back over every join so the bands melt into each other. Dab the brightest Pale gold near the sky's upper right corner, where the sun glows.
When you stop, no white canvas shows. If a hard line forms where two colors meet, add more of the lighter color there and blend again.

words: This first coat covers the whole canvas and reaches all four edges. It is the misty sky, and every tree and the ground will be painted over it later, so paint straight across where they will go.

Start with the darkest paint, Blue-violet mist, stroking side to side across the bottom of the sky and up its right side. Without rinsing, pick up Misty blue and work it across the middle, then Pale gold into the sky's upper left corner.
Stroke back over each join while it is wet, so the gold melts into blue and the blue into violet. If you see a hard line, add a little more of the lighter paint there and blend again.
When you stop, there is no white canvas left: a soft glowing haze, warmest in the sky's upper left corner and coolest on its right side.
Let the misty sky dry to the touch first, so the Sun cream stays clean and bright instead of turning muddy.
The sun sits right at the left edge of the canvas, inside the gold glow. Its top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
With the tip of the brush, start at the sun's brightest middle and make small circles, moving outward toward its edge. Keep the edge bumpy and soft.
Then smooth it over with the same circling motion. If the edge looks hard and cut out, soften it with lighter passes, or smudge it with a finger.
When you stop, the sun is a small glowing disk at the edge, and the rest of the sky is untouched haze.
Let the misty sky dry to the touch first, or this trunk will melt into it. This step is one soft far trunk near the middle of the canvas: its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge.
Start at the trunk's foot. Press the full width of the brush to make a soft, wide foot. Then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull straight up, so the trunk thins to a hair-fine top in the haze.
On the side of the trunk that faces the sun, lay a few short thick-to-thin strokes into one soft hazy patch partway up. Keep its edges blurry.
Leave all the haze around it showing. When you stop, you have one faint, plain trunk with no light side.
A common mistake is a hard dark line. Wipe the brush often so it stays pale.
Let the Blue-violet mist trunk dry first. The firs fill the right side of the canvas: their tops start about 3/4 in from the top edge, and the group reaches the right edge.

Begin with Misty blue for the hazy firs at the back: the small one at the end nearest the far trunk, and a soft mass rising behind the others. Tap from each tip down in a zigzag, pressing harder as the tree widens.
Then use Deep pine green for three or four dark firs in front, the tallest nearly up to the group's top. Each one is a narrow tip widening downward.
Let the bottoms fade ragged into the mist, and let the earlier trunk lines show through gaps. Stop when the firs are flat dark shapes with no lighter side.
Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick. Thin it, spread the fan, and stamp with the middle tips.
The firs must be dry, or this green will mix into mud. The sun is at the upper left of the canvas, so most of this light goes on the left side of the fir trees and in their bottom half.
Start at the foot of the small hazy fir and the bottom of the first dark fir. That patch's left side is about 8 in from the left edge. Tap with the middle tips in short strokes going different ways.
Next, tap a narrow upright strip down the sunny edge of the pale fir that stands among the big dark ones. Add a small patch at the foot of the tallest fir, and a few single taps.
Leave the tops and shaded sides dark. When you stop, the light shows only in a few scattered patches.
Wait until the far trunk and the firs are dry. These trunks stand in the left half of the canvas, left of the fir trees.

Start with Smoky brown on the tallest trunk. Its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge and its top about 3/4 in from the top edge. Press the full width at its foot and pull straight up, lightening so it narrows. Pull one Blue-violet mist stroke down it so it grays into the haze.

Then pull three Blue-violet mist trunks, each shorter, stepping toward the firs. Start each at its wide, soft top with the full brush width, then pull down and lighten to a thin stem. Add one very short one last.
Leave the sky and far trunk showing around them. Keep them plain, with no bark marks.
Pressing evenly the whole way makes a stiff post instead of a taper.
Let the misty sky and the fir trees dry first, because the ground goes right up against them.

Start at the back of the forest floor, where it meets the mist; its top is about 7 in from the top edge. Lay Golden ochre there in long, level strokes, left and right, running from the left edge all the way to the right edge. Tuck the strokes in around the feet of the far trunks and the firs.

Work down toward the bottom edge in bands. Bring in more Leaf brown as you come forward, so the front is darker and rougher. Let some brown streaks run across the gold bands; they read as long shadows lying on the ground.
Stop when the whole lower part of the canvas is covered, light at the back and dark at the bottom edge. Don't tilt the strokes; the ground must lie flat.
Let the forest floor dry before you start, because the path goes on top of it.

Mark one dot where the path disappears into the mist, low under the firs. Its middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. Draw three to five faint chalk lines fanning out from that dot down to the bottom edge.

Pull Path mauve along those lines, from the bottom edge back toward the dot: wide in front, and thinner and thinner as you reach the dot. Keep the edges ragged where the path meets the floor; leaves will cover them later.
Leave a patch of the gold floor showing in the front of the path, and some floor peeking between the strokes.
If the strokes run side by side instead of closing toward the dot, the path will stand up. Check them with your brush handle held from the dot.
Let the forest floor and the path dry first, or the dabs will smear into them. Wipe most of the paint off the old stiff brush and tap with its tip; don't brush.

Start at the bottom edge with Leaf brown and Burnt orange, tapping big dabs across the ground and over the path. Work up toward the mist and make the dabs smaller as you go. Leave the far end of the path showing.
Tap Burnt orange into the bushes on both sides of the path. Tap Moss green into the bush right of the path, around the feet of the firs.
Add a few broken Burnt orange patches in the treetops. One sits at the top edge, its left side about 10 3/4 in from the left edge. Stop while the ground reads as a dark, dappled carpet.
Wait until the dark dabs are dry so the yellow stays clean.

Start at the top edge in the treetops with Golden yellow, tapping loose clusters that hang down into the mist. Most of it goes on the left side, near the sun. The thickest mass is a tall cluster against the left edge, its top about 2 in from the top edge, and it grows into the bush left of the path. Tap there until that bush glows almost solid.
Then scatter single dabs over the ground and on the bushes right of the path. Leave plenty of orange and brown showing between them.
A common mistake is a loaded brush that makes blobs. Wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.
Let the golden yellow dry first.
Start in the treetops at the upper left, near the sun, with a nearly dry brush of Pale gold. Tap light dabs onto the tips of the golden clusters, the side that faces the sun.

Work down the arc of hanging leaves that ends over the bush left of the path. The lowest taps start about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, right at the left edge. Put only a few taps in the treetops on the right side of the canvas.
Leave the golden yellow showing underneath, and keep the ground bare of Pale gold. Stop while the upper left looks lit from behind and the rest stays warm gold.

Let the leaf dabs dry first, because the rock goes straight over them. The mossy rock sits on the leaves just right of the path: its left side is about 10 3/4 in from the left edge, and its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

Start with one wide, low oval of Moss green, flat on the bottom like a stone resting on the ground. Then add a smaller rounded piece at each end, curving like ( ), so the whole boulder is about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Fill it in solid, with no canvas or leaves showing through. Soften the joins between the pieces so it reads as one boulder.
When you stop, it is one flat olive-green shape with no light or shadow. Beginners often make it too round and tall, like a ball. Keep it a low, wide hump.
Wait until the Moss green rock is dry. Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Deep pine green, wipe it, and test it on a scrap.

Start along the flat bottom of the rock, where it sits in the leaves, and skim light strokes along it. Then work up the right end and across the middle, following the round of the rock. Keep the shading from about 11 1/4 in from the left edge onward.
The light comes from the upper left, so the left end and the top-left curve stay Moss green, with scraps of green peeking through the dark everywhere else.
When you stop, most of the rock reads as a cool, dark, mottled stone. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded. Let it dry, then dry-brush Moss green back over part of it.
Let the Deep pine green shading dry first. Load only the tip of the dry brush with Moss light.

Start at the low left end of the rock and skim a curving stroke up and along its top edge, as if the sun from the upper left is catching the rim. Add a couple of tiny touches a little further along the top.
This is only a thin, broken band of light along the top-left rim. Leave all the dark underneath and across the rest of the rock showing, so the stone keeps its shadow.
When you stop, the rock has a pale sage glint along its top-left curve and is dark everywhere else. Don't drag the light down into the shadow. Too much of it flattens the rock.
Let the leaves, bushes and rock dry first, because these trunks go straight over them. Start at the foot of each trunk, down in the fallen leaves, and give it a wide, flared base.

Press the full width of the brush and pull up to the top edge of the canvas, easing the pressure a little as you rise. Paint five trunks: a slim one along the left edge of the canvas, two big ones that lean as they climb, and two near the right edge. The first of those two has its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
Cover each trunk solidly so no leaves show through. Keep the edges clean, and leave the leaves, firs and haze around the trunks as they are.

When you stop, five plain, pale gray-white trunks stand from the leaves to the top edge, with no shading or marks. Most of the new paint is on the left side. Don't make them thin like the far trunks: these are wide, close-up trees.
Wait until the Birch gray trunks are dry. Start at the top edge of the canvas on the big trunk whose middle is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge.
Dip only the tip of the brush in Birch shadow and skim it lightly down the trunk in long strokes. Lay it heaviest on the side away from the sun, then shade the other four trunks the same way.

Let the shadow break up as it goes. Leave ragged patches of Birch gray showing, mostly on the sunny side and toward the trunk feet, which stay mostly pale. Touch a little Moss green where each foot meets the leaves.

When you stop, the trunks read lavender gray with pale patches, and most of the paint is on the left side. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry, then dry-brush Birch gray back over part of it.
Let the shading dry first. Start on the big trunk whose middle is about 2 in from the left edge, low down near its foot.

Load Bark dark and press the full width of the brush at one edge of the trunk. Pull across the trunk, turning onto the brush's edge as you go so each patch tapers. Lay the patches in broken rows up the trunk, with gaps between them, then do the same on every trunk.

Make the patches heavier toward the base, so the lower parts of the two big trunks go mostly dark. On the trunk whose middle is about 14 1/4 in from the left edge, the dark foot's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. Higher up, keep the patches small and far apart.
Leave plenty of lavender and pale gray between the patches. When you stop, most of the dark sits in the bottom half. Don't space the patches evenly like ladder rungs.
The bark patches must be fully dry first, because lines laid over wet paint spread and feather.

Thin Bark dark with water and hold the liner upright. Start at the top of the big trunk whose middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge. Pull short, wobbly lines down the shaded side of the trunk, the side away from the sun, through and between the patches. Start each line thick and lighten as you go.
Let the lines fork and overlap in a narrow band, then do the same on the other trunks. Most of the lines go in the top half, and the trunk feet get none.
Leave the sunny side pale. When you stop, each trunk has a streaky, barky shadow side. If a line skips, add water, and reload often.
Let the thin bark lines dry first, or the white will smear them into gray.

Start at the top edge on the big leaning trunk nearest the left edge. With only the tip of the brush in the Birch white and no water, skim lightly down the trunk. Then do the second big leaning trunk, then the two slim trunks near the right edge.

Keep the light on the edge of each trunk that faces the sun, and let it break over the dark bark patches in places. Most of the light goes on the two big trunks in the left half. Stop high: the lowest light is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, so the trunk feet stay dark and moss green.
When you stop, the upper trunks should look sunlit and rough, with lavender gray still showing. If a stroke goes on solid, your brush was too loaded.
Wait until the Birch white on the trunks is dry, because you will tap right up to the trunk feet.

Start where the path meets the leaves near the rock. Wipe most of the Pale gold off the #12 round, then tap with its tip along both edges of the path and around the rock's base. Work outward to the trunk feet, and on toward the left and right edges.

Keep the taps in a band across the middle of the ground. Its top is about 8 in from the top edge, and its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge. Most of the taps go in the right half, where the path and the rock are.
Leave plenty of the orange and brown leaves showing between the taps. When you stop, the ground should glint, not shine. If you get blobs, wipe the brush and tap again.
