A common mistake is a hard dark line. Wipe the brush often so it stays pale.

stamp-pines.text: Let the Blue-violet mist trunk dry first. The firs fill the right side of the canvas: their tops start about 3/4 in from the top edge, and the group reaches the right edge.

Begin with Misty blue for the hazy firs at the back: the small one at the end nearest the far trunk, and a soft mass rising behind the others. Tap from each tip down in a zigzag, pressing harder as the tree widens.
Then use Deep pine green for three or four dark firs in front, the tallest nearly up to the group's top. Each one is a narrow tip widening downward.
Let the bottoms fade ragged into the mist, and let the earlier trunk lines show through gaps. Stop when the firs are flat dark shapes with no lighter side.
Heavy, clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick. Thin it, spread the fan, and stamp with the middle tips.

light-pines.text: The firs must be dry, or this green will mix into mud. The sun is at the upper left of the canvas, so most of this light goes on the left side of the fir trees and in their bottom half.
Start at the foot of the small hazy fir and the bottom of the first dark fir. That patch's left side is about 8 in from the left edge. Tap with the middle tips in short strokes going different ways.
Next, tap a narrow upright strip down the sunny edge of the pale fir that stands among the big dark ones. Add a small patch at the foot of the tallest fir, and a few single taps.
Leave the tops and shaded sides dark. When you stop, the light shows only in a few scattered patches.

pull-middle-trunks.text: Wait until the far trunk and the firs are dry. These trunks stand in the left half of the canvas, left of the fir trees.

Start with Smoky brown on the tallest trunk. Its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge and its top about 3/4 in from the top edge. Press the full width at its foot and pull straight up, lightening so it narrows. Pull one Blue-violet mist stroke down it so it grays into the haze.

Then pull three Blue-violet mist trunks, each shorter, stepping toward the firs. Start each at its wide, soft top with the full brush width, then pull down and lighten to a thin stem. Add one very short one last.
Leave the sky and far trunk showing around them. Keep them plain, with no bark marks.
Pressing evenly the whole way makes a stiff post instead of a taper.

lay-floor.text: Let the misty sky and the fir trees dry first, because the ground goes right up against them.

Start at the back of the forest floor, where it meets the mist; its top is about 7 in from the top edge. Lay Golden ochre there in long, level strokes, left and right, running from the left edge all the way to the right edge. Tuck the strokes in around the feet of the far trunks and the firs.

Work down toward the bottom edge in bands. Bring in more Leaf brown as you come forward, so the front is darker and rougher. Let some brown streaks run across the gold bands; they read as long shadows lying on the ground.
Stop when the whole forest floor is covered, light at the back near the mist and dark in front. Don't tilt the strokes; the ground must lie flat.

pull-path.text: Let the forest floor dry before you start, because the path goes on top of it.

Mark one dot where the path disappears into the mist, low under the firs. Its middle is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. Draw three to five faint chalk lines fanning out from that dot toward the front of the canvas.

Pull Path mauve along those lines, from the bottom edge back toward the dot: wide in front, and thinner and thinner as you reach the dot. Keep the edges ragged where the path meets the floor; leaves will cover them later.
Leave a patch of the gold floor showing in the front of the path, and some floor peeking between the strokes.
If the strokes run side by side instead of closing toward the dot, the path will stand up. Check them with your brush handle held from the dot.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the forest floor and the path dry first, or the dabs will smear into them. Wipe most of the paint off the old stiff brush and tap with its tip; don't brush.

Start at the bottom edge with Leaf brown and Burnt orange, tapping big dabs across the ground and over the path. Work up toward the mist and make the dabs smaller as you go. Leave the far end of the path showing.
Tap Burnt orange into the bushes along both sides of the path. Tap Moss green into the low bush around the feet of the dark firs.
Add a few broken Burnt orange patches in the treetops. One sits at the top edge, its left side about 10 3/4 in from the left edge. Stop while the ground reads as a dark, dappled carpet.

dab-mid-leaves.text: Wait until the dark dabs are dry so the yellow stays clean.

Start at the top edge in the treetops with Golden yellow, tapping loose clusters that hang down into the mist. Most of it goes on the left side, near the sun. The thickest mass is a tall cluster against the left edge, its top about 2 in from the top edge, and it grows into the big near bush. Tap there until that bush glows almost solid.
Then scatter single dabs over the ground and on the orange bushes at the feet of the dark firs. Leave plenty of orange and brown showing between them.
A common mistake is a loaded brush that makes blobs. Wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.

dab-sunlit-canopy.text: Let the golden yellow dry first.
Start in the treetops at the upper left, near the sun, with a nearly dry brush of Pale gold. Tap light dabs onto the tips of the golden clusters, the side that faces the sun.

Work down the arc of hanging leaves that ends over the big golden bush. The lowest taps start about 3 1/4 in from the top edge, right at the left edge. Put only a few taps in the treetops toward the dark firs.
Leave the golden yellow showing underneath, and keep the ground bare of Pale gold. Stop while the upper left looks lit from behind and the rest stays warm gold.

block-in-rock.text: Let the leaf dabs dry first, because the rock goes straight over them. The mossy rock sits on the leaves just right of the path: its left side is about 10 3/4 in from the left edge, and its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

Start with one wide, low oval of Moss green, flat on the bottom like a stone resting on the ground. Then add a smaller rounded piece at each end, curving like ( ), so the whole boulder is about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Fill it in solid, with no canvas or leaves showing through. Soften the joins between the pieces so it reads as one boulder.
When you stop, it is one flat olive-green shape with no light or shadow. Beginners often make it too round and tall, like a ball. Keep it a low, wide hump.

shade-rock.text: Wait until the Moss green rock is dry. Dip only the tip of the dry brush in Deep pine green, wipe it, and test it on a scrap.

Start along the flat bottom of the rock, where it sits in the leaves, and skim light strokes along it. Then work up the far end and across the middle, following the round of the rock. Leave the end nearest the path untouched.
Scraps of green should peek through the dark everywhere else.
When you stop, most of the rock reads as a cool, dark, mottled stone. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded. Let it dry, then dry-brush Moss green back over part of it.

light-rock.text: Let the Deep pine green shading dry first. Load only the tip of the dry brush with Moss light.
Start at the end of the rock nearest the path and skim a curving stroke up and over its rounded rim, as if the low sun is catching it. Add a couple of tiny touches a little further along the top.
This is only a thin, broken band of light along the top-left rim. Leave all the dark underneath and across the rest of the rock showing, so the stone keeps its shadow.
When you stop, the rock has a pale sage glint along its top-left curve and is dark everywhere else. Don't drag the light down into the shadow. Too much of it flattens the rock.

pull-birches.text: Let the leaves, bushes and rock dry first, because these trunks go straight over them. Start at the foot of each trunk, down in the fallen leaves, and give it a wide, flared base.

Press the full width of the brush and pull up, easing the pressure a little as you rise. Paint five front birch trunks: a slim one at the left edge of the canvas, two big ones that lean as they climb, and two near the right edge. The first of those two has its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
Cover each trunk solidly so no leaves show through. Keep the edges clean, and leave the leaves, firs and haze around the trunks as they are.

When you stop, the front birch trunks stand plain and pale gray-white from the leaves to the top edge of the canvas, with no shading or marks. Most of the new paint is on the left side. Don't make them thin like the far trunks: these are wide, close-up trees.

shade-birches.text: Wait until the Birch gray trunks are dry. Start at the top edge of the canvas on the big trunk whose middle is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge.
Dip only the tip of the brush in Birch shadow and skim it lightly down the trunk in long strokes. Lay it heaviest on the side away from the sun, then shade the other four trunks the same way.

Let the shadow break up as it goes. Leave ragged patches of Birch gray showing, mostly on the sunny side and toward the trunk feet, which stay mostly pale. Touch a little Moss green where each foot meets the leaves.

When you stop, the trunks read lavender gray with pale patches, and most of the paint is on the left side. If it went on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry, then dry-brush Birch gray back over part of it.

mark-bark.text: Let the shading dry first. Start on the big trunk whose middle is about 2 in from the left edge, low down near its foot.

Load Bark dark and press the full width of the brush at one edge of the trunk. Pull across the trunk, turning onto the brush's edge as you go so each patch tapers. Lay the patches in broken rows up the trunk, with gaps between them, then do the same on every trunk.

Make the patches heavier toward the base, so the lower parts of the two big trunks go mostly dark. On the trunk whose middle is about 14 1/4 in from the left edge, the dark foot's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. Higher up, keep the patches small and far apart.
Leave plenty of lavender and pale gray between the patches. When you stop, most of the dark sits in the bottom half. Don't space the patches evenly like ladder rungs.

line-bark.text: The bark patches must be fully dry first, because lines laid over wet paint spread and feather.

Thin Bark dark with water and hold the liner upright. Start high on the first big trunk, the one nearest the slim trunk. Pull short, wobbly lines down the shaded side of the trunk, the side away from the sun, through and between the patches. Start each line thick and lighten as you go.
Let the lines fork and overlap in a narrow band, then do the same on the other trunks. Most of the lines go in the top half, and the trunk feet get none.
Leave the sunny side pale. When you stop, each trunk has a streaky, barky shadow side. If a line skips, add water, and reload often.

light-bark.text: Let the thin bark lines dry first, or the white will smear them into gray.

Start at the top edge on the big leaning trunk nearest the left edge. With only the tip of the brush in the Birch white and no water, skim lightly down the trunk. Then do the second big leaning trunk, then the two slim trunks near the right edge.

Keep the light on the edge of each trunk that faces the sun, and let it break over the dark bark patches in places. Most of the light goes on the two big trunks in the left half. Stop high: the lowest light is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, so the trunk feet stay dark and moss green.
When you stop, the upper trunks should look sunlit and rough, with lavender gray still showing. If a stroke goes on solid, your brush was too loaded.

tap-sunlit-leaves.text: Wait until the Birch white on the trunks is dry, because you will tap right up to the trunk feet.

Start where the path meets the leaves near the rock. Wipe most of the Pale gold off the #12 round, then tap with its tip along both edges of the path and around the rock's base. Work outward to the trunk feet, and on toward the left and right edges.

Keep the taps in a band across the middle of the ground. Its top is about 8 in from the top edge, and its bottom is about 1/2 in from the bottom edge. Most of the taps go in the right half, where the path and the rock are.
Leave plenty of the orange and brown leaves showing between the taps. When you stop, the ground should glint, not shine. If you get blobs, wipe the brush and tap again.

blend-sky.start: Start with Sky blue along the top edge of the canvas, stroking side to side from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Keep every stroke long and level, all the way across the 12 in width. Without rinsing, pick up the next colour and paint it under the last band. Then stroke back up over each join while it is still wet.
blend-sky.inside: Lay the sky in bands: blue at the top, Pale gold just under it, wide blue through the upper middle, then mostly Pale gold low down, with thin blue at the bottom edge. Use Cream gold where blue meets gold to soften the join. The ground goes over the lower sky later.
blend-sky.leave: No bare white: the sky reaches all four edges. Keep the soft, streaky band edges; don't smooth them flat.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas reads as glowing sunset bands with soft joins. If a hard line shows, add more of the lighter colour there and blend again.

dry-brush-clouds.first: Let the blended sky dry completely, so the dry brush skims over it instead of stirring it up.
dry-brush-clouds.start: Begin at the top edge of the canvas with the Warm peach, laying the first long streaks so they run all the way to the left and right edges.
dry-brush-clouds.strokes: Dip just the tip of the dry brush, wipe it, and skim it lightly sideways across the sky with a gentle slant, letting each streak break up and feather out at its ends. Work down the sky in several light passes.
dry-brush-clouds.inside: Keep the Warm peach along the upper edge of each streak and run the Dusky rose along its lower edge, as if the sun is lighting the clouds from beyond the far hills. Make the streaks thinner and smaller as you go down toward the horizon.
dry-brush-clouds.leave: Let the blue and gold sky show through the broken edges of every streak and in the wide gaps between them.
dry-brush-clouds.stop: Stop when soft, see-through peach and rose streaks lie across the whole sky, never solid patches. If one goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim a little sky color back over it.

light-cloud-tops.first: Wait until the Warm peach and Dusky rose streaks are dry to the touch.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, on the cloud streaks nearest the setting sun.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: With only the brush tip in the Pale gold and no water, skim short, light sideways strokes along the upper edge of each streak, following its slant and lifting off so the gold breaks up.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Put the gold only on the edge of each cloud that faces the sun, and give more of it to the clouds on the right side of the sky, nearest the sun.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the peach in the middle of each streak and the Dusky rose along its lower edge showing, with the blue sky between the clouds.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when the streaks have small glowing gold tops scattered over the sky, brightest on the right, with the rose still clearly showing underneath.

lay-mountains.first: The sky and the clouds must be fully dry, so the mountain paint doesn't drag the gold into it.
lay-mountains.start: Start with Far violet on the far range's peaks, where the gold sky is. The top of the far blue mountains is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-mountains.strokes: Pull long, level strokes left and right. Let the top edge rise and dip in soft, low peaks.
lay-mountains.inside: Far violet is the far range, high and pale. Mountain blue goes on below it as the nearer ridge, overlapping the far range's foot and running from the left edge to the right edge. It is darker because it is closer.
lay-mountains.leave: Leave the gold sky and the clouds showing above the far peaks.
lay-mountains.stop: Stop when two flat bands cross the canvas: pale violet peaks behind and slate blue in front. The bottom of the slate band is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, with a ragged lower edge. There is no warm light on them yet.

light-ridges.first: Let the Far violet and Mountain blue dry completely first, or the peach will smear into them.
light-ridges.start: Start on the right side of the far blue mountains, along the very top of the far range's peaks.
light-ridges.strokes: Dip only the tip of a dry brush and skim it lightly along the ridge line, following each peak's slope. Use short touches, not one long line.
light-ridges.inside: The peach sits only on the topmost edge of the peaks that face the setting sun. Most of it is on the right side of the far blue mountains, plus one tiny touch on a peak near the middle.
light-ridges.leave: Leave the rest of both ranges their flat blue and violet. The peach is a rim, not a fill.
light-ridges.stop: Stop when a few thin, broken peach glints catch the ridge tops. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush violet back over part of it.

lay-lake.first: The Mountain blue must be dry, so the cream stays clean where it meets the ridge.
lay-lake.start: Start at the right edge, just under the foot of the slate-blue ridge. The lake's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-lake.strokes: Pull short, level strokes from the right edge toward the left. Let each stroke get shorter so the strip tapers to a point.
lay-lake.inside: The cream is one flat sliver of shining water, thickest where it meets the right edge and thinning to a sharp point. It is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
lay-lake.leave: Keep the dark Mountain blue line of the ridge's foot crisp along the lake's top.
lay-lake.stop: Stop when a thin, pale, glowing strip sits at the right edge, pointing left like a sliver of light.

lay-hills-meadow.first: Let the sky, the far blue mountains and the glimpse of lake dry before you start.
lay-hills-meadow.start: Start just below the far blue mountains at the left edge of the canvas. The top of the green is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-hills-meadow.strokes: Keep the 1 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right. On the hills, let each band slope gently down toward the right, the way the slopes roll.
lay-hills-meadow.inside: Use Yellow green for the far slopes, where the sun reaches. Lower down, lay a solid band of Hill green across the meadow, lit Yellow green along its top. Below that, keep the strokes short and broken.
lay-hills-meadow.leave: Let the sunset sky show between the hill bands and between the broken strokes near the bottom edge.
lay-hills-meadow.stop: Stop when green bands reach the left, right and bottom edges. A solid green band should cross the middle, and some sky should still show between the strokes.

darken-bands.first: Let the Yellow green and Hill green dry first, so the dark doesn't mix into them.
darken-bands.start: Start with a dark ridge right under the far blue mountains, running from the left edge of the canvas toward the lake.
darken-bands.strokes: Use level strokes that follow each hill's roll, sloping down toward the right. At the meadow front, pull long strokes all the way across to the bottom edge.
darken-bands.inside: Lay Deep green in bands across the hills to put them in shadow, filling the spots where sky showed through. Darken the meadow front, whose top is about 9 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of the dark goes in the bottom half.
darken-bands.leave: Keep light Yellow green bands between the dark ones. Leave the broad lit band across the meadow's middle alone.
darken-bands.stop: Stop when no sky shows anywhere. The hills should be striped dark and light, and the meadow should be dark at the front. A common mistake is covering the light bands, which flattens the hills.

dab-bushes.first: Let the Deep green bands dry, or the taps will smear into them.
dab-bushes.start: Start with the cluster of bushes near the left edge of the canvas, on the far slopes just under the far blue mountains.
dab-bushes.strokes: Use a light load and no water. Tap with the tip of the #6 round, a few taps for each round clump, and set the clumps in rows along the Deep green bands.
dab-bushes.inside: Put the bushes on the shadowed bands of the hills: a cluster at the left, one lone clump near the middle, and a long row toward the right edge. They all sit between about 4 in from the top edge and 7 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
dab-bushes.leave: Leave the lit Yellow green bands and the whole meadow untouched.
dab-bushes.stop: Stop when rows of small, dark, rounded bushes dot the hills. If you get blobs instead, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

block-in-cow.first: The green hills and meadow must be dry, because the cow goes right over them.
block-in-cow.start: Start in the middle of the cow's body with one big upright oval. The cow's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 9 in tall.
block-in-cow.strokes: Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), every stroke pulled downward the way long hair hangs. Put the rounded head on as a bump at the top right of the body, with a small lump where the chin pokes out.
block-in-cow.inside: Fill the whole cow flat with Rust brown, body and head alike. Shadows and locks come later.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave the hills, bushes and meadow showing all around the cow. Let the bottom edge break into ragged points of hair; don't close it off.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop at one flat rust-brown blob with a shaggy, pointed lower edge. A beginner often outlines it neatly first. Don't: it should look rough.

shade-cow.first: The Rust brown cow must be dry, or the dark will mix into mud.
shade-cow.start: Start on the left side of the cow, at the top of the back, where the body is turned away from the sun.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the back toward the meadow, bending with the round of the coat. Skim lighter, broken strokes over the rest of the cow so the rust looks streaky like hair.
shade-cow.inside: Lay the darkest paint down the left side of the cow, where the head sits over the body, under the fringe and chin, and in a dark run low on the body between the legs. The sun is behind the cow at the right.
shade-cow.leave: Keep most of the rust showing on the sunny side of the head and body.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks round and hairy, dark on one side and warm rust on the other. A common mistake is covering it all evenly dark.

block-in-horns.first: The Dark umber shading on the head must be dry, so the horn bases stay clean.
block-in-horns.start: Start each horn with a wide piece where it leaves the top of the head. The taller horn's top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge; the shorter horn's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-horns.strokes: From each wide base, add a curving piece that narrows to a sharp point. The taller horn sweeps up and out from the head. The shorter horn reaches out from the head and then bends straight up.
block-in-horns.inside: Fill both horns flat with Horn tan, base to tip.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the sky, mountains and the cow's coat around the horns untouched.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop at two flat pale horns, wide at the head and pointed at the tips. Beginners often make them the same width all along; taper them.

shade-horns.first: The Horn tan must be dry, so the dark sits on top and doesn't smear.
shade-horns.start: Start at the very tip of each horn, where the dark is strongest.
shade-horns.strokes: Pull each stroke from the tip back along the horn's curve toward the head, following the bend, and press lighter as you go so the dark fades.
shade-horns.inside: Put the dark on the tips and along the underside of each horn's curve, plus a little at the base where it meets the coat. The tops catch the sunset light, so they stay pale.
shade-horns.leave: Leave a strip of pale Horn tan along the top edge of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when the horns look round: dark tips, dark undersides, pale tops. Don't paint a hard band across the tip; let it fade along the curve.

pull-orange-locks.first: Let the Dark umber shadows and the horns dry first, so the locks don't smear them.
pull-orange-locks.start: Start on the fringe at the crown of the head, just below the cow's horns; the coat's top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge.
pull-orange-locks.strokes: Press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull down, so it tapers to a point. Curve the locks down over the eyes, over the round of the shoulders, then straight down the body to the ragged hem.
pull-orange-locks.inside: Lay locks over the whole cow, fringe, head and body, overlapping like hair hanging from the crown and spine.
pull-orange-locks.leave: Leave Dark umber showing in the gaps between locks, most where the fringe meets the face and the chin meets the chest. Keep off the horns.
pull-orange-locks.stop: Stop when the whole coat, about 6 in wide, is long tapering locks with dark gaps. Don't paint even-width stripes: every lock starts wide and ends in a point.

pull-gold-locks.first: Let the Rust brown locks dry, so the gold sits on top instead of mixing in.
pull-gold-locks.start: Start on the top of the cow's shoulder, where the coat rounds over the back; the first lock's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
pull-gold-locks.strokes: Use the same stroke, smaller: full width at the top, then onto the edge, pulling down along the hair to a point.
pull-gold-locks.inside: Put a few short Honey gold locks on the shoulder and down the upper body behind it, where the coat rounds toward the light, and one by the ear near the right horn, its left side about 8 in from the left edge. Most go in the top half of the coat.
pull-gold-locks.leave: Leave nearly all the Rust brown locks and Dark umber gaps showing; the gold only tops a few locks.
pull-gold-locks.stop: Stop at a handful of small gold locks, each on a ginger lock. Beginners add too many: if the coat looks gold all over, you've gone too far.

flick-dark-grass.first: Let the cow's coat and the green meadow base dry first, so the grass blades stay crisp instead of smearing.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom left corner of the canvas, where the biggest, darkest clumps of grass go.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Touch the fan's tip down where a clump grows and flick quickly upward and a little to the right, lifting off as you go so each blade thins at its top. Make two or three flicks side by side for each clump.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Scatter the clumps below the Highland cow and on both sides of it. Most of them go in the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass, bigger and closer together near the bottom edge, smaller toward the hills, because near grass looks bigger.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave plenty of the green base showing between the clumps, and keep the cow's coat clean.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Dark slanted clumps dot the meadow from the left edge to the right edge, the highest about 10 in from the top edge. A common mistake is too much paint, which makes flat blobs instead of tapering blades.

flick-green-grass.first: Let the Deep green grass marks dry, so the lighter green sits on top instead of turning muddy.
flick-green-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge and work upward; the highest marks stop about 6 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
flick-green-grass.strokes: With a light load, flick quickly upward and a little to the right, the same slant as the dark blades, lifting off so each tip breaks. Lay the flicks in the gaps between the dark clumps.
flick-green-grass.inside: This is the sunlit grass, so it covers more than the dark did: thick across the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass and right up to the bottom of the Highland cow, with most of it on the right side, toward the sun. Toward the hills, it thins to small flecks.
flick-green-grass.leave: Let the Deep green grass marks show between your strokes, and keep the cow itself clean.
flick-green-grass.stop: The meadow reads as a mix of bright and dark blades all leaning the same way. A common mistake is covering the dark clumps completely; the dark gives the grass its depth.

flick-gold-grass.first: Let the Yellow green grass marks dry first.
flick-gold-grass.start: Start right of the Highland cow, on the right side of the meadow's tall grass, where the gold catches the low sun most.
flick-gold-grass.strokes: Use a light load and quick upward flicks, slanting a little to the right, lifting off so each golden blade tapers at its tip. Group them in short clumps of two or three.
flick-gold-grass.inside: Most of it goes on the right side, toward the setting sun: a band of clumps right of the Highland cow, a few left of the Highland cow at the left edge, and a scatter across the bottom of the meadow's tall grass. The highest strokes stop about 8 1/2 in from the top edge.
flick-gold-grass.leave: Leave the Deep green and Yellow green grass marks showing between the gold, and keep the cow untouched.
flick-gold-grass.stop: The meadow looks full and sunlit, gold blades glinting among the greens. Don't spread gold evenly everywhere, or the meadow goes flat.

rim-light-cow.first: Let the Honey gold locks and the meadow's tall grass around the cow dry first, so the new gold stays bright and clean.
rim-light-cow.start: Start at the top of the cow's head between the horns, where the fringe meets the sky; the rim's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
rim-light-cow.strokes: Press the full width of the brush at the coat's outer edge, then turn onto its edge and lift as you pull down the way the hair hangs, so each stroke tapers to a point. Down the cow's chest and side, pull each stroke straight down.
rim-light-cow.inside: The gold goes only on the edges facing the low sun: the top of the head and fringe, the edge of the head and chest nearest the lake, down that side to the grass, and the top of the back, about 5 in from the top edge.
rim-light-cow.leave: Leave the Dark umber shadows down the far side of the body and under the fringe and chin, and keep ginger and Honey gold locks showing between your strokes.
rim-light-cow.stop: Stop when the head, fringe, chest and back glow with a thin gold rim, much smaller than the locks under it. A common mistake is painting whole locks gold: keep it to the edges.

light-horns.first: Let the Dark umber tips and undersides of the cow's horns dry first, so the cream does not turn muddy.
light-horns.start: Start on the left horn where it leaves the head, and work toward its tip; its light's top is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge. Then do the right horn the same way, from its base.
light-horns.strokes: Use the tip of the brush and pull one long curved stroke along the top of each horn, bending with the horn as it curves up toward the tip.
light-horns.inside: The cream sits only along the top of each horn, the side facing the sky and the setting sun, and fades out before the tip.
light-horns.leave: Leave the Dark umber tips and undersides showing, with a band of Horn tan between them and the cream.
light-horns.stop: Stop when each horn has a thin pale cream line along its top that fades before the dark tip. Don't widen it into a stripe that covers the tan.

paint-nose.first: Let the Pale gold rim and the locks on the face dry, so the nose doesn't drag them.
paint-nose.start: Start on the cow's face, under the fringe, at the broad top of the nose. The area you work in is about 2 1/2 in tall, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Curve each stroke around the nose. Go across its top, then down and around the edge of the muzzle facing the sun. Finish with one curved stroke along the jaw, where the chin meets the chest.
paint-nose.inside: Most of the Rosy nose goes on the left side of the cow's face. It makes a solid patch on the shadow side of the nose, away from the sun. The rest is thin curved edges and a couple of small dabs low on the shadowed chin.
paint-nose.leave: Leave the ginger and gold locks showing across the middle of the muzzle, and the whole fringe above it.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when the muzzle reads as a round snout. Don't fill it in flat, or it turns into a mask. There is no shine, no nostrils and no mouth yet.

nose-shine.first: Let the Rosy nose dry to the touch, or the pale pink will turn muddy.
nose-shine.start: Start at the very top of the nose, where it faces up to the sky. The area's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
nose-shine.strokes: Lay short curved strokes across the top of the nose. Bend them over its round like a cap, working from the middle out.
nose-shine.inside: The Nose pink sits only on the top of the nose, between where the nostrils will go, because that's the part the sky lights. The sides and the lower nose stay Rosy nose.
nose-shine.leave: Leave the Rosy nose showing all around the shine, and leave the chin and the fringe untouched.
nose-shine.stop: Stop at a small pale pink cap, about 1 1/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall. Beginners often make it too big, so keep it smaller than feels right.

nostrils-mouth.first: Let the Nose pink and the Rosy nose dry, or the dark lines will spread and feather.
nostrils-mouth.start: Start with the two nostrils, one at each end of the Nose pink cap.
nostrils-mouth.strokes: Hold the liner upright and use light, steady pressure. Curl one short curved stroke down for each nostril. Then make one short, slightly wobbly line for the mouth, where the nose meets the chin. Then pull overlapping lines from the chin down the throat to darken it.
nostrils-mouth.inside: Most of the Dark umber goes on the left side of the cow's face. The throat and jaw on the shadow side, away from the sun, get the most, so the head stands forward off the chest.
nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave the Nose pink cap clean between the nostrils, and leave the gold rim on the muzzle untouched.
nostrils-mouth.stop: Stop at two dark nostrils, a short mouth and a dark shadow under the chin. The whole area is about 2 1/2 in tall. If the lines skip, add water.

blend-sky.start: Start with Sky blue along the top edge of the canvas, stroking side to side from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Keep every stroke long and level, all the way across the sky, which is about 12 in wide. Without rinsing, pick up the next colour and paint it under the last band. Then stroke back up over each join while it is still wet.
blend-sky.inside: Lay the sky in bands: blue at the top, Pale gold just under it, wide blue through the upper middle, then mostly Pale gold low down, with thin blue at the bottom edge. Use Cream gold where blue meets gold to soften the join. The ground goes over the lower sky later.
blend-sky.leave: No bare white: the sky reaches all four edges. Keep the soft, streaky band edges; don't smooth them flat.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas reads as glowing sunset bands with soft joins. If a hard line shows, add more of the lighter colour there and blend again.

dry-brush-clouds.first: Let the blended sky dry completely, so the dry brush skims over it instead of stirring it up.
dry-brush-clouds.start: Begin at the top edge of the canvas with the Warm peach, laying the first long streaks so they run all the way to the left and right edges.
dry-brush-clouds.strokes: Dip just the tip of the dry brush, wipe it, and skim it lightly sideways across the sky with a gentle slant, letting each streak break up and feather out at its ends. Work down the sky in several light passes.
dry-brush-clouds.inside: Keep the Warm peach along the upper edge of each streak and run the Dusky rose along its lower edge, as if the sun is lighting the clouds from beyond the far hills. Make the streaks thinner and smaller as you go down toward the horizon.
dry-brush-clouds.leave: Let the blue and gold sky show through the broken edges of every streak and in the wide gaps between them.
dry-brush-clouds.stop: Stop when soft, see-through peach and rose streaks lie across the whole sky, never solid patches. If one goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim a little sky color back over it.

light-cloud-tops.first: Wait until the Warm peach and Dusky rose streaks are dry to the touch.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start at the top edge of the canvas, on the cloud streaks nearest the setting sun.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: With only the brush tip in the Pale gold and no water, skim short, light sideways strokes along the upper edge of each streak, following its slant and lifting off so the gold breaks up.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Put the gold only on the edge of each cloud that faces the sun, and give more of it to the clouds on the right side of the sky, nearest the sun.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the peach in the middle of each streak and the Dusky rose along its lower edge showing, with the blue sky between the clouds.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Stop when the streaks have small glowing gold tops scattered over the sky, brightest on the right, with the rose still clearly showing underneath.

lay-mountains.first: The sky and the clouds must be fully dry, so the mountain paint doesn't drag the gold into it.
lay-mountains.start: Start with Far violet on the far range's peaks, where the gold sky is. The top of the far blue mountains is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-mountains.strokes: Pull long, level strokes left and right. Let the top edge rise and dip in soft, low peaks.
lay-mountains.inside: Far violet is the far range, high and pale. Mountain blue is the nearer ridge, overlapping the far range's foot and running from the left edge to the right edge; it is darker because it is closer.
lay-mountains.leave: Leave the gold sky and the clouds showing where they meet the far range's peaks.
lay-mountains.stop: Stop when two flat bands cross the canvas: pale violet peaks behind and slate blue in front. The bottom of the slate band is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, with a ragged lower edge. There is no warm light on them yet.

light-ridges.first: Let the Far violet and Mountain blue dry completely first, or the peach will smear into them.
light-ridges.start: Start on the right side of the far blue mountains, along the very top of the far range's peaks.
light-ridges.strokes: Dip only the tip of a dry brush and skim it lightly along the ridge line, following each peak's slope. Use short touches, not one long line.
light-ridges.inside: The peach sits only on the topmost edge of the peaks that face the setting sun. Most of it is on the right side of the far blue mountains, plus one tiny touch on a peak near the middle.
light-ridges.leave: Leave the rest of both ranges their flat blue and violet. The peach is a rim, not a fill.
light-ridges.stop: Stop when a few thin, broken peach glints catch the ridge tops. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush violet back over part of it.

lay-lake.first: The Mountain blue must be dry, so the cream stays clean where it meets the ridge.
lay-lake.start: Start at the right edge, just under the foot of the slate-blue ridge. The lake's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-lake.strokes: Pull short, level strokes from the right edge toward the left. Let each stroke get shorter so the strip tapers to a point.
lay-lake.inside: The cream is one flat sliver of shining water, thickest where it meets the right edge and thinning to a sharp point. It is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
lay-lake.leave: Keep the dark Mountain blue line of the ridge's foot crisp along the lake's top.
lay-lake.stop: Stop when a thin, pale, glowing strip sits at the right edge, pointing left like a sliver of light.

lay-hills-meadow.first: Let the sky, the far blue mountains and the glimpse of lake dry before you start.
lay-hills-meadow.start: Start just below the far blue mountains at the left edge of the canvas. The top of the green is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
lay-hills-meadow.strokes: Keep the 1 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right. On the hills, let each band slope gently down toward the right, the way the slopes roll.
lay-hills-meadow.inside: Use Yellow green for the far slopes, where the sun reaches. Lower down, lay a solid band of Hill green across the meadow, lit Yellow green along its top. Toward the bottom edge of the canvas, keep the strokes short and broken.
lay-hills-meadow.leave: Let the sunset sky show between the hill bands and between the broken strokes near the bottom edge.
lay-hills-meadow.stop: Stop when green bands reach the left, right and bottom edges. A solid green band should cross the middle, and some sky should still show between the strokes.

darken-bands.first: Let the Yellow green and Hill green dry first, so the dark doesn't mix into them.
darken-bands.start: Start with a dark ridge right under the far blue mountains, running from the left edge of the canvas toward the lake.
darken-bands.strokes: Use level strokes that follow each hill's roll, sloping down toward the right. At the meadow front, pull long strokes all the way across to the bottom edge.
darken-bands.inside: Lay Deep green in bands across the hills to put them in shadow, filling the spots where sky showed through. Darken the meadow front, whose top is about 9 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of the dark goes in the bottom half.
darken-bands.leave: Keep light Yellow green bands between the dark ones. Leave the broad lit band across the meadow's middle alone.
darken-bands.stop: Stop when no sky shows anywhere. The hills should be striped dark and light, and the meadow should be dark at the front. A common mistake is covering the light bands, which flattens the hills.

dab-bushes.first: Let the Deep green bands dry, or the taps will smear into them.
dab-bushes.start: Start with the cluster of bushes near the left edge of the canvas, on the far slopes just under the far blue mountains.
dab-bushes.strokes: Use a light load and no water. Tap with the tip of the #6 round, a few taps for each round clump, and set the clumps in rows along the Deep green bands.
dab-bushes.inside: Put the bushes on the shadowed bands of the hills: a cluster at the left, one lone clump near the middle, and a long row toward the right edge. They all sit between about 4 in from the top edge and 7 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
dab-bushes.leave: Leave the lit Yellow green bands and the whole meadow untouched.
dab-bushes.stop: Stop when rows of small, dark, rounded bushes dot the hills. If you get blobs instead, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

block-in-cow.first: The green hills and meadow must be dry, because the cow goes right over them.
block-in-cow.start: Start in the middle of the cow's body with one big upright oval. The cow's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 9 in tall.
block-in-cow.strokes: Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), every stroke pulled downward the way long hair hangs. Put the rounded head on as a bump at the top right of the body, with a small lump where the chin pokes out.
block-in-cow.inside: Fill the whole cow flat with Rust brown, body and head alike. Shadows and locks come later.
block-in-cow.leave: Leave the hills, bushes and meadow showing all around the cow. Let the bottom edge break into ragged points of hair; don't close it off.
block-in-cow.stop: Stop at one flat rust-brown blob with a shaggy, pointed lower edge. A beginner often outlines it neatly first. Don't: it should look rough.

shade-cow.first: The Rust brown cow must be dry, or the dark will mix into mud.
shade-cow.start: Start on the left side of the cow, at the top of the back, where the body is turned away from the sun.
shade-cow.strokes: Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the back toward the meadow, bending with the round of the coat. Skim lighter, broken strokes over the rest of the cow so the rust looks streaky like hair.
shade-cow.inside: Lay the darkest paint down the left side of the cow, where the head sits over the body, under the fringe and chin, and in a dark run low on the body between the legs. The sun is behind the cow at the right.
shade-cow.leave: Keep most of the rust showing on the sunny side of the head and body.
shade-cow.stop: Stop when the cow looks round and hairy, dark on one side and warm rust on the other. A common mistake is covering it all evenly dark.

block-in-horns.first: The Dark umber shading on the head must be dry, so the horn bases stay clean.
block-in-horns.start: Start each horn with a wide piece where it leaves the top of the head. The taller horn's top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge; the shorter horn's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-horns.strokes: From each wide base, add a curving piece that narrows to a sharp point. The taller horn sweeps up and out from the head. The shorter horn reaches out from the head and then bends straight up.
block-in-horns.inside: Fill both horns flat with Horn tan, base to tip.
block-in-horns.leave: Leave the sky, mountains and the cow's coat around the horns untouched.
block-in-horns.stop: Stop at two flat pale horns, wide at the head and pointed at the tips. Beginners often make them the same width all along; taper them.

shade-horns.first: The Horn tan must be dry, so the dark sits on top and doesn't smear.
shade-horns.start: Start at the very tip of each horn, where the dark is strongest.
shade-horns.strokes: Pull each stroke from the tip back along the horn's curve toward the head, following the bend, and press lighter as you go so the dark fades.
shade-horns.inside: Put the dark on the tips and along the underside of each horn's curve, plus a little at the base where it meets the coat. The tops catch the sunset light, so they stay pale.
shade-horns.leave: Leave a strip of pale Horn tan along the top edge of each horn.
shade-horns.stop: Stop when the horns look round: dark tips, dark undersides, pale tops. Don't paint a hard band across the tip; let it fade along the curve.

pull-orange-locks.first: Let the Dark umber shadows and the horns dry first, so the locks don't smear them.
pull-orange-locks.start: Start on the fringe at the crown of the head, just below the cow's horns; the coat's top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge.
pull-orange-locks.strokes: Press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull down, so it tapers to a point. Curve the locks down over the eyes, over the round of the shoulders, then straight down the body to the ragged hem.
pull-orange-locks.inside: Lay locks over the whole cow, fringe, head and body, overlapping like hair hanging from the crown and spine.
pull-orange-locks.leave: Leave Dark umber showing in the gaps between locks, most where the fringe meets the face and the chin meets the chest. Keep off the horns.
pull-orange-locks.stop: Stop when the whole coat, about 6 in wide, is long tapering locks with dark gaps. Don't paint even-width stripes: every lock starts wide and ends in a point.

pull-gold-locks.first: Let the Rust brown locks dry, so the gold sits on top instead of mixing in.
pull-gold-locks.start: Start on the top of the cow's shoulder, where the coat rounds over the back; the first lock's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
pull-gold-locks.strokes: Use the same stroke, smaller: full width at the top, then onto the edge, pulling down along the hair to a point.
pull-gold-locks.inside: Put a few short Honey gold locks on the shoulder and down the upper body behind it, where the coat rounds toward the light, and one by the ear near the right horn, its left side about 8 in from the left edge. Most go in the top half of the coat.
pull-gold-locks.leave: Leave nearly all the Rust brown locks and Dark umber gaps showing; the gold only tops a few locks.
pull-gold-locks.stop: Stop at a handful of small gold locks, each on a ginger lock. Beginners add too many: if the coat looks gold all over, you've gone too far.

flick-dark-grass.first: Let the cow's coat and the green meadow base dry first, so the grass blades stay crisp instead of smearing.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start at the bottom left corner of the canvas, where the biggest, darkest clumps of grass go.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Touch the fan's tip down where a clump grows and flick quickly upward and a little to the right, lifting off as you go so each blade thins at its top. Make two or three flicks side by side for each clump.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Scatter the clumps below the Highland cow and on both sides of it. Most of them go in the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass, bigger and closer together near the bottom edge, smaller toward the hills, because near grass looks bigger.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave plenty of the green base showing between the clumps, and keep the cow's coat clean.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Dark slanted clumps dot the meadow from the left edge to the right edge, the highest about 10 in from the top edge. A common mistake is too much paint, which makes flat blobs instead of tapering blades.

flick-green-grass.first: Let the Deep green grass marks dry, so the lighter green sits on top instead of turning muddy.
flick-green-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge and work upward through the meadow, stopping short of the hills.
flick-green-grass.strokes: With a light load, flick quickly upward and a little to the right, the same slant as the dark blades, lifting off so each tip breaks. Lay the flicks in the gaps between the dark clumps.
flick-green-grass.inside: This is the sunlit grass, so it covers more than the dark did: thick across the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass and right up to the bottom of the Highland cow, with most of it on the right side, toward the sun. Toward the hills, it thins to small flecks.

flick-gold-grass.first: Let the Yellow green grass marks dry first.
flick-gold-grass.start: Start right of the Highland cow, on the right side of the meadow's tall grass, where the gold catches the low sun most.
flick-gold-grass.strokes: Use a light load and quick upward flicks, slanting a little to the right, lifting off so each golden blade tapers at its tip. Group them in short clumps of two or three.
flick-gold-grass.inside: Most of it goes on the right side, toward the setting sun: a band of clumps right of the Highland cow, a few left of the Highland cow at the left edge, and a scatter across the bottom of the meadow's tall grass. The highest strokes stop about 8 1/2 in from the top edge.

flick-gold-grass.stop: The meadow looks full and sunlit, gold blades glinting among the greens. Don't spread gold evenly everywhere, or the meadow goes flat.

Stop when the whole canvas reads as glowing sunset bands with soft joins. If a hard line shows, add more of the lighter colour there and blend again.

Begin at the top edge of the canvas with the Warm peach, laying the first long streaks so they run all the way to the left and right edges.

light-cloud-tops.text: Wait until the Warm peach and Dusky rose streaks are dry to the touch.
Start at the top edge of the canvas, on the cloud streaks nearest the setting sun.
With only the brush tip in the Pale gold and no water, skim short, light sideways strokes along the upper edge of each streak, following its slant and lifting off so the gold breaks up.
Put the gold only on the edge of each cloud that faces the sun, and give more of it to the clouds on the right side of the sky, nearest the sun.
Leave the peach in the middle of each streak and the Dusky rose along its lower edge showing, with the blue sky between the clouds.
Stop when the streaks have small glowing gold tops scattered over the sky, brightest on the right, with the rose still clearly showing underneath.

lay-mountains.text: The sky and the clouds must be fully dry, so the mountain paint doesn't drag the gold into it.
Start with Far violet on the far range's peaks, where the gold sky is. The top of the far blue mountains is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge.
Pull long, level strokes left and right. Let the top edge rise and dip in soft, low peaks.
Far violet is the far range, high and pale. Mountain blue is the nearer ridge, overlapping the far range's foot and running from the left edge to the right edge; it is darker because it is closer.
Leave the gold sky and the clouds showing where they meet the far range's peaks.

Stop when two flat bands cross the canvas: pale violet peaks behind and slate blue in front. The bottom of the slate band is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, with a ragged lower edge. There is no warm light on them yet.

light-ridges.text: Let the Far violet and Mountain blue dry completely first, or the peach will smear into them.
Start on the right side of the far blue mountains, along the very top of the far range's peaks.
Dip only the tip of a dry brush and skim it lightly along the ridge line, following each peak's slope. Use short touches, not one long line.
The peach sits only on the topmost edge of the peaks that face the setting sun. Most of it is on the right side of the far blue mountains, plus one tiny touch on a peak near the middle.
Leave the rest of both ranges their flat blue and violet. The peach is a rim, not a fill.
Stop when a few thin, broken peach glints catch the ridge tops. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush violet back over part of it.

lay-lake.text: The Mountain blue must be dry, so the cream stays clean where it meets the ridge.
Start at the right edge, just under the foot of the slate-blue ridge. The lake's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Pull short, level strokes from the right edge toward the left. Let each stroke get shorter so the strip tapers to a point.
The cream is one flat sliver of shining water, thickest where it meets the right edge and thinning to a sharp point. It is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
Keep the dark Mountain blue line of the ridge's foot crisp along the lake's top.
Stop when a thin, pale, glowing strip sits at the right edge, pointing left like a sliver of light.

lay-hills-meadow.text: Let the sky, the far blue mountains and the glimpse of lake dry before you start.
Start just below the far blue mountains at the left edge of the canvas. The top of the green is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge.
Keep the 1 inch flat level and pull long strokes left and right. On the hills, let each band slope gently down toward the right, the way the slopes roll.

Use Yellow green for the far slopes, where the sun reaches. Lower down, lay a solid band of Hill green across the meadow, lit Yellow green along its top. Toward the bottom edge of the canvas, keep the strokes short and broken.
Let the sunset sky show between the hill bands and between the broken strokes near the bottom edge.
Stop when green bands reach the left, right and bottom edges. A solid green band should cross the middle, and some sky should still show between the strokes.

darken-bands.text: Let the Yellow green and Hill green dry first, so the dark doesn't mix into them.
Start with a dark ridge right under the far blue mountains, running from the left edge of the canvas toward the lake.
Use level strokes that follow each hill's roll, sloping down toward the right. At the meadow front, pull long strokes all the way across to the bottom edge.

Lay Deep green in bands across the hills to put them in shadow, filling the spots where sky showed through. Darken the meadow front, whose top is about 9 1/2 in from the top edge. Most of the dark goes in the bottom half.
Keep light Yellow green bands between the dark ones. Leave the broad lit band across the meadow's middle alone.
Stop when no sky shows anywhere. The hills should be striped dark and light, and the meadow should be dark at the front. A common mistake is covering the light bands, which flattens the hills.

dab-bushes.text: Let the Deep green bands dry, or the taps will smear into them.
Start with the cluster of bushes near the left edge of the canvas, on the far slopes just under the far blue mountains.
Use a light load and no water. Tap with the tip of the #6 round, a few taps for each round clump, and set the clumps in rows along the Deep green bands.

Put the bushes on the shadowed bands of the hills: a cluster at the left, one lone clump near the middle, and a long row toward the right edge. They all sit between about 4 in from the top edge and 7 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Leave the lit Yellow green bands and the whole meadow untouched.
Stop when rows of small, dark, rounded bushes dot the hills. If you get blobs instead, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

block-in-cow.text: The green hills and meadow must be dry, because the cow goes right over them.
Start in the middle of the cow's body with one big upright oval. The cow's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 9 in tall.

Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), every stroke pulled downward the way long hair hangs. Put the rounded head on as a bump at the top right of the body, with a small lump where the chin pokes out.
Fill the whole cow flat with Rust brown, body and head alike. Shadows and locks come later.
Leave the hills, bushes and meadow showing all around the cow. Let the bottom edge break into ragged points of hair; don't close it off.
Stop at one flat rust-brown blob with a shaggy, pointed lower edge. A beginner often outlines it neatly first. Don't: it should look rough.

shade-cow.text: The Rust brown cow must be dry, or the dark will mix into mud.
Start on the left side of the cow, at the top of the back, where the body is turned away from the sun.
Pull long curved strokes down the body, from the back toward the meadow, bending with the round of the coat. Skim lighter, broken strokes over the rest of the cow so the rust looks streaky like hair.

Lay the darkest paint down the left side of the cow, where the head sits over the body, under the fringe and chin, and in a dark run low on the body between the legs. The sun is behind the cow at the right.
Keep most of the rust showing on the sunny side of the head and body.
Stop when the cow looks round and hairy, dark on one side and warm rust on the other. A common mistake is covering it all evenly dark.

block-in-horns.text: The Dark umber shading on the head must be dry, so the horn bases stay clean.
Start each horn with a wide piece where it leaves the top of the head. The taller horn's top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge; the shorter horn's middle is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge.
From each wide base, add a curving piece that narrows to a sharp point. The taller horn sweeps up and out from the head. The shorter horn reaches out from the head and then bends straight up.
Fill both horns flat with Horn tan, base to tip.
Leave the sky, mountains and the cow's coat around the horns untouched.
Stop at two flat pale horns, wide at the head and pointed at the tips. Beginners often make them the same width all along; taper them.

shade-horns.text: The Horn tan must be dry, so the dark sits on top and doesn't smear.
Start at the very tip of each horn, where the dark is strongest.
Pull each stroke from the tip back along the horn's curve toward the head, following the bend, and press lighter as you go so the dark fades.
Put the dark on the tips and along the underside of each horn's curve, plus a little at the base where it meets the coat. The tops catch the sunset light, so they stay pale.
Leave a strip of pale Horn tan along the top edge of each horn.
Stop when the horns look round: dark tips, dark undersides, pale tops. Don't paint a hard band across the tip; let it fade along the curve.

pull-orange-locks.text: Let the Dark umber shadows and the horns dry first, so the locks don't smear them.
Start on the fringe at the crown of the head, just below the cow's horns; the coat's top is about 5 3/4 in from the top edge.

Press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull down, so it tapers to a point. Curve the locks down over the eyes, over the round of the shoulders, then straight down the body to the ragged hem.
Lay locks over the whole cow, fringe, head and body, overlapping like hair hanging from the crown and spine.
Leave Dark umber showing in the gaps between locks, most where the fringe meets the face and the chin meets the chest. Keep off the horns.
Stop when the whole coat, about 6 in wide, is long tapering locks with dark gaps. Don't paint even-width stripes: every lock starts wide and ends in a point.

pull-gold-locks.text: Let the Rust brown locks dry, so the gold sits on top instead of mixing in.
Start on the top of the cow's shoulder, where the coat rounds over the back; the first lock's left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge.
Use the same stroke, smaller: full width at the top, then onto the edge, pulling down along the hair to a point.

Put a few short Honey gold locks on the shoulder and down the upper body behind it, where the coat rounds toward the light, and one by the ear near the right horn, its left side about 8 in from the left edge. Most go in the top half of the coat.
Leave nearly all the Rust brown locks and Dark umber gaps showing; the gold only tops a few locks.
Stop at a handful of small gold locks, each on a ginger lock. Beginners add too many: if the coat looks gold all over, you've gone too far.

flick-dark-grass.text: Let the cow's coat and the green meadow base dry first, so the grass blades stay crisp instead of smearing.
Start at the bottom left corner of the canvas, where the biggest, darkest clumps of grass go.

Touch the fan's tip down where a clump grows and flick quickly upward and a little to the right, lifting off as you go so each blade thins at its top. Make two or three flicks side by side for each clump.

Scatter the clumps below the Highland cow and on both sides of it. Most of them go in the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass, bigger and closer together near the bottom edge, smaller toward the hills, because near grass looks bigger.
Leave plenty of the green base showing between the clumps, and keep the cow's coat clean.

Dark slanted clumps dot the meadow from the left edge to the right edge, the highest about 10 in from the top edge. A common mistake is too much paint, which makes flat blobs instead of tapering blades.

flick-green-grass.text: Let the Deep green grass marks dry, so the lighter green sits on top instead of turning muddy.
Start at the bottom edge and work upward through the meadow, stopping short of the hills.
With a light load, flick quickly upward and a little to the right, the same slant as the dark blades, lifting off so each tip breaks. Lay the flicks in the gaps between the dark clumps.

This is the sunlit grass, so it covers more than the dark did: thick across the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass and right up to the bottom of the Highland cow, with most of it on the right side, toward the sun. Toward the hills, it thins to small flecks.
Let the Deep green grass marks show between your strokes, and keep the cow itself clean.
The meadow reads as a mix of bright and dark blades all leaning the same way. A common mistake is covering the dark clumps completely; the dark gives the grass its depth.

flick-gold-grass.text: Let the Yellow green grass marks dry first.
Start right of the Highland cow, on the right side of the meadow's tall grass, where the gold catches the low sun most.
Use a light load and quick upward flicks, slanting a little to the right, lifting off so each golden blade tapers at its tip. Group them in short clumps of two or three.

Most of it goes on the right side, toward the setting sun: a band of clumps right of the Highland cow, a few left of the Highland cow at the left edge, and a scatter across the bottom of the meadow's tall grass. The highest strokes stop about 8 1/2 in from the top edge.
Leave the Deep green and Yellow green grass marks showing between the gold, and keep the cow untouched.
The meadow looks full and sunlit, gold blades glinting among the greens. Don't spread gold evenly everywhere, or the meadow goes flat.

rim-light-cow.text: Let the Honey gold locks and the meadow's tall grass around the cow dry first, so the new gold stays bright and clean.
Start at the top of the cow's head between the horns, where the fringe meets the sky; the rim's top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.

Press the full width of the brush at the coat's outer edge, then turn onto its edge and lift as you pull down the way the hair hangs, so each stroke tapers to a point. Down the cow's chest and side, pull each stroke straight down.

The gold goes only on the edges facing the low sun: the top of the head and fringe, the edge of the head and chest nearest the lake, down that side to the grass, and the top of the back, about 5 in from the top edge.
Leave the Dark umber shadows down the far side of the body and under the fringe and chin, and keep ginger and Honey gold locks showing between your strokes.
Stop when the head, fringe, chest and back glow with a thin gold rim, much smaller than the locks under it. A common mistake is painting whole locks gold: keep it to the edges.

light-horns.text: Let the Dark umber tips and undersides of the cow's horns dry first, so the cream does not turn muddy.
Start on the left horn where it leaves the head, and work toward its tip; its light's top is about 3 3/4 in from the top edge. Then do the right horn the same way, from its base.
Use the tip of the brush and pull one long curved stroke along the top of each horn, bending with the horn as it curves up toward the tip.
The cream sits only along the top of each horn, the side facing the sky and the setting sun, and fades out before the tip.
Leave the Dark umber tips and undersides showing, with a band of Horn tan between them and the cream.
Stop when each horn has a thin pale cream line along its top that fades before the dark tip. Don't widen it into a stripe that covers the tan.

paint-nose.text: Let the Pale gold rim and the locks on the face dry, so the nose doesn't drag them.
Start on the cow's face, under the fringe, at the broad top of the nose. The area you work in is about 2 1/2 in tall, and its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
Curve each stroke around the nose. Go across its top, then down and around the edge of the muzzle facing the sun. Finish with one curved stroke along the jaw, where the chin meets the chest.

Most of the Rosy nose goes on the left side of the cow's face. It makes a solid patch on the shadow side of the nose, away from the sun. The rest is thin curved edges and a couple of small dabs low on the shadowed chin.
Leave the ginger and gold locks showing across the middle of the muzzle, and leave the whole fringe untouched.
Stop when the muzzle reads as a round snout. Don't fill it in flat, or it turns into a mask. There is no shine, no nostrils and no mouth yet.

nose-shine.text: Let the Rosy nose dry to the touch, or the pale pink will turn muddy.
Start at the very top of the nose, where it faces up to the sky. The area's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
Lay short curved strokes across the top of the nose. Bend them over its round like a cap, working from the middle out.
The Nose pink sits only on the top of the nose, between where the nostrils will go, because that's the part the sky lights. The sides and the lower nose stay Rosy nose.
Leave the Rosy nose showing all around the shine, and leave the chin and the fringe untouched.
Stop at a small pale pink cap, about 1 1/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall. Beginners often make it too big, so keep it smaller than feels right.

nostrils-mouth.text: Let the Nose pink and the Rosy nose dry, or the dark lines will spread and feather.
Start with the two nostrils, one at each end of the Nose pink cap.

Hold the liner upright and use light, steady pressure. Curl one short curved stroke down for each nostril. Then make one short, slightly wobbly line for the mouth, where the nose meets the chin. Then pull overlapping lines from the chin down the throat to darken it.
Most of the Dark umber goes on the left side of the cow's face. The throat and jaw on the shadow side, away from the sun, get the most, so the head stands forward off the chest.
Leave the Nose pink cap clean between the nostrils, and leave the gold rim on the muzzle untouched.
Stop at two dark nostrils, a short mouth and a dark shadow under the chin. The whole area is about 2 1/2 in tall. If the lines skip, add water.
