blend-sky.start: Begin at the top of the canvas near its right edge with Blue-violet mist, and lay a band across in side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Misty blue and paint below it, across the middle and down to the bottom edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Keep every stroke going side to side, and stroke back over each join several times while both colors are wet so the colors melt into each other.
blend-sky.inside: Rinse, then work Pale gold into the upper left corner of the canvas and in soft patches low on the left side of the canvas, where the sun will glow. Let a few soft violet streaks stay on the right side of the canvas as a far haze.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas should show anywhere. The paint reaches all four edges, about 16 in wide and 12 in tall.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze with no hard lines: gold glowing on the left, misty blue through the middle and bottom, violet haze on the right. If a hard line or a green stripe shows where gold meets blue, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

glow-sun.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the cream will mix into the blue.
glow-sun.start: Place the sun against the left edge of the canvas, its top about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, in the brightest part of the gold glow.
glow-sun.strokes: Load the tip of the brush and paint small circles, starting at the sun's bright middle and moving outward toward its edge.
glow-sun.inside: Keep the cream thickest and brightest at the middle of the sun, and let it thin out into a bumpy edge. The sun runs off the left edge of the canvas, so you paint only part of a circle.
glow-sun.leave: Leave the pale gold glow around the sun and all the rest of the misty sky untouched.
glow-sun.stop: Stop when a small soft sun, about 1 1/4 in wide, glows against the left edge with a bumpy edge. If its edge looks hard, soften it with lighter circles or smudge it with a finger.

pull-far-trunks.first: Let the misty sky and the sun dry to the touch, so the new trunk sits on the haze instead of mixing into it.
pull-far-trunks.start: This step is one trunk. Start at its foot, low in the haze: its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge, and its middle is about 7 1/4 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch flat at the foot and pull straight up, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you rise, so the trunk tapers to a thin line at its tip.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Widest at the foot and thinnest at the top, with one short soft stroke out on the left side of the misty far trunks, about a third of the way down. It stays one pale color, with no light side, because it is far away in the mist.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave all the haze around it untouched, and keep its edges soft so it melts into the mist.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Stop when one faint violet-gray trunk stands in the haze, flared at the foot and tapering to a thin tip, with its short arm part way up.

stamp-pines.first: Let the haze and the far trunk dry first, so the firs stay crisp.
stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tall dark fir in the group. The group's top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, its left side is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge, and it reaches the right edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Stamp only the middle tips of the fan. Tap a narrow tip at the top of each fir, then zigzag down, pressing harder as you go so the tree widens toward its base.
stamp-pines.inside: Use Deep pine green for the big dark firs. Use Misty blue for the paler firs at the left end of the group, between the dark ones, and behind them, because they stand deeper in the mist. Each fir is flat, with no light side yet.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the misty sky showing between the treetops. Keep the misty far trunks clear of fir paint.
stamp-pines.stop: Stop when a band of firs fills that corner, dark ones in front and hazy blue ones behind, with their bases fading softly into the mist. If the marks turn heavy and clumpy, the paint is too thick: thin it a little and spread the fan.

light-pines.first: Let the Deep pine green and Misty blue firs dry, or this paint will turn to mud.
light-pines.start: Start low at the left end of the fir trees. The first patch is about 2 in wide, and its top is about 5 in from the top edge.
light-pines.strokes: Spread the fan and tap lightly with the middle tips. Make short taps in different directions, so the patch looks like needles and not a smear.
light-pines.inside: Most of it goes on the left side of the fir trees, low down, the side facing the sun. Add one narrow upright strip in the gap left of the second dark fir. Then tap a few small dabs low on the tall fir, around the foot of its trunk.
light-pines.leave: Leave the tops and the shaded sides of the firs dark, and keep the hazy blue firs plain.
light-pines.stop: Stop when only a few small patches show, most of them on the left side and in the lower part of the firs. The firs still read as mostly dark.

pull-middle-trunks.first: Let the firs and the far trunk dry first, so these trunks stay clean where they cross the haze.
pull-middle-trunks.start: The trunks start right of the sun: the left side of the group is about 2 1/2 in from the left edge. Start with the smoky-brown trunk. Its middle is about 3 1/4 in from the left edge, and it is about 8 in tall.
pull-middle-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat at each trunk's foot and pull straight up, lifting onto the edge so each trunk tapers as it rises.
pull-middle-trunks.inside: The first trunk is Smoky brown, because it is the nearest. Pull the three trunks that follow it toward the middle of the canvas in Blue-violet mist, each one shorter and fainter, because they stand deeper in the mist. Two of them have a soft wider patch at their top. All of them stay plain, with no bark marks.
pull-middle-trunks.leave: Leave clear haze between the trunks, and keep the misty far trunks and the fir trees untouched.
pull-middle-trunks.stop: Stop when four plain trunks stand in a row, the brown one darkest and the violet ones paler, with their feet fading into the low mist.

lay-floor.first: Let the misty sky and the fir trees dry to the touch. The floor goes right over the low haze and touches the bottoms of the fir trees.
lay-floor.start: Start with Golden ochre at the floor's top line, about 7 in from the top edge, where the ground meets the bottoms of the fir trees and the misty far trunks.
lay-floor.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, laying one band under the next all the way down to the bottom edge. Don't tilt the strokes: a slanted band makes the ground look like it's sliding.
lay-floor.inside: Golden ochre bands are the sunlit ground. Pull Leaf brown bands between them like long shadows, and use more Leaf brown as you near the bottom edge. That keeps the back light near the mist and the front dark.
lay-floor.leave: Leave the fir trees and the misty far trunks as they are; the floor stops at their feet. Let streaks of Golden ochre show between the Leaf brown in front.
lay-floor.stop: The floor reaches the left, right and bottom edges and is about 5 in tall. It reads as level gold and brown bands, smooth at the back and streakier in front, with no path yet.

pull-path.first: Let the forest floor dry first, or the Path mauve will mix into the gold and turn muddy.
pull-path.start: Mark one dot where the path vanishes into the mist, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge and below the fir trees. Draw three to five faint chalk lines fanning from it down to the bottom edge.
pull-path.strokes: Start at the bottom edge and pull each stroke back along a chalk line toward the dot. Make it wide in front and let it thin to a thread as you reach the dot. If the path's edges run parallel, the path stands up like a wall, so go back to your chalk lines.
pull-path.inside: Most of the paint sits in the front of the path, where it is widest and nearest you. At the far end there is only a thin thread, with one short thin crossing stroke where the track meets the mist.
pull-path.leave: Keep the strokes broken so the Golden ochre floor shows through. Leave a patch of floor in the middle of the path near the bottom edge, like a hump between two ruts.
pull-path.stop: A mauve path runs from the bottom edge back into the mist, its middle about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. It is wide in front and a thread at the back. Check a few edges with the brush handle held from the dot.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the forest floor and the path dry to the touch first, or the dabs will smear into them.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start on the ground at the bottom edge of the canvas, tapping Burnt orange and Leaf brown leaves across the front of the forest floor and the path.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap straight down with the tip of the dry brush: big leaf-sized dabs near the bottom edge, smaller ones as you work back toward the mist at the end of the path. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: This is the dark of every leaf, so most of it goes low, in the bottom half. Tap Burnt orange into the bushes left of and right of the path, with Moss green in the big bush right of the path. Up top, only a few loose Burnt orange dabs; their biggest cluster's middle is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Let small bits of the floor and the path show between the dabs on the ground, and keep the treetop dabs broken, with misty sky between them.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the leaf carpet and the bushes cover the lower canvas, their top about 3 in from the top edge. It reads as a warm, dark, patchy autumn ground.

dab-mid-leaves.first: Let the Burnt orange, Moss green and Leaf brown dabs dry first, so the gold sits on top instead of turning muddy.
dab-mid-leaves.start: Start in the treetops at the top edge of the canvas, tapping Golden yellow clusters that hang down from the top edge.
dab-mid-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush, letting each cluster droop downward like hanging leaves. Then build a big full golden bush left of the path, and finish with single scattered dabs on the ground. Wipe off extra paint if dabs turn into blobs.
dab-mid-leaves.inside: Most of the gold goes on the left side, because the sun is at the upper left: the bush left of the path gets it thickest. The ground and the bush right of the path get only scattered dabs.
dab-mid-leaves.leave: Leave plenty of Burnt orange and Leaf brown showing between the gold dabs on the ground, and blue sky gaps between the hanging clusters.
dab-mid-leaves.stop: Golden leaves hang from the top edge and fill the bush left of the path. The ground is still mostly orange and brown, dotted with gold.

dab-sunlit-canopy.first: Let the Golden yellow dabs dry first, so the pale taps stay clean.
dab-sunlit-canopy.start: Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, around the sun, on the Golden yellow treetop leaves.
dab-sunlit-canopy.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the brush on the tops and outer edges of the gold clusters. Work from the upper left corner across the treetops and down the left edge. Keep the brush nearly dry so you get dots, not blobs.
dab-sunlit-canopy.inside: Pale gold goes only where the low sun hits: the treetop leaves on the left side, nearly all of it in the top half. The lowest taps sit on the edges of the clusters that hang over the bush left of the path.
dab-sunlit-canopy.leave: Leave most of each Golden yellow cluster showing under the taps. Don't touch the ground leaves.
dab-sunlit-canopy.stop: The treetops on the left side glow pale near the sun and fade to plain gold toward the middle. The ground has no pale gold yet.

block-in-rock.first: Let the leaf dabs right of the path dry first, so the green doesn't pick up orange.
block-in-rock.start: The mossy rock sits on the leaves just right of the path. Start with one wide, low oval in its middle. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and it's about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
block-in-rock.strokes: Add a smaller rounded piece at each end of the oval, curving like ( ). Then brush over where the pieces meet so they join into one smooth boulder.
block-in-rock.inside: Fill the whole shape with Moss green, edge to edge. It is one flat color for now; the shadow and light come next.
block-in-rock.leave: Leave the leaf dabs all round the rock and the bush above it untouched.
block-in-rock.stop: Stop at a flat, low, dome-topped moss-green boulder with a flat base. A common mistake is making it round like a ball: keep it wide and low.

shade-rock.first: The Moss green rock must be fully dry before you start.
shade-rock.start: Start along the bottom of the mossy rock, where it sits in the leaves.
shade-rock.strokes: Dip only the tip of a dry brush in the paint. Skim lightly along the base of the boulder, then up and over the right side of the mossy rock in short broken passes.
shade-rock.inside: The Deep pine green goes heaviest along the base and on the right side, away from the sun at the upper left. Thinner, broken touches spread across the middle.
shade-rock.leave: Leave the Moss green showing along the top left of the mossy rock, where the sun lands.
shade-rock.stop: Stop when the boulder looks mottled and grayed, dark underneath and on its right side. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush Moss green back over part of it.

light-rock.first: Let the Deep pine green dry completely first.
light-rock.start: Start at the left end of the mossy rock, on its top edge. This light reaches about 3 in from the right edge.
light-rock.strokes: Use only the tip of a dry brush. Skim one light, broken stroke along the top edge of the mossy rock, curving down over the rounded left end. Add a couple of tiny touches on the top, nearer the middle.
light-rock.inside: The Moss light goes only where the sun from the upper left hits: the top edge and the left end.
light-rock.leave: Leave the dark underside, the right side and the mottled middle as they are.
light-rock.stop: Stop at a thin rim of pale light along the top and left end. Beginners often cover the whole top; keep it a narrow line.

pull-birches.first: Let the leaves, the rock and the fir trees dry to the touch so the Birch gray stays clean.
pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of the slim trunk at the left edge of the canvas, down in the leaves. Then do the two big trunks left of the middle of the canvas, and last the two at the right. The inner one of those has its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full width of the 1 inch flat at each trunk's foot, flaring it into the leaves. Then pull straight up to the top edge, easing off so the trunk narrows as it climbs. Lean the two big trunks toward the middle of the canvas as they rise, and keep the other three nearly upright.
pull-birches.inside: Each trunk is one flat, even gray with no shading yet. The feet are the widest part because a birch flares where it meets the ground. Most of the paint goes in the left half of the canvas, where the nearest trunks stand.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves, the path, the rock, the firs and the thin far trunks showing in the gaps between the five trunks. Paint straight over everything, and don't try to paint around it.
pull-birches.stop: Stop when five solid, plain gray trunks stand from the leaves to the top edge, with the two big ones much wider than the rest. A common mistake is making all five the same width.

shade-birches.first: The Birch gray trunks must be fully dry, or the dry brush will drag and smear them.
shade-birches.start: Start at the top edge on the big trunk nearest the left edge, on its shadow side, the side away from the sun. Do the other four trunks the same way.
shade-birches.strokes: Use almost no Birch shadow on a dry brush, and skim it lightly down the length of each trunk from the top edge. Let it break into feathery patches. At the very rim of each foot, touch in a little Moss green where the trunk meets the leaves.
shade-birches.inside: The shadow covers most of each trunk's width, thickest on the side away from the sun because the light comes from the upper left. It thins out low down, so the lower trunks stay mostly pale.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged patches of the Birch gray showing, most of them on the sunny edge and on the lower trunk and feet.
shade-birches.stop: Stop when each trunk reads as a lavender-gray, rounded column spotted with irregular pale patches. Most of the shading is on the three trunks in the left half of the canvas. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

mark-bark.first: Let the Birch shadow dry first, so the Bark dark doesn't turn muddy.
mark-bark.start: Start at the foot of the big trunk nearest the left edge, where the dark is heaviest. Then work up that trunk before moving to the other four.
mark-bark.strokes: For each patch, press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat across the trunk, then lift onto the edge so the patch tapers off to a point. At each foot, press thick at the ground and pull up a short way, thinning as you go.
mark-bark.inside: Put the patches in broken bands across each trunk, with gaps between them. Crowd them toward the base, so most of the dark sits in the bottom half of the canvas. The feet go nearly solid dark, like old bark near the ground.
mark-bark.leave: Leave plenty of the pale trunk and lavender shadow between the patches, especially high up.
mark-bark.stop: Stop when each trunk shows scattered black-brown birch marks that thicken into a dark, rough foot. Don't make the patches even stripes; keep them broken and uneven.

line-bark.first: Everything on the trunks must be dry, or the thin lines will spread and feather.
line-bark.start: Start near the top edge on the big trunk nearest the left edge, on its shadow side between the dark patches.
line-bark.strokes: Load the #2 liner with thinned Bark dark and hold it upright. Make short, light marks across the trunk, starting thick and lifting off. Let them wobble, fork and overlap, and reload often.
line-bark.inside: Set the lines close together in a band down the shadow side of each trunk, linking the patches, and keep most of them on the upper trunks. Do the trunk whose left side is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge the same way. Most of the lines are in the left half of the canvas.
line-bark.leave: Leave the pale sunny edge of each trunk and the white gaps clean.
line-bark.stop: Stop when the shaded part of each trunk looks finely cracked and rough, like real bark, with no broad new dark. If a line skips, add water.

light-bark.first: Let the thin Bark dark lines dry first, because this light skims straight over them.
light-bark.start: Start at the top edge on the big leaning birch whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, then do the other front birch trunks one by one.
light-bark.strokes: Pull the dry brush lightly down each trunk from the top, skimming the edge that faces the sun. Lift before the trunk's foot. Give a few lighter pulls to the thin pale trunks above the mossy rock.
light-bark.inside: The light sits on the sunny edge of each trunk, because the sun is low in the upper left. It goes over the bark patches in places and fades out partway down.
light-bark.leave: Leave the lavender-gray shadow edge, most of the dark bark patches and the dark, mossy trunk feet showing.
light-bark.stop: Stop when each trunk's sunny edge reads bright and broken, near-white with canvas texture showing. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the gray back over part of it.

tap-sunlit-leaves.first: Let the Birch white on the trunks dry before you tap around their feet.
tap-sunlit-leaves.start: Start on the far stretch of the path where it narrows into the mist, and tap your way forward down the path toward you.
tap-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap with just the tip, wiping the brush on a paper towel so you get dots, not blobs. Make the dots small near the mist and bigger as you come forward.
tap-sunlit-leaves.inside: Most of it goes on the right side: along the path and across the ground toward the rock and the right birch. Add smaller clusters at the left edge and around the feet of the two big leaning trunks. This is where the sun lands on the open ground.
tap-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the dark orange and brown leaf dabs showing between your taps, and keep the darkest front row of leaves mostly untouched.
tap-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when a glinting band of pale gold crosses the ground, thickest on the path, with its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge. The painting is finished.

blend-sky.start: Begin at the top of the canvas near its right edge with Blue-violet mist, and lay a band across in side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Misty blue and carry it down from that violet band, across the middle and on to the bottom edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Keep every stroke going side to side, and stroke back over each join several times while both colors are wet so the colors melt into each other.
blend-sky.inside: Rinse, then work Pale gold into the upper left corner of the canvas and in soft patches low on the left side of the canvas, where the sun will glow. Let a few soft violet streaks stay on the right side of the canvas as a far haze.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas should show anywhere. The paint reaches all four edges, about 16 in wide and 12 in tall.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze with no hard lines: gold glowing on the left, misty blue through the middle and bottom, violet haze on the right. If a hard line or a green stripe shows where gold meets blue, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

glow-sun.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the cream will mix into the blue.
glow-sun.start: Place the sun against the left edge of the canvas, its top about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, in the brightest part of the gold glow.
glow-sun.strokes: Load the tip of the brush and paint small circles, starting at the sun's bright middle and moving outward toward its edge.
glow-sun.inside: Keep the cream thickest and brightest at the middle of the sun, and let it thin out into a bumpy edge. The sun runs off the left edge of the canvas, so you paint only part of a circle.
glow-sun.leave: Leave the pale gold glow around the sun and all the rest of the misty sky untouched.
glow-sun.stop: Stop when a small soft sun, about 1 1/4 in wide, glows against the left edge with a bumpy edge. If its edge looks hard, soften it with lighter circles or smudge it with a finger.

pull-far-trunks.first: Let the misty sky and the sun dry to the touch, so the new trunk sits on the haze instead of mixing into it.
pull-far-trunks.start: This step is one trunk. Start at its foot, low in the haze: its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge, and its middle is about 7 1/4 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch flat at the foot and pull straight up, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you rise, so the trunk tapers to a thin line at its tip.
pull-far-trunks.inside: Widest at the foot and thinnest at the top, with one short soft stroke out on the left side of the misty far trunks, about a third of the way down. It stays one pale color, with no light side, because it is far away in the mist.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave all the haze around it untouched, and keep its edges soft so it melts into the mist.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Stop when one faint violet-gray trunk stands in the haze, flared at the foot and tapering to a thin tip, with its short arm part way up.

stamp-pines.first: Let the haze and the far trunk dry first, so the firs stay crisp.
stamp-pines.start: Start at the tip of the tall dark fir in the group. The group's top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, its left side is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge, and it reaches the right edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Stamp only the middle tips of the fan. Tap a narrow tip at the top of each fir, then zigzag down, pressing harder as you go so the tree widens toward its base.
stamp-pines.inside: Use Deep pine green for the big dark firs. Use Misty blue for the paler firs at the left end of the group, between the dark ones, and behind them, because they stand deeper in the mist. Each fir is flat, with no light side yet.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the misty sky showing between the treetops. Keep the misty far trunks clear of fir paint.
stamp-pines.stop: Stop when a band of firs fills that corner, dark ones in front and hazy blue ones behind, with their bases fading softly into the mist. If the marks turn heavy and clumpy, the paint is too thick: thin it a little and spread the fan.

light-pines.first: Let the Deep pine green and Misty blue firs dry, or this paint will turn to mud.
light-pines.start: Start low at the left end of the fir trees. The first patch is about 2 in wide, and its top is about 5 in from the top edge.
light-pines.strokes: Spread the fan and tap lightly with the middle tips. Make short taps in different directions, so the patch looks like needles and not a smear.
light-pines.inside: Most of it goes on the left side of the fir trees, low down, the side facing the sun. Add one narrow upright strip in the gap between the first two dark firs. Then tap a few small dabs low on the tall fir, around the foot of its trunk.
light-pines.leave: Leave the tops and the shaded sides of the firs dark, and keep the hazy blue firs plain.
light-pines.stop: Stop when only a few small patches show, most of them on the left side and in the lower part of the firs. The firs still read as mostly dark.

pull-middle-trunks.first: Let the firs and the far trunk dry first, so these trunks stay clean where they cross the haze.
pull-middle-trunks.start: Start with the smoky-brown trunk, the first of the middle trunks. The middle trunks' left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, and this first trunk is about 8 in tall.
pull-middle-trunks.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat at each trunk's foot and pull straight up, lifting onto the edge so each trunk tapers as it rises.
pull-middle-trunks.inside: The first trunk is Smoky brown, because it is the nearest. Pull the three trunks that follow it toward the middle of the canvas in Blue-violet mist, each one shorter and fainter, because they stand deeper in the mist. Two of them have a soft wider patch at their top. All of them stay plain, with no bark marks.
pull-middle-trunks.leave: Leave clear haze between the trunks, and keep the misty far trunks and the fir trees untouched.
pull-middle-trunks.stop: Stop when four plain trunks stand in a row, the brown one darkest and the violet ones paler, with their feet fading into the low mist.

lay-floor.first: Let the misty sky and the fir trees dry to the touch. The floor goes right over the low haze and touches the bottoms of the fir trees.
lay-floor.start: Start with Golden ochre at the floor's top line, about 7 in from the top edge, where the ground meets the bottoms of the fir trees and the misty far trunks.
lay-floor.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, laying one band under the next all the way down to the bottom edge. Don't tilt the strokes: a slanted band makes the ground look like it's sliding.
lay-floor.inside: Golden ochre bands are the sunlit ground. Pull Leaf brown bands between them like long shadows, and use more Leaf brown as you near the bottom edge. That keeps the back light near the mist and the front dark.
lay-floor.leave: Leave the fir trees and the misty far trunks as they are; the floor stops at their feet. Let streaks of Golden ochre show between the Leaf brown in front.
lay-floor.stop: The floor reaches the left, right and bottom edges and is about 5 in tall. It reads as level gold and brown bands, smooth at the back and streakier in front, with no path yet.

pull-path.first: Let the forest floor dry first, or the Path mauve will mix into the gold and turn muddy.
pull-path.start: Mark one dot where the path vanishes into the mist, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge and below the fir trees. Draw three to five faint chalk lines fanning out from the dot and spreading wider as they come toward you across the floor.
pull-path.strokes: Start at the bottom edge and pull each stroke back along a chalk line toward the dot. Make it wide in front and let it thin to a thread as you reach the dot. If the path's edges run parallel, the path stands up like a wall, so go back to your chalk lines.
pull-path.inside: Most of the paint sits in the front of the path, where it is widest and nearest you. At the far end there is only a thin thread, with one short thin crossing stroke where the track meets the mist.
pull-path.leave: Keep the strokes broken so the Golden ochre floor shows through. Leave a patch of floor in the middle of the path near the bottom edge, like a hump between two ruts.
pull-path.stop: A mauve path runs from the bottom edge back into the mist, its middle about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. It is wide in front and a thread at the back. Check a few edges with the brush handle held from the dot.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the forest floor and the path dry to the touch first, or the dabs will smear into them.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start on the ground at the bottom edge of the canvas, tapping Burnt orange and Leaf brown leaves across the front of the forest floor and the path.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap straight down with the tip of the dry brush: big leaf-sized dabs near the bottom edge, smaller ones as you work back toward the mist at the end of the path. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: This is the dark of every leaf, so most of it goes low, in the bottom half. Tap Burnt orange into the bushes along the path, with Moss green in the big bush that sits against the dark firs. Up top, only a few loose Burnt orange dabs; their biggest cluster's middle is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Let small bits of the floor and the path show between the dabs on the ground, and keep the treetop dabs broken, with misty sky between them.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the leaf carpet and the bushes cover the lower canvas, their top about 3 in from the top edge. It reads as a warm, dark, patchy autumn ground.

dab-mid-leaves.first: Let the Burnt orange, Moss green and Leaf brown dabs dry first, so the gold sits on top instead of turning muddy.
dab-mid-leaves.start: Start in the treetops at the top edge of the canvas, tapping Golden yellow clusters that hang down from the top edge.
dab-mid-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of the dry brush, letting each cluster droop downward like hanging leaves. Then build a big full golden bush left of the path, and finish with single scattered dabs on the ground. Wipe off extra paint if dabs turn into blobs.
dab-mid-leaves.inside: Most of the gold goes on the left side, the side the sunlight comes from: the big round bush nearest the sun gets it thickest. The ground and the bush against the dark firs get only scattered dabs.
dab-mid-leaves.leave: Leave plenty of Burnt orange and Leaf brown showing between the gold dabs on the ground, and blue sky gaps between the hanging clusters.
dab-mid-leaves.stop: Golden leaves hang from the top edge and fill the big round bush. The ground is still mostly orange and brown, dotted with gold.

dab-sunlit-canopy.first: Let the Golden yellow dabs dry first, so the pale taps stay clean.
dab-sunlit-canopy.start: Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, around the sun, on the Golden yellow treetop leaves.
dab-sunlit-canopy.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the brush on the tops and outer edges of the gold clusters. Work from the upper left corner across the treetops and down the left edge. Keep the brush nearly dry so you get dots, not blobs.
dab-sunlit-canopy.inside: Pale gold goes only where the low sun hits: the treetop leaves on the left side, nearly all of it in the top half. The lowest taps sit on the edges of the clusters that hang over the big golden bush.
dab-sunlit-canopy.leave: Leave most of each Golden yellow cluster showing under the taps. Don't touch the ground leaves.
dab-sunlit-canopy.stop: The treetops on the left side glow pale near the sun and fade to plain gold toward the middle. The ground has no pale gold yet.

block-in-rock.first: Let the leaf dabs right of the path dry first, so the green doesn't pick up orange.
block-in-rock.start: The mossy rock sits on the leaves just right of the path. Start with one wide, low oval in its middle. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and it's about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
block-in-rock.strokes: Add a smaller rounded piece at each end of the oval, curving like ( ). Then brush over where the pieces meet so they join into one smooth boulder.
block-in-rock.inside: Fill the whole shape with Moss green, right out to its outline. It is one flat color for now; the shadow and light come next.
block-in-rock.leave: Leave the leaf dabs around the rock, and the bush behind it, untouched.
block-in-rock.stop: Stop at a flat, low, dome-topped moss-green boulder with a flat base. A common mistake is making it round like a ball: keep it wide and low.

shade-rock.first: The Moss green rock must be fully dry before you start.
shade-rock.start: Start along the bottom of the mossy rock, where it sits in the leaves.
shade-rock.strokes: Dip only the tip of a dry brush in the paint. Skim lightly along the base of the boulder, then up and over the right side of the mossy rock in short broken passes.
shade-rock.inside: The Deep pine green goes heaviest along the base and on the right side, the side turned away from the sun. Thinner, broken touches spread across the middle.
shade-rock.leave: Leave the Moss green showing along the top left of the mossy rock, where the sun lands.
shade-rock.stop: Stop when the boulder looks mottled and grayed, dark underneath and on its right side. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush Moss green back over part of it.

light-rock.first: Let the Deep pine green dry completely first.
light-rock.start: Start at the left end of the mossy rock, on the curved rim of its dome. This light reaches about 3 in from the right edge.
light-rock.strokes: Use only the tip of a dry brush. Skim one light, broken stroke along the rim of the dome, curving down over the rounded end of the rock. Add a couple of tiny touches nearer the middle.
light-rock.inside: The Moss light goes only on the rim of the dome and the rounded end, where the sun hits the rock.
light-rock.leave: Leave the Deep pine green and the mottled middle of the rock as they are.
light-rock.stop: Stop at a thin line of pale light along the rim of the dome. Beginners often cover the whole dome; keep it a narrow line.

Lean the two big trunks toward the middle of the canvas as they rise, and keep the other three nearly upright.

pull-birches.stop: Stop when five solid, plain gray trunks run the full height of the canvas from the leaves up, with the two big ones much wider than the rest. A common mistake is making all five the same width.

shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged patches of the Birch gray showing, most of them on the sunny edge and on the lower trunk and feet.
shade-birches.stop: Stop when each trunk reads as a lavender-gray, rounded column spotted with irregular pale patches. Most of the shading is on the three trunks in the left half of the canvas. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

line-bark.start: Start near the top edge on the big trunk nearest the left edge, on its shadow side between the dark patches.
line-bark.strokes: Load the #2 liner with thinned Bark dark and hold it upright. Make short, light marks across the trunk, starting thick and lifting off. Let them wobble, fork and overlap, and reload often.
line-bark.inside: Set the lines close together in a band down the shadow side of each trunk, linking the patches, and keep most of them on the upper trunks. Do the trunk whose left side is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge the same way. Most of the lines are in the left half of the canvas.

line-bark.stop: Stop when the shaded part of each trunk looks finely cracked and rough, like real bark, with no broad new dark. If a line skips, add water.

light-bark.strokes: Pull the dry brush lightly down each trunk from the top, skimming the edge that faces the sun. Lift before the trunk's foot. Give a few lighter pulls to the thin pale trunks above the mossy rock.

tap-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when a glinting band of pale gold crosses the ground, thickest on the path, with its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge. The painting is finished.

Keep every stroke going side to side, and stroke back over each join several times while both colors are wet so the colors melt into each other.

Rinse, then work Pale gold into the upper left corner of the canvas and in soft patches low on the left side of the canvas, where the sun will glow. Let a few soft violet streaks stay on the right side of the canvas as a far haze.
No white canvas should show anywhere. The paint reaches all four edges, about 16 in wide and 12 in tall.

Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze with no hard lines: gold glowing on the left, misty blue through the middle and bottom, violet haze on the right. If a hard line or a green stripe shows where gold meets blue, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

glow-sun.text: Let the sky dry completely, or the cream will mix into the blue.
Place the sun against the left edge of the canvas, its top about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, in the brightest part of the gold glow.
Load the tip of the brush and paint small circles, starting at the sun's bright middle and moving outward toward its edge.
Keep the cream thickest and brightest at the middle of the sun, and let it thin out into a bumpy edge. The sun runs off the left edge of the canvas, so you paint only part of a circle.
Leave the pale gold glow around the sun and all the rest of the misty sky untouched.
Stop when a small soft sun, about 1 1/4 in wide, glows against the left edge with a bumpy edge. If its edge looks hard, soften it with lighter circles or smudge it with a finger.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the misty sky and the sun dry to the touch, so the new trunk sits on the haze instead of mixing into it.
This step is one trunk. Start at its foot, low in the haze: its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge, and its middle is about 7 1/4 in from the left edge.
Press the full width of the 1/4 inch flat at the foot and pull straight up, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you rise, so the trunk tapers to a thin line at its tip.

Widest at the foot and thinnest at the top, with one short soft stroke out on the left side of the misty far trunks, about a third of the way down. It stays one pale color, with no light side, because it is far away in the mist.
Leave all the haze around it untouched, and keep its edges soft so it melts into the mist.
Stop when one faint violet-gray trunk stands in the haze, flared at the foot and tapering to a thin tip, with its short arm part way up.

stamp-pines.text: Let the haze and the far trunk dry first, so the firs stay crisp.
Start at the tip of the tall dark fir in the group. The group's top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, its left side is about 9 1/4 in from the left edge, and it reaches the right edge.
Stamp only the middle tips of the fan. Tap a narrow tip at the top of each fir, then zigzag down, pressing harder as you go so the tree widens toward its base.

Use Deep pine green for the big dark firs. Use Misty blue for the paler firs at the left end of the group, between the dark ones, and behind them, because they stand deeper in the mist. Each fir is flat, with no light side yet.
Leave the misty sky showing between the treetops. Keep the misty far trunks clear of fir paint.

Stop when a band of firs fills that corner, dark ones in front and hazy blue ones behind, with their bases fading softly into the mist. If the marks turn heavy and clumpy, the paint is too thick: thin it a little and spread the fan.

light-pines.text: Let the Deep pine green and Misty blue firs dry, or this paint will turn to mud.
Start low at the left end of the fir trees. The first patch is about 2 in wide, and its top is about 5 in from the top edge.
Spread the fan and tap lightly with the middle tips. Make short taps in different directions, so the patch looks like needles and not a smear.

Most of it goes on the left side of the fir trees, low down, the side facing the sun. Add one narrow upright strip in the gap between the first two dark firs. Then tap a few small dabs low on the tall fir, around the foot of its trunk.
Leave the tops and the shaded sides of the firs dark, and keep the hazy blue firs plain.
Stop when only a few small patches show, most of them on the left side and in the lower part of the firs. The firs still read as mostly dark.

pull-middle-trunks.text: Let the firs and the far trunk dry first, so these trunks stay clean where they cross the haze.
Start with the smoky-brown trunk, the first of the middle trunks.
Press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat at each trunk's foot and pull straight up, lifting onto the edge so each trunk tapers as it rises.

The first trunk is Smoky brown, because it is the nearest. Pull the three trunks that follow it toward the middle of the canvas in Blue-violet mist, each one shorter and fainter, because they stand deeper in the mist. Two of them have a soft wider patch at their top. All of them stay plain, with no bark marks.
Leave clear haze between the trunks, and keep the misty far trunks and the fir trees untouched.
Stop when four plain trunks stand in a row, the brown one darkest and the violet ones paler, with their feet fading into the low mist.

lay-floor.text: Let the misty sky and the fir trees dry to the touch. The floor goes right over the low haze and touches the bottoms of the fir trees.
Start with Golden ochre at the floor's top line, about 7 in from the top edge, where the ground meets the bottoms of the fir trees and the misty far trunks.

Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right, laying one band under the next all the way down to the bottom edge. Don't tilt the strokes: a slanted band makes the ground look like it's sliding.

Golden ochre bands are the sunlit ground. Pull Leaf brown bands between them like long shadows, and use more Leaf brown as you near the bottom edge. That keeps the back light near the mist and the front dark.
Leave the fir trees and the misty far trunks as they are; the floor stops at their feet. Let streaks of Golden ochre show between the Leaf brown in front.
The floor reaches the left, right and bottom edges and is about 5 in tall. It reads as level gold and brown bands, smooth at the back and streakier in front, with no path yet.

pull-path.text: Let the forest floor dry first, or the Path mauve will mix into the gold and turn muddy.

Mark one dot where the path vanishes into the mist, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge and below the fir trees. Draw three to five faint chalk lines fanning out from the dot and spreading wider as they come toward you across the floor.

Start at the bottom edge and pull each stroke back along a chalk line toward the dot. Make it wide in front and let it thin to a thread as you reach the dot. If the path's edges run parallel, the path stands up like a wall, so go back to your chalk lines.
Most of the paint sits in the front of the path, where it is widest and nearest you. At the far end there is only a thin thread, with one short thin crossing stroke where the track meets the mist.
Keep the strokes broken so the Golden ochre floor shows through. Leave a patch of floor in the middle of the path near the bottom edge, like a hump between two ruts.

A mauve path runs from the bottom edge back into the mist, its middle about 9 1/2 in from the left edge. It is wide in front and a thread at the back. Check a few edges with the brush handle held from the dot.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the forest floor and the path dry to the touch first, or the dabs will smear into them.
Start on the ground at the bottom edge of the canvas, tapping Burnt orange and Leaf brown leaves across the front of the forest floor and the path.

Tap straight down with the tip of the dry brush: big leaf-sized dabs near the bottom edge, smaller ones as you work back toward the mist at the end of the path. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

This is the dark of every leaf, so most of it goes low, in the bottom half. Tap Burnt orange into the bushes along the path, with Moss green in the big bush that sits against the dark firs. Up top, only a few loose Burnt orange dabs; their biggest cluster's middle is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.
Let small bits of the floor and the path show between the dabs on the ground, and keep the treetop dabs broken, with misty sky between them.
Stop when the leaf carpet and the bushes cover the lower canvas, their top about 3 in from the top edge. It reads as a warm, dark, patchy autumn ground.

dab-mid-leaves.text: Let the Burnt orange, Moss green and Leaf brown dabs dry first, so the gold sits on top instead of turning muddy.
Start in the treetops at the top edge of the canvas, tapping Golden yellow clusters that hang down from the top edge.

Tap with the tip of the dry brush, letting each cluster droop downward like hanging leaves. Then build a big full golden bush left of the path, and finish with single scattered dabs on the ground. Wipe off extra paint if dabs turn into blobs.
Most of the gold goes on the left side, the side the sunlight comes from: the big round bush nearest the sun gets it thickest. The ground and the bush against the dark firs get only scattered dabs.
Leave plenty of Burnt orange and Leaf brown showing between the gold dabs on the ground, and blue sky gaps between the hanging clusters.
Golden leaves hang from the top edge and fill the big round bush. The ground is still mostly orange and brown, dotted with gold.

dab-sunlit-canopy.text: Let the Golden yellow dabs dry first, so the pale taps stay clean.
Start at the upper left corner of the canvas, around the sun, on the Golden yellow treetop leaves.

Tap lightly with the tip of the brush on the tops and outer edges of the gold clusters. Work from the upper left corner across the treetops and down the left edge. Keep the brush nearly dry so you get dots, not blobs.
Pale gold goes only where the low sun hits: the treetop leaves on the left side, nearly all of it in the top half. The lowest taps sit on the edges of the clusters that hang over the big golden bush.
Leave most of each Golden yellow cluster showing under the taps. Don't touch the ground leaves.
The treetops on the left side glow pale near the sun and fade to plain gold toward the middle. The ground has no pale gold yet.

block-in-rock.text: Let the leaf dabs right of the path dry first, so the green doesn't pick up orange.
The mossy rock sits on the leaves just right of the path. Start with one wide, low oval in its middle. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and it's about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Add a smaller rounded piece at each end of the oval, curving like ( ). Then brush over where the pieces meet so they join into one smooth boulder.
Fill the whole shape with Moss green, right out to its outline. It is one flat color for now; the shadow and light come next.
Leave the leaf dabs around the rock, and the bush behind it, untouched.
Stop at a flat, low, dome-topped moss-green boulder with a flat base. A common mistake is making it round like a ball: keep it wide and low.

shade-rock.text: The Moss green rock must be fully dry before you start.
Start along the bottom of the mossy rock, where it sits in the leaves.
Dip only the tip of a dry brush in the paint. Skim lightly along the base of the boulder, then up and over the right side of the mossy rock in short broken passes.
The Deep pine green goes heaviest along the base and on the right side, the side turned away from the sun. Thinner, broken touches spread across the middle.
Leave the Moss green showing along the top left of the mossy rock, where the sun lands.
Stop when the boulder looks mottled and grayed, dark underneath and on its right side. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush Moss green back over part of it.

light-rock.text: Let the Deep pine green dry completely first.
Start at the left end of the mossy rock, on the curved rim of its dome. This light reaches about 3 in from the right edge.
Use only the tip of a dry brush. Skim one light, broken stroke along the rim of the dome, curving down over the rounded end of the rock. Add a couple of tiny touches nearer the middle.
The Moss light goes only on the rim of the dome and the rounded end, where the sun hits the rock.
Leave the Deep pine green and the mottled middle of the rock as they are.
Stop at a thin line of pale light along the rim of the dome. Beginners often cover the whole dome; keep it a narrow line.

pull-birches.text: Let the leaves, the rock and the fir trees dry to the touch so the Birch gray stays clean.

Start at the foot of the slim trunk at the left edge of the canvas, down in the leaves. Then do the two big trunks left of the middle of the canvas, and last the two at the right. The inner one of those has its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge.

Press the full width of the 1 inch flat at each trunk's foot, flaring it into the leaves. Then pull straight up to the top edge, easing off so the trunk narrows as it climbs. Lean the two big trunks toward the middle of the canvas as they rise, and keep the other three nearly upright.

Each trunk is one flat, even gray with no shading yet. The feet are the widest part because a birch flares where it meets the ground. Most of the paint goes in the left half of the canvas, where the nearest trunks stand.
Leave the leaves, the path, the rock, the firs and the thin far trunks showing in the gaps between the five trunks. Paint straight over everything, and don't try to paint around it.
Stop when five solid, plain gray trunks run the full height of the canvas from the leaves up, with the two big ones much wider than the rest. A common mistake is making all five the same width.

shade-birches.text: The Birch gray trunks must be fully dry, or the dry brush will drag and smear them.
Start at the top edge on the big trunk nearest the left edge, on its shadow side, the side away from the sun. Do the other four trunks the same way.

Use almost no Birch shadow on a dry brush, and skim it lightly down the length of each trunk, starting at its top. Let it break into feathery patches. At the very rim of each foot, touch in a little Moss green where the trunk meets the leaves.
The shadow covers most of each trunk's width, thickest on the side away from the sun because the light comes from the upper left. It thins out low down, so the lower trunks stay mostly pale.
Leave ragged patches of the Birch gray showing, most of them on the sunny edge and on the lower trunk and feet.

Stop when each trunk reads as a lavender-gray, rounded column spotted with irregular pale patches. Most of the shading is on the three trunks in the left half of the canvas. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

mark-bark.text: Let the Birch shadow dry first, so the Bark dark doesn't turn muddy.
Start at the foot of the big trunk nearest the left edge, where the dark is heaviest. Then work up that trunk before moving to the other four.

For each patch, press the full width of the 1/2 inch flat across the trunk, then lift onto the edge so the patch tapers off to a point. At each foot, press thick at the ground and pull up a short way, thinning as you go.

Put the patches in broken bands across each trunk, with gaps between them. Crowd them toward the base, so most of the dark sits in the bottom half of the canvas. The feet go nearly solid dark, like old bark near the ground.
Leave plenty of the pale trunk and lavender shadow between the patches, especially high up.
Stop when each trunk shows scattered black-brown birch marks that thicken into a dark, rough foot. Don't make the patches even stripes; keep them broken and uneven.

line-bark.text: Everything on the trunks must be dry, or the thin lines will spread and feather.
Start near the top edge on the big trunk nearest the left edge, on its shadow side between the dark patches.
Load the #2 liner with thinned Bark dark and hold it upright. Make short, light marks across the trunk, starting thick and lifting off. Let them wobble, fork and overlap, and reload often.

Set the lines close together in a band down the shadow side of each trunk, linking the patches, and keep most of them on the upper trunks. Do the trunk whose left side is about 13 1/2 in from the left edge the same way. Most of the lines are in the left half of the canvas.
Leave the pale sunny edge of each trunk and the white gaps clean.
Stop when the shaded part of each trunk looks finely cracked and rough, like real bark, with no broad new dark. If a line skips, add water.

light-bark.text: Let the thin Bark dark lines dry first, because this light skims straight over them.
Start at the top edge on the big leaning birch whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, then do the other front birch trunks one by one.
Pull the dry brush lightly down each trunk from the top, skimming the edge that faces the sun. Lift before the trunk's foot. Give a few lighter pulls to the thin pale trunks above the mossy rock.
The light sits on the sunny edge of each trunk, because the sun is low in the upper left. It goes over the bark patches in places and fades out partway down.
Leave the lavender-gray shadow edge, most of the dark bark patches and the dark, mossy trunk feet showing.
Stop when each trunk's sunny edge reads bright and broken, near-white with canvas texture showing. If it went on solid, let it dry and dry-brush the gray back over part of it.

tap-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the Birch white on the trunks dry before you tap around their feet.
Start on the far stretch of the path where it narrows into the mist, and tap your way forward down the path toward you.
Tap with just the tip, wiping the brush on a paper towel so you get dots, not blobs. Make the dots small near the mist and bigger as you come forward.

Most of it goes on the right side: along the path and across the ground toward the rock and the right birch. Add smaller clusters at the left edge and around the feet of the two big leaning trunks. This is where the sun lands on the open ground.
Leave the dark orange and brown leaf dabs showing between your taps, and keep the darkest front row of leaves mostly untouched.
Stop when a glinting band of pale gold crosses the ground, thickest on the path, with its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge. The painting is finished.
