blend-window-sky.start: Begin in the canvas's top left corner, at the top edge, with Pale sky blue. This is the sky through the window. Its top is at the top edge and its left side is at the left edge.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the sky, working down from the top edge. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white and paint the lower part of the sky. Then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The sky is bluest at the top edge and turns paler low down, toward the window's bottom, like a real sky near the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave all the rest of the canvas bare white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the sky is a smooth patch about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall: blue at the top edge, fading softly paler lower down, with no hard line where the two colours meet.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky dry fully first, or the dabs will smear into it.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start the leaf clumps with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side about 1 in from the left edge. Tap the first clumps there, over the sky.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Hold the old stiff brush upright and tap with its tip. Don't drag it. Tap more in one spot to make a clump more solid, and tap more lightly at a clump's edges so it stays ragged and leafy.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Most of the Leaf green goes in the top half of the leaves, in clumps across the sky. Let one ragged arm of leaves hang down the far side of the window.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave pale sky showing in gaps between the clumps, and in the rounded holes low in the window.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when loose dark green clumps cover most of the sky, with pale sky peeking through. Wipe the brush if the dabs come out as blobs.

dab-sunlit-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green dabs dry first, so the new taps sit on top instead of mixing in.
dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Begin on the highest Leaf green clumps, with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the old stiff brush, using smaller taps than before. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel first, so each tap leaves dots rather than a solid patch.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Put the Sunny leaf green on the tops of the clumps, where the daylight from the window falls. Keep the undersides of the clumps dark.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the Leaf green showing on the underside of each clump, and leave the pale sky gaps open.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when every clump has a bright, dotted top over its darker green, against the pale sky. If a patch goes too solid, tap a little Leaf green back over it.

blend-wall.first: Let the sky and the leaves dry before you paint up against them.
blend-wall.start: Start with Deep wall blue at the top edge of the canvas, right next to the leaves outside the window.
blend-wall.strokes: Lay an even, creamy coat with side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and paint it beside the deep blue, out to the right edge. Then stroke back and forth over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-wall.inside: The deep blue stays nearest the window and Wall blue fills the rest, because the wall is darkest by the window. Run it straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the leaves and the scrap of sky in the canvas's upper left corner showing, and paint carefully around them.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the whole canvas outside that corner is blue, from the top edge to the bottom edge. It should be deeper by the window and softer toward the right edge, with no hard line where the blues meet. If a line shows, add more Wall blue at the join and blend again.

block-in-frame.first: The blue wall must be dry to the touch, or the white will turn pale blue.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide upright post, between the window and the blue wall. Make it one long rectangle from the top edge straight down to the bottom edge. Its white reaches about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-frame.strokes: Pull long, straight strokes down the post. Then add the other pieces: a thin crossbar across the window near the top, and the wide bottom ledge, a band that slants from the left edge into the post. Brush the joins smooth, because the frame is plain painted wood.
block-in-frame.inside: Make it all one flat cream white with no shading. The shadows come in the next step.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two window panes. Leave the blue wall showing in the corner the ledge cuts off at the canvas's lower left, and beyond the post.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when you have a crisp cream post from top edge to bottom edge, a thin crossbar and a slanting ledge. Beginners often get a wobbly edge where the post meets the wall, so keep that edge straight.

shade-frame.first: Let the Warm white frame dry completely, or the lavender will smear into it.
shade-frame.start: Start on the post at the top edge, along the side of the post that meets the blue wall. At the frame's middle, this band runs from about 3 in to 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay that band as one long, straight piece from the top edge to the bottom edge. Then add the smaller pieces: a thin line along the shadowed edge of the crossbar, a band across the ledge's front face, and a softer band down the post where it runs on past the ledge.
shade-frame.inside: The daylight comes through the window at the upper left. So the lavender goes only on the faces turned away from it: the post's wall side, the crossbar's shadowed edge and the ledge's front face.
shade-frame.leave: Leave cream white showing on the post's window-facing side, on the top of the ledge and the crossbar, and as a lit streak on the post where it runs past the ledge.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when the frame reads as solid wood: cream where the light hits, lavender bands where it turns away. Beginners often cover the whole post, so keep the cream showing.

block-in-sill.first: Let the blue wall and the white window frame dry first, so the brown doesn't drag into them along the sill's back edge.
block-in-sill.start: Start at the left edge, just under the white window frame. The sill's top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
block-in-sill.strokes: First lay one long slanted rectangle for the sill's top. Pull the flat brush across from the left edge to the right edge, with the back edge sloping gently down toward the right edge. Then lay a strip along the bottom edge for the sill's front edge.
block-in-sill.inside: Make the whole sill one flat warm brown, right through where the blanket will lie. Its shading and sunlight come in the next steps.
block-in-sill.leave: Leave the blue wall and the white window frame clean above the sill's back edge. Let a faint line show where the top meets the front edge.
block-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat brown sill covers the bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, about 16 in wide, with a straight back edge. A wobbly back edge is the usual slip. Fix it now while the paint is wet.

shade-sill.first: Let the flat Warm wood brown sill dry completely. Dry brush over wet paint just smears.
shade-sill.start: Start at the right edge on the sill's top. Work back toward the left edge along the grain.
shade-sill.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush and wipe off the excess. Skim lightly along the length of the sill in long strokes, building up over several light passes. Then skim broken strokes along the front edge, which reaches the bottom edge.
shade-sill.inside: The paint sits over most of the sill's top and its front edge. That darkens the wood away from the window's light, which comes from the upper left.
shade-sill.leave: Leave the shape of the coming sunny patch at the left, below the window, untouched as flat brown. Also leave streaks of the flat brown between your strokes.
shade-sill.stop: Stop when the sill reads as streaky, darker wood from the left edge to the right edge. A pale wedge shape should be waiting at the left. If it went on solid, let it dry and skim the base brown back over part of it.

light-sill.first: Let the Warm wood brown dry-brushing dry first, so the peach stays clean.
light-sill.start: Start with the biggest piece. It is a long slanted wedge on the sill's top at the left, and its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge.
light-sill.strokes: Fill the wedge first, pulling along its length and tapering it to a point toward the window's far side. Next lay a narrower bar nearer the white window frame, its left side about 2 in from the left edge. Then lay a small piece at the left edge.
light-sill.inside: This is the sunlight from the window falling on the sill. The brown bands between the pieces are the frame's shadow.
light-sill.leave: Leave two brown bands between the three peach pieces. Keep the dark front edge and the brown sill around the patch.
light-sill.stop: Stop when a peach patch sits at the left edge, about 6 1/2 in wide, crossed by two brown bands. Its tip should break into a few dabs.

block-in-blanket.first: Let the sill's Sunny peach patch and the blue wall dry to the touch, because the blanket goes on over both.
block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long, low oval for the blanket's rolled bed. Its left end is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, it runs off the right edge of the canvas, and its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes along the oval. Then add a curved roll along its front and a folded front edge in ( ) shaped pieces, rounding the left end.
block-in-blanket.inside: Lay one flat coat of Golden yellow over the whole shape, with no shading yet. The cat will lie on it later.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave the window frame and the sill's sunny patch showing where the blanket's left end meets them. Leave the blue wall above the roll and the front of the sill below.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when it is one smooth, solid golden shape, about 15 in wide, with no wall or sill showing through it.

shade-blanket.first: The Golden yellow must be fully dry, or the dark loops will smear into it.
shade-blanket.start: Start along the inside of the roll at the back of the blanket, where it curves down into the hollow of the bed.
shade-blanket.strokes: Touch the tip of the brush down, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Set these commas in rows that follow the roll. On the front fold, lean them in pairs like little Vs, the way knit stitches sit.
shade-blanket.inside: Pack the Dark ochre loops thickest under the roll, along the fold and on the lower front, where the blanket turns away from the light. Scatter a few loose patches across the hollow.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave gold showing between the loops, most of all along the top of the roll and the top of the front fold.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket reads as a rolled knit bed with a sunken middle, darkest in its folds. If you get a blob instead of a teardrop, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.first: The Dark ochre loops must be dry first.
light-blanket.start: Start on the blanket's rounded left end, the end facing the window, about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
light-blanket.strokes: Use the same press and lift: touch the tip down, press, pull and lift to a point. Make these commas smaller and fewer than the dark ones. Curve them around the left end, then dot them along the tops of the roll and the front fold.
light-blanket.inside: The Pale yellow goes where the window light from the upper left hits: thickest down the rounded left end, then thinly across the hollow and the tops of the folds. Most of it sits in the left half of the blanket.
light-blanket.leave: Leave the Dark ochre loops showing in the folds and under the roll, and leave most of the gold untouched.
light-blanket.stop: Stop when the left end and the tops glow a little lighter and the knit looks rounded and lit from the window. Don't cover the whole blanket.

block-in-cat.first: The blanket's pale yellow knit loops must be dry, because the gray goes straight over them.
block-in-cat.start: Start with one big oval for the curled body on the blanket. The sleeping tabby cat's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and its back end reaches the right edge of the canvas.
block-in-cat.strokes: Add a round head at the end nearest the window, one ear triangle pointing toward the window frame and one standing up from the top of the head. Pull each stroke around the curve of the back.
block-in-cat.inside: Fill the whole cat with one flat Mid gray, with no darker or lighter spots, since all the shading comes later.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket's front roll and fold showing all along the cat's lower edge, and the blue wall above its back.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop at one smooth gray shape about 15 in wide. Soften where the pieces meet, and give thin spots a second pass so no yellow peeks through.

shade-cat.first: Let the Mid gray dry fully, or the Dark gray will smear into it.
shade-cat.start: Start at the top of the back where it meets the head. Curve one wide stroke down through the deep fold behind the head, all the way to the blanket.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend every stroke with the body. Sweep the tail's curl along the bottom of the body, from the front paws to the back end. Then wrap curved strokes around the back end, where the paint reaches the right edge of the canvas.
shade-cat.inside: The daylight comes from the window, so the dark goes on the far, rounded back end, the tail and the fold. Add a few small curved dabs over the back to suggest fur.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the head, the top of the back, the two paw shapes and the patch on the cat's side in Mid gray.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the fold, the tail and the back end read clearly darker. A common mistake is painting over the paws; keep them gray.

paint-white-patches.first: Let the Dark gray dry first, so the white stays clean.
paint-white-patches.start: Start on the muzzle. Pull a white stroke down from the face to the chin, the part whose top is about 5 in from the top edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: Curve the strokes around each of the two front paws like small round mounds tucked against the chin. For the side patch, pull short curved strokes toward the back, letting their tips make a ragged, pointed edge.
paint-white-patches.inside: The white goes on the muzzle and chin, the two paws, and one patch in the middle of the cat's side. That patch's left side is about 8 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 3/4 in wide.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave a thin gray line between the two paws, and keep the dark tail curl showing below the side patch.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop when the white is solid. If gray shows through, let it dry and go over it once more.

paint-stripes.first: Let the Warm white patches and the Dark gray shading dry to the touch. A wet stripe dragged into wet white turns gray.
paint-stripes.start: Start on the top of the cat's back, where the body is highest. Work across the body first, then do the tail, then the top of the head and the cheeks.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush at the spine. Then pull down around the curve of the body toward the blanket, turning onto the edge and pressing lighter so each stripe tapers to a point. On the tail, pull short bands across it. On the head, pull short tapered marks from the top of the head down the cheeks.
paint-stripes.inside: The stripes wrap around the round body like curved rings, not straight bars. That curve is what makes the body look full. The middle of all the striping is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge, so most of it lands on the big body and the tail.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave gray showing between the stripes, about as wide as the stripes. Keep the white muzzle, chest patch and paws clean, and leave the ears gray inside.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when the body, tail, head and cheeks all carry curving charcoal stripes over the gray. A likely mistake is pressing hard all the way through, which gives blunt even bars with no taper.

paint-ears.first: Let the Charcoal stripes on the head dry first, so the pink doesn't smear into them.
paint-ears.start: Start in the far ear, whose middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge. Then paint the ear nearest the window, whose middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ears.strokes: Touch the #4 round down near the base of the ear and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear's tip and lift, so the stroke ends on a point inside the tip. Use two or three of these strokes side by side to fill each ear.
paint-ears.inside: The pink fills the middle of each ear triangle. It is widest at the base and narrows into the tip, the way the inside of a real ear does.
paint-ears.leave: Leave a thin gray rim along both edges of each ear. Leave all the head and body stripes untouched.
paint-ears.stop: Stop when both ears are pink inside, each with a gray rim, and nothing else has changed. If a stroke turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

flick-fur.first: Let the Charcoal stripes and the pink in the ears dry fully first, so the flicks don't drag the dark into the gray.
flick-fur.start: Start on the top of the cat's back, where the big curled body rounds over, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
flick-fur.strokes: Use very little paint. Set each flick down in the fur and lift off quickly as you go, so it thins at the tip. Follow the way the fur lies: around the curve of the body, along the tail, and over the top of the head and the cheeks.
flick-fur.inside: Most of the flicks go on the right half of the cat's fur, across the big body and the tail. Cross the edges of the stripes so they look soft and furry.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the middle of each Charcoal stripe dark, and keep the white muzzle, chest patch, paws and pink ears clean.
flick-fur.stop: The whole coat reads lighter and furry, with the darker gray and stripes showing between the flicks. The face stays blank.

paint-nose.first: Let the white muzzle and the pink inside the ears dry first.
paint-nose.start: Start with the nose on the white muzzle, just under where the sleeping eyes will go. Its top is about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and it's about 3/4 in wide.
paint-nose.strokes: Touch the tip down at one top corner of the nose, press, then pull toward the point and lift. Repeat from the other top corner so the two marks meet in a small triangle pointing down toward the paws.
paint-nose.inside: The nose is solid pink at the tip of the muzzle, where the face presses toward the paws. Then add a few small press-and-lift touches inside each ear, along the edge of the pink where it meets the gray rim, to deepen it.
paint-nose.leave: Keep white muzzle all round the nose. Leave each ear's gray rim and the lighter pink in its middle showing.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a small, neat pink triangle sits on the white muzzle and each ear has a deeper pink edge inside. There are no eyes, mouth or whiskers yet. If the nose comes out as a round blob, you used too much paint: use less and lift faster.

line-eyes.first: Let the pink nose dry first, or the dark lines will spread into it.
line-eyes.start: Start with the upper closed eye, a curve on the gray face just above the white muzzle, under the upright ear.
line-eyes.strokes: Hold the liner upright. Pull each eye as one smile-shaped curve with its ends dipping, a little thicker at the end nearer the nose and lighter as you go. Then pull the lower eye across the cheek nearer the window. Add a short mouth line under the nose, a thin dark edge along the outer rim of each ear, and three short lines on the gray cheek beside the muzzle.
line-eyes.inside: The lines sit where the eyelids close. The lower eye crosses the middle of the sleeping face about 6 in from the top edge. Add a small dark tuck where the chin meets the paw.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the white muzzle, the pink nose and the pink inside the ears clear.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the cat reads as fast asleep, with closed eyes, a tiny mouth and crisp ear edges. If a line skips, add water.

line-whiskers.first: Let the Charcoal lines and the pink nose dry first, or the white will turn gray.
line-whiskers.start: Start each whisker at the edge of the white muzzle, beside the pink nose.
line-whiskers.strokes: Hold the liner upright and pull each whisker outward in one long, gently curved line. Press a little at the start and lighten so it tapers to nothing. Pull three or four down and out across the cheek toward the window, then three or four up and out over the dark fold toward the white chest patch.
line-whiskers.inside: Most of what you add sits in the bottom half of the sleeping face. The whiskers nearer the window reach to about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, ending over the white paws.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave fur showing between the whiskers, and keep them off the closed eyes and the nose.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop when fine white whiskers fan out from both sides of the muzzle, a few each way. The painting is finished. If the lines break up, add water and reload often.

blend-window-sky.start: Begin in the canvas's top left corner, at the top edge, with Pale sky blue. This is the sky through the window. Its top is at the top edge and its left side is at the left edge.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the sky, working down from the top edge. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white and paint the lower part of the sky. Then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The sky is bluest at the top edge and turns paler low down, toward the window's bottom, like a real sky near the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave all the rest of the canvas bare white.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the sky is a smooth patch about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall: blue at the top edge, fading softly paler lower down, with no hard line where the two colours meet.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky dry fully first, or the dabs will smear into it.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start the leaf clumps with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side about 1 in from the left edge. Tap the first clumps there, over the sky.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Hold the old stiff brush upright and tap with its tip. Don't drag it. Tap more in one spot to make a clump more solid, and tap more lightly at a clump's edges so it stays ragged and leafy.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Most of the Leaf green goes in the top half of the leaves, in clumps across the sky. Let one ragged arm of leaves hang down the far side of the window.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave pale sky showing in gaps between the clumps, and in the rounded holes low in the window.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when loose dark green clumps cover most of the sky, with pale sky peeking through. Wipe the brush if the dabs come out as blobs.

dab-sunlit-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green dabs dry first, so the new taps sit on top instead of mixing in.
dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Begin on the highest Leaf green clumps, with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap lightly with the tip of the old stiff brush, using smaller taps than before. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel first, so each tap leaves dots rather than a solid patch.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Put the Sunny leaf green on the tops of the clumps, where the daylight from the window falls. Keep the undersides of the clumps dark.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the Leaf green showing on the underside of each clump, and leave the pale sky gaps open.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when every clump has a bright, dotted top over its darker green, against the pale sky. If a patch goes too solid, tap a little Leaf green back over it.

blend-wall.first: Let the sky and the leaves dry before you paint up against them.
blend-wall.start: Start with Deep wall blue at the top edge of the canvas, right next to the leaves outside the window.
blend-wall.strokes: Lay an even, creamy coat with side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it on across to the right edge. Then stroke back and forth over the join several times while both are wet.
blend-wall.inside: The deep blue stays nearest the window and Wall blue fills the rest, because the wall is darkest by the window. Run it straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the leaves and the scrap of sky in the canvas's upper left corner showing, and paint carefully around them.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when the whole canvas outside that corner is blue, from the top edge to the bottom edge. It should be deeper by the window and softer toward the right edge, with no hard line where the blues meet. If a line shows, add more Wall blue at the join and blend again.

block-in-frame.first: The blue wall must be dry to the touch, or the white will turn pale blue.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide upright post, between the window and the blue wall. Make it one long rectangle from the top edge straight down to the bottom edge.
block-in-frame.strokes: Pull long, straight strokes down the post. Then add the other pieces: a thin crossbar across the window near the top, and the wide bottom ledge, a band that slants from the left edge into the post. Brush the joins smooth, because the frame is plain painted wood.
block-in-frame.inside: Make it all one flat cream white with no shading. The shadows come in the next step.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two window panes. Leave the blue wall showing in the corner the ledge cuts off at the canvas's lower left, and beyond the post.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when you have a crisp cream post from top edge to bottom edge, a thin crossbar and a slanting ledge. Beginners often get a wobbly edge where the post meets the wall, so keep that edge straight.

shade-frame.first: Let the Warm white frame dry completely, or the lavender will smear into it.
shade-frame.start: Start on the post at the top edge, along the side of the post that meets the blue wall. The band begins about 3 in from the left edge.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay that band as one long, straight piece from the top edge to the bottom edge. Then add the smaller pieces: a thin line along the shadowed edge of the crossbar, a band across the ledge's front face, and a softer band down the post where it runs on past the ledge.
shade-frame.inside: The daylight comes through the window at the upper left. So the lavender goes only on the faces turned away from it: the post's wall side, the crossbar's shadowed edge and the ledge's front face.
shade-frame.leave: Leave cream white showing on the post's window-facing side, on the top of the ledge and the crossbar, and as a lit streak on the post where it runs past the ledge.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when the frame reads as solid wood: cream where the light hits, lavender bands where it turns away. Beginners often cover the whole post, so keep the cream showing.

block-in-sill.first: Let the blue wall and the white window frame dry first, so the brown doesn't drag into them along the sill's back edge.
block-in-sill.start: Start at the left edge, just under the white window frame, where the sill's back edge meets it.
block-in-sill.strokes: First lay one long slanted rectangle for the sill's top. Pull the flat brush across from the left edge to the right edge, with the back edge sloping gently down toward the right edge. Then lay a strip along the bottom edge for the sill's front edge.
block-in-sill.inside: Make the whole sill one flat warm brown, right through where the blanket will lie. Its shading and sunlight come in the next steps.
block-in-sill.leave: Leave the blue wall and the white window frame clean above the sill's back edge. Let a faint line show where the top meets the front edge.
block-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat brown sill covers the bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, about 16 in wide, with a straight back edge. A wobbly back edge is the usual slip. Fix it now while the paint is wet.

shade-sill.first: Let the flat Warm wood brown sill dry completely. Dry brush over wet paint just smears.
shade-sill.start: Start at the right edge on the sill's top. Work back toward the left edge along the grain.
shade-sill.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush and wipe off the excess. Skim lightly along the length of the sill in long strokes, building up over several light passes. Then skim broken strokes along the front edge, which reaches the bottom edge.
shade-sill.inside: The paint sits over most of the sill's top and its front edge. That darkens the wood away from the window's light, which comes from the upper left.
shade-sill.leave: Leave the shape of the coming sunny patch at the left, below the window, untouched as flat brown. Also leave streaks of the flat brown between your strokes.
shade-sill.stop: Stop when the sill reads as streaky, darker wood from the left edge to the right edge. A pale wedge shape should be waiting at the left. If it went on solid, let it dry and skim the base brown back over part of it.

light-sill.first: Let the Warm wood brown dry-brushing dry first, so the peach stays clean.
light-sill.start: Start with the biggest piece. It is a long slanted wedge on the sill's top at the left, and its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge.
light-sill.strokes: Fill the wedge first, pulling along its length and tapering it to a point toward the window's far side. Next lay a narrower bar between the wedge and the window, with a brown band separating the two. Then lay a small piece at the left edge.
light-sill.inside: This is the sunlight from the window falling on the sill. The brown bands between the pieces are the frame's shadow.
light-sill.leave: Leave two brown bands between the three peach pieces. Keep the dark front edge and the brown sill around the patch.
light-sill.stop: Stop when a peach patch sits at the left edge, about 6 1/2 in wide, crossed by two brown bands. Its tip should break into a few dabs.

block-in-blanket.first: Let the sill's Sunny peach patch and the blue wall dry to the touch, because the blanket goes on over both.
block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long, low oval for the blanket's rolled bed. Its left end is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, it runs off the right edge of the canvas, and its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes along the oval. Then add a curved roll along its front and a folded front edge in ( ) shaped pieces, rounding the end nearest the window.
block-in-blanket.inside: Lay one flat coat of Golden yellow over the whole shape, with no shading yet. The cat will lie on it later.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave the window frame and the sill's sunny patch showing where the blanket's rounded end meets them. Keep the blue wall clean along the blanket's top edge, and keep the front of the wooden windowsill clean along its bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when it is one smooth, solid golden shape, about 15 in wide, with no wall or sill showing through it.

shade-blanket.first: The Golden yellow must be fully dry, or the dark loops will smear into it.
shade-blanket.start: Start along the inside of the roll at the back of the blanket, where it curves down into the hollow of the bed.
shade-blanket.strokes: Touch the tip of the brush down, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Set these commas in rows that follow the roll. On the front fold, lean them in pairs like little Vs, the way knit stitches sit.
shade-blanket.inside: Pack the Dark ochre loops thickest under the roll, along the fold and on the lower front, where the blanket turns away from the light. Scatter a few loose patches across the hollow.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave gold showing between the loops, most of all along the top of the roll and the top of the front fold.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the blanket reads as a rolled knit bed with a sunken middle, darkest in its folds. If you get a blob instead of a teardrop, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.first: The Dark ochre loops must be dry first.
light-blanket.start: Start on the blanket's rounded end, the one nearest the window.
light-blanket.strokes: Use the same press and lift: touch the tip down, press, pull and lift to a point. Make these commas smaller and fewer than the dark ones. Curve them around the rounded end, then dot them along the tops of the roll and the front fold.
light-blanket.inside: The Pale yellow goes where the window light from the upper left hits: thickest down the rounded end, then thinly across the hollow and the tops of the folds. Most of it sits in the left half of the blanket.
light-blanket.leave: Leave the Dark ochre loops showing in the folds and under the roll, and leave most of the gold untouched.
light-blanket.stop: Stop when the rounded end and the tops glow a little lighter and the knit looks rounded and lit from the window. Don't cover the whole blanket.

block-in-cat.first: The blanket's pale yellow knit loops must be dry, because the gray goes straight over them.
block-in-cat.start: Start with one big oval for the curled body on the blanket. The sleeping tabby cat's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and its back end reaches the right edge of the canvas.
block-in-cat.strokes: Add a round head at the end nearest the window, one ear triangle pointing toward the window frame and one standing up from the top of the head. Pull each stroke around the curve of the back.
block-in-cat.inside: Fill the whole cat with one flat Mid gray, with no darker or lighter spots, since all the shading comes later.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket's front roll and fold showing all along the cat's lower edge, and keep the blue wall showing around the curve of the back.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop at one smooth gray shape about 15 in wide. Soften where the pieces meet, and give thin spots a second pass so no yellow peeks through.

shade-cat.first: Let the Mid gray dry fully, or the Dark gray will smear into it.
shade-cat.start: Start at the top of the back where it meets the head. Curve one wide stroke down through the deep fold behind the head, all the way to the blanket.
shade-cat.strokes: Bend every stroke with the body. Sweep the tail's curl along the bottom of the body, from the front paws to the back end. Then wrap curved strokes around the back end, where the paint reaches the right edge of the canvas.
shade-cat.inside: The daylight comes from the window, so the dark goes on the far, rounded back end, the tail and the fold. Add a few small curved dabs over the back to suggest fur.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the head, the top of the back, the two paw shapes and the patch on the cat's side in Mid gray.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the fold, the tail and the back end read clearly darker. A common mistake is painting over the paws; keep them gray.

paint-white-patches.first: Let the Dark gray dry first, so the white stays clean.
paint-white-patches.start: Start on the muzzle. Pull a white stroke down from the face to the chin, the part whose top is about 5 in from the top edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: Curve the strokes around each of the two front paws like small round mounds tucked against the chin. For the side patch, pull short curved strokes toward the back, letting their tips make a ragged, pointed edge.
paint-white-patches.inside: The white goes on the muzzle and chin, the two paws, and one patch in the middle of the cat's side. That patch's left side is about 8 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 3/4 in wide.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave a thin gray line between the two paws, and keep the dark tail curl showing where it meets the white patch on the side.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop when the white is solid. If gray shows through, let it dry and go over it once more.

paint-stripes.first: Let the Warm white patches and the Dark gray shading dry to the touch. A wet stripe dragged into wet white turns gray.
paint-stripes.start: Start on the top of the cat's back, where the body is highest. Work across the body first, then do the tail, then the top of the head and the cheeks.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush at the spine. Then pull down around the curve of the body toward the blanket, turning onto the edge and pressing lighter so each stripe tapers to a point. On the tail, pull short bands across it. On the head, pull short tapered marks from the top of the head down the cheeks.
paint-stripes.inside: The stripes wrap around the round body like curved rings, not straight bars. That curve is what makes the body look full. The middle of all the striping is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge, so most of it lands on the big body and the tail.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave gray showing between the stripes, about as wide as the stripes. Keep the white muzzle, chest patch and paws clean, and leave the ears gray inside.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when the body, tail, head and cheeks all carry curving charcoal stripes over the gray. A likely mistake is pressing hard all the way through, which gives blunt even bars with no taper.

paint-ears.first: Let the Charcoal stripes on the head dry first, so the pink doesn't smear into them.
paint-ears.start: Start in the far ear, whose middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge. Then paint the other ear the same way.
paint-ears.strokes: Touch the #4 round down near the base of the ear and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear's point and lift, so the stroke ends sharp at the point. Use two or three of these strokes side by side to fill each ear.
paint-ears.inside: The pink fills the middle of each ear triangle. It is widest at the base and narrows toward the point, the way a real cat's ear looks.
paint-ears.leave: Leave a thin gray rim along both edges of each ear. Leave all the head and body stripes untouched.
paint-ears.stop: Stop when both ears are pink inside, each with a gray rim, and nothing else has changed. If a stroke turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

flick-fur.first: Let the Charcoal stripes and the pink in the ears dry fully first, so the flicks don't drag the dark into the gray.
flick-fur.start: Start on the top of the cat's back, where the big curled body rounds over, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.
flick-fur.strokes: Use very little paint. Set each flick down in the fur and lift off quickly as you go, so it thins at the tip. Follow the way the fur lies: around the curve of the body, along the tail, and over the top of the head and the cheeks.
flick-fur.inside: Most of the flicks go on the right half of the cat's fur, across the big body and the tail. Cross the edges of the stripes so they look soft and furry.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the middle of each Charcoal stripe dark, and keep the white muzzle, chest patch, paws and pink ears clean.
flick-fur.stop: The whole coat reads lighter and furry, with the darker gray and stripes showing between the flicks. The face stays blank.

paint-nose.first: Let the white muzzle and the pink inside the ears dry first.
paint-nose.start: Start with the nose on the white muzzle, just under where the sleeping eyes will go. Its top is about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and it's about 3/4 in wide.
paint-nose.strokes: Touch the tip down at one top corner of the nose, press, then pull toward the point and lift. Repeat from the other top corner so the two marks meet in a small triangle pointing down toward the paws.
paint-nose.inside: The nose is solid pink at the tip of the muzzle, where the face presses toward the paws. Then deepen the pink of both ears with a few small press-and-lift touches along the edge where the pink meets the gray rim.
paint-nose.leave: Keep white muzzle all round the nose. Leave each ear's gray rim and the lighter pink in its middle showing.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a small, neat pink triangle sits on the white muzzle and each ear has a deeper pink edge. There are no eyes, mouth or whiskers yet. If the nose comes out as a round blob, you used too much paint: use less and lift faster.

line-eyes.first: Let the pink nose dry first, or the dark lines will spread into it.
line-eyes.start: Start with the upper closed eye, a curve on the gray face just above the white muzzle, under the upright ear.
line-eyes.strokes: Hold the liner upright. Pull each eye as one smile-shaped curve with its ends dipping, a little thicker at the end nearer the nose and lighter as you go. Then pull the lower eye across the cheek nearer the window. Add a short mouth line under the nose, a thin dark edge along the outer rim of each ear, and three short lines on the gray cheek where the whiskers will start.
line-eyes.inside: The lines sit where the eyelids close. Add a small dark tuck where the chin meets the paw.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the white muzzle, the pink nose and the pink inside the ears clear.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the cat reads as fast asleep, with closed eyes, a tiny mouth and crisp ear edges. If a line skips, add water.

line-whiskers.first: Let the Charcoal lines and the pink nose dry first, or the white will turn gray.
line-whiskers.start: Start each whisker at the edge of the white muzzle.
line-whiskers.strokes: Hold the liner upright and pull each whisker outward in one long, gently curved line. Press a little at the start and lighten so it tapers to nothing. Pull three or four down and out across the cheek toward the window, then three or four up and out over the dark fold toward the white chest patch.
line-whiskers.inside: Most of what you add sits in the bottom half of the sleeping face. The whiskers nearer the window end on the white paws.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave fur showing between the whiskers, and keep them off the closed eyes and the nose.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop when fine white whiskers fan out from both sides of the muzzle, a few each way. The painting is finished. If the lines break up, add water and reload often.

blend-window-sky.text: Begin in the canvas's top left corner, at the top edge, with Pale sky blue. This is the sky through the window. Its top is at the top edge and its left side is at the left edge.

Stroke side to side across the sky, working down from the top edge. Without rinsing, pick up Warm white and paint the lower part of the sky. Then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
The sky is bluest at the top edge and turns paler low down, toward the window's bottom, like a real sky near the horizon.
Leave all the rest of the canvas bare white.
Stop when the sky is a smooth patch about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall: blue at the top edge, fading softly paler lower down, with no hard line where the two colours meet.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky dry fully first, or the dabs will smear into it.
Start the leaf clumps with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge and its left side about 1 in from the left edge. Tap the first clumps there, over the sky.
Hold the old stiff brush upright and tap with its tip. Don't drag it. Tap more in one spot to make a clump more solid, and tap more lightly at a clump's edges so it stays ragged and leafy.
Most of the Leaf green goes in the top half of the leaves, in clumps across the sky. Let one ragged arm of leaves hang down the far side of the window.
Leave pale sky showing in gaps between the clumps, and in the rounded holes low in the window.
Stop when loose dark green clumps cover most of the sky, with pale sky peeking through. Wipe the brush if the dabs come out as blobs.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green dabs dry first, so the new taps sit on top instead of mixing in.
Begin on the highest Leaf green clumps, with the leaf area's top about 1/2 in from the top edge.
Tap lightly with the tip of the old stiff brush, using smaller taps than before. Wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel first, so each tap leaves dots rather than a solid patch.
Put the Sunny leaf green on the tops of the clumps, where the daylight from the window falls. Keep the undersides of the clumps dark.
Leave the Leaf green showing on the underside of each clump, and leave the pale sky gaps open.
Stop when every clump has a bright, dotted top over its darker green, against the pale sky. If a patch goes too solid, tap a little Leaf green back over it.

blend-wall.text: Let the sky and the leaves dry before you paint up against them.
Start with Deep wall blue at the top edge of the canvas, right next to the leaves outside the window.

Lay an even, creamy coat with side-to-side strokes, working down to the bottom edge. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it on across to the right edge. Then stroke back and forth over the join several times while both are wet.
The deep blue stays nearest the window and Wall blue fills the rest, because the wall is darkest by the window. Run it straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go.
Leave the leaves and the scrap of sky in the canvas's upper left corner showing, and paint carefully around them.

Stop when the whole canvas outside that corner is blue, from the top edge to the bottom edge. It should be deeper by the window and softer toward the right edge, with no hard line where the blues meet. If a line shows, add more Wall blue at the join and blend again.

block-in-frame.text: The blue wall must be dry to the touch, or the white will turn pale blue.
Start with the wide upright post, between the window and the blue wall. Make it one long rectangle from the top edge straight down to the bottom edge.

Pull long, straight strokes down the post. Then add the other pieces: a thin crossbar across the window near the top, and the wide bottom ledge, a band that slants from the left edge into the post. Brush the joins smooth, because the frame is plain painted wood.
Make it all one flat cream white with no shading. The shadows come in the next step.
Leave the sky and leaves showing in the two window panes. Leave the blue wall showing in the corner the ledge cuts off at the canvas's lower left, and beyond the post.
Stop when you have a crisp cream post from top edge to bottom edge, a thin crossbar and a slanting ledge. Beginners often get a wobbly edge where the post meets the wall, so keep that edge straight.

shade-frame.text: Let the Warm white frame dry completely, or the lavender will smear into it.
Start on the post at the top edge, along the side of the post that meets the blue wall. The band begins about 3 in from the left edge.

Lay that band as one long, straight piece from the top edge to the bottom edge. Then add the smaller pieces: a thin line along the shadowed edge of the crossbar, a band across the ledge's front face, and a softer band down the post where it runs on past the ledge.
The daylight comes through the window at the upper left. So the lavender goes only on the faces turned away from it: the post's wall side, the crossbar's shadowed edge and the ledge's front face.
Leave cream white showing on the post's window-facing side, on the top of the ledge and the crossbar, and as a lit streak on the post where it runs past the ledge.
Stop when the frame reads as solid wood: cream where the light hits, lavender bands where it turns away. Beginners often cover the whole post, so keep the cream showing.

block-in-sill.text: Let the blue wall and the white window frame dry first, so the brown doesn't drag into them along the sill's back edge.
Start at the left edge, just under the white window frame, where the sill's back edge meets it.

First lay one long slanted rectangle for the sill's top. Pull the flat brush across from the left edge to the right edge, with the back edge sloping gently down toward the right edge. Then lay a strip along the bottom edge for the sill's front edge.
Make the whole sill one flat warm brown, right through where the blanket will lie. Its shading and sunlight come in the next steps.
Leave the blue wall and the white window frame clean above the sill's back edge. Let a faint line show where the top meets the front edge.

Stop when a flat brown sill covers the bottom of the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, about 16 in wide, with a straight back edge. A wobbly back edge is the usual slip. Fix it now while the paint is wet.

shade-sill.text: Let the flat Warm wood brown sill dry completely. Dry brush over wet paint just smears.
Start at the right edge on the sill's top. Work back toward the left edge along the grain.

Dip only the tip of the dry brush and wipe off the excess. Skim lightly along the length of the sill in long strokes, building up over several light passes. Then skim broken strokes along the front edge, which reaches the bottom edge.
The paint sits over most of the sill's top and its front edge. That darkens the wood away from the window's light, which comes from the upper left.
Leave the shape of the coming sunny patch at the left, below the window, untouched as flat brown. Also leave streaks of the flat brown between your strokes.

Stop when the sill reads as streaky, darker wood from the left edge to the right edge. A pale wedge shape should be waiting at the left. If it went on solid, let it dry and skim the base brown back over part of it.

light-sill.text: Let the Warm wood brown dry-brushing dry first, so the peach stays clean.
Start with the biggest piece. It is a long slanted wedge on the sill's top at the left, and its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge.

Fill the wedge first, pulling along its length and tapering it to a point toward the window's far side. Next lay a narrower bar between the wedge and the window, with a brown band separating the two. Then lay a small piece at the left edge.
This is the sunlight from the window falling on the sill. The brown bands between the pieces are the frame's shadow.
Leave two brown bands between the three peach pieces. Keep the dark front edge and the brown sill around the patch.
Stop when a peach patch sits at the left edge, about 6 1/2 in wide, crossed by two brown bands. Its tip should break into a few dabs.

block-in-blanket.text: Let the sill's Sunny peach patch and the blue wall dry to the touch, because the blanket goes on over both.

Start with a long, low oval for the blanket's rolled bed. Its left end is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, it runs off the right edge of the canvas, and its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.
Pull long side-to-side strokes along the oval. Then add a curved roll along its front and a folded front edge in ( ) shaped pieces, rounding the end nearest the window.
Lay one flat coat of Golden yellow over the whole shape, with no shading yet. The cat will lie on it later.

Leave the window frame and the sill's sunny patch showing where the blanket's rounded end meets them. Keep the blue wall clean along the blanket's top edge, and keep the front of the wooden windowsill clean along its bottom edge.
Stop when it is one smooth, solid golden shape, about 15 in wide, with no wall or sill showing through it.

shade-blanket.text: The Golden yellow must be fully dry, or the dark loops will smear into it.
Start along the inside of the roll at the back of the blanket, where it curves down into the hollow of the bed.

Touch the tip of the brush down, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so each mark ends in a point. Set these commas in rows that follow the roll. On the front fold, lean them in pairs like little Vs, the way knit stitches sit.
Pack the Dark ochre loops thickest under the roll, along the fold and on the lower front, where the blanket turns away from the light. Scatter a few loose patches across the hollow.
Leave gold showing between the loops, most of all along the top of the roll and the top of the front fold.
Stop when the blanket reads as a rolled knit bed with a sunken middle, darkest in its folds. If you get a blob instead of a teardrop, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.text: The Dark ochre loops must be dry first.
Start on the blanket's rounded end, the one nearest the window.

Use the same press and lift: touch the tip down, press, pull and lift to a point. Make these commas smaller and fewer than the dark ones. Curve them around the rounded end, then dot them along the tops of the roll and the front fold.

The Pale yellow goes where the window light from the upper left hits: thickest down the rounded end, then thinly across the hollow and the tops of the folds. Most of it sits in the left half of the blanket.
Leave the Dark ochre loops showing in the folds and under the roll, and leave most of the gold untouched.
Stop when the rounded end and the tops glow a little lighter and the knit looks rounded and lit from the window. Don't cover the whole blanket.

block-in-cat.text: The blanket's pale yellow knit loops must be dry, because the gray goes straight over them.
Start with one big oval for the curled body on the blanket. The sleeping tabby cat's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and its back end reaches the right edge of the canvas.
Add a round head at the end nearest the window, one ear triangle pointing toward the window frame and one standing up from the top of the head. Pull each stroke around the curve of the back.
Fill the whole cat with one flat Mid gray, with no darker or lighter spots, since all the shading comes later.
Leave the blanket's front roll and fold showing all along the cat's lower edge, and keep the blue wall showing around the curve of the back.
Stop at one smooth gray shape about 15 in wide. Soften where the pieces meet, and give thin spots a second pass so no yellow peeks through.

shade-cat.text: Let the Mid gray dry fully, or the Dark gray will smear into it.
Start at the top of the back where it meets the head. Curve one wide stroke down through the deep fold behind the head, all the way to the blanket.

Bend every stroke with the body. Sweep the tail's curl along the bottom of the body, from the front paws to the back end. Then wrap curved strokes around the back end, where the paint reaches the right edge of the canvas.
The daylight comes from the window, so the dark goes on the far, rounded back end, the tail and the fold. Add a few small curved dabs over the back to suggest fur.
Leave the head, the top of the back, the two paw shapes and the patch on the cat's side in Mid gray.
Stop when the fold, the tail and the back end read clearly darker. A common mistake is painting over the paws; keep them gray.

paint-white-patches.text: Let the Dark gray dry first, so the white stays clean.
Start on the muzzle. Pull a white stroke down from the face to the chin, the part whose top is about 5 in from the top edge.

Curve the strokes around each of the two front paws like small round mounds tucked against the chin. For the side patch, pull short curved strokes toward the back, letting their tips make a ragged, pointed edge.
The white goes on the muzzle and chin, the two paws, and one patch in the middle of the cat's side. That patch's left side is about 8 in from the left edge, and it is about 2 3/4 in wide.
Leave a thin gray line between the two paws, and keep the dark tail curl showing where it meets the white patch on the side.
Stop when the white is solid. If gray shows through, let it dry and go over it once more.

paint-stripes.text: Let the Warm white patches and the Dark gray shading dry to the touch. A wet stripe dragged into wet white turns gray.
Start on the top of the cat's back, where the body is highest. Work across the body first, then do the tail, then the top of the head and the cheeks.

Press the full width of the 1/4 inch angle brush at the spine. Then pull down around the curve of the body toward the blanket, turning onto the edge and pressing lighter so each stripe tapers to a point. On the tail, pull short bands across it. On the head, pull short tapered marks from the top of the head down the cheeks.

The stripes wrap around the round body like curved rings, not straight bars. That curve is what makes the body look full. The middle of all the striping is about 9 1/2 in from the left edge, so most of it lands on the big body and the tail.
Leave gray showing between the stripes, about as wide as the stripes. Keep the white muzzle, chest patch and paws clean, and leave the ears gray inside.
Stop when the body, tail, head and cheeks all carry curving charcoal stripes over the gray. A likely mistake is pressing hard all the way through, which gives blunt even bars with no taper.

paint-ears.text: Let the Charcoal stripes on the head dry first, so the pink doesn't smear into them.
Start in the far ear, whose middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge. Then paint the other ear the same way.

Touch the #4 round down near the base of the ear and press so the belly spreads. Then pull toward the ear's point and lift, so the stroke ends sharp at the point. Use two or three of these strokes side by side to fill each ear.
The pink fills the middle of each ear triangle. It is widest at the base and narrows toward the point, the way a real cat's ear looks.
Leave a thin gray rim along both edges of each ear. Leave all the head and body stripes untouched.
Stop when both ears are pink inside, each with a gray rim, and nothing else has changed. If a stroke turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.

flick-fur.text: Let the Charcoal stripes and the pink in the ears dry fully first, so the flicks don't drag the dark into the gray.
Start on the top of the cat's back, where the big curled body rounds over, about 3 3/4 in from the top edge of the canvas.

Use very little paint. Set each flick down in the fur and lift off quickly as you go, so it thins at the tip. Follow the way the fur lies: around the curve of the body, along the tail, and over the top of the head and the cheeks.
Most of the flicks go on the right half of the cat's fur, across the big body and the tail. Cross the edges of the stripes so they look soft and furry.
Leave the middle of each Charcoal stripe dark, and keep the white muzzle, chest patch, paws and pink ears clean.
The whole coat reads lighter and furry, with the darker gray and stripes showing between the flicks. The face stays blank.

paint-nose.text: Let the white muzzle and the pink inside the ears dry first.
Start with the nose on the white muzzle, just under where the sleeping eyes will go. Its top is about 6 1/4 in from the top edge, and it's about 3/4 in wide.
Touch the tip down at one top corner of the nose, press, then pull toward the point and lift. Repeat from the other top corner so the two marks meet in a small triangle pointing down toward the paws.

The nose is solid pink at the tip of the muzzle, where the face presses toward the paws. Then deepen the pink of both ears with a few small press-and-lift touches along the edge where the pink meets the gray rim.
Keep white muzzle all round the nose. Leave each ear's gray rim and the lighter pink in its middle showing.

Stop when a small, neat pink triangle sits on the white muzzle and each ear has a deeper pink edge. There are no eyes, mouth or whiskers yet. If the nose comes out as a round blob, you used too much paint: use less and lift faster.

line-eyes.text: Let the pink nose dry first, or the dark lines will spread into it.
Start with the upper closed eye, a curve on the gray face just above the white muzzle, under the upright ear.

Hold the liner upright. Pull each eye as one smile-shaped curve with its ends dipping, a little thicker at the end nearer the nose and lighter as you go. Then pull the lower eye across the cheek nearer the window. Add a short mouth line under the nose, a thin dark edge along the outer rim of each ear, and three short lines on the gray cheek where the whiskers will start.
The lines sit where the eyelids close. Add a small dark tuck where the chin meets the paw.
Leave the white muzzle, the pink nose and the pink inside the ears clear.
Stop when the cat reads as fast asleep, with closed eyes, a tiny mouth and crisp ear edges. If a line skips, add water.

line-whiskers.text: Let the Charcoal lines and the pink nose dry first, or the white will turn gray.
Start each whisker at the edge of the white muzzle.

Hold the liner upright and pull each whisker outward in one long, gently curved line. Press a little at the start and lighten so it tapers to nothing. Pull three or four down and out across the cheek toward the window, then three or four up and out over the dark fold toward the white chest patch.
Most of what you add sits in the bottom half of the sleeping face. The whiskers nearer the window end on the white paws.
Leave fur showing between the whiskers, and keep them off the closed eyes and the nose.
Stop when fine white whiskers fan out from both sides of the muzzle, a few each way. The painting is finished. If the lines break up, add water and reload often.

words: Start in the top left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, at the very top edge and the very left edge. Stroke side to side, working downward.
Keep this sky small. It is a patch about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall, tucked into the corner. Let its lower edge be soft and uneven, like clouds.
Without rinsing, pick up Warm white for the lowest strokes so the sky gets paler as it comes down. Stroke back over the join while both are wet.

When you stop, the corner is a smooth pale blue, lighter low down, and the rest of the canvas is still bare white. Don't stop with a hard line where the two colours meet: add a little more Warm white there and blend again.
Let the sky dry first. Wipe the old stiff brush nearly dry, then tap Leaf green with its tip into the sky patch, starting at the top edge in the corner.
Tap loose clumps, mostly in the upper part of the sky through the window, and work down its outer edge in a ragged line. Leave pale sky showing in spots, mostly low down where the sky is lightest.
When you stop, the corner is a deeper, dappled patch with a few pale gaps. If the paint goes on as blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.
Wait until the Leaf green is dry. Load the old stiff brush lightly with Sunny leaf green and tap over the same corner patch.
Use smaller, fewer taps than before. Put them on the tops of the clumps, the side toward the light, and leave the darker taps showing underneath.

When you stop, the patch looks lit and leafy, with dark green still between the bright taps and pale sky in the gaps. The rest of the canvas is still bare. If one spot goes solid, break it up with a few taps of the darker green.
Let the window view dry. Start with Deep wall blue just beside the window view in the upper left corner, and stroke side to side down that side of the canvas.
Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it across to the right edge. Stroke back over the join several times so the deep blue fades softly into the lighter one.
Cover the whole canvas, out to all four edges, right through where the sill, blanket and cat will go. Paint around the leaves and sky, leaving them showing in the corner.
When you stop, the canvas is one smooth blue wall, deeper near the window, softer to the right. A hard line at the join means more Wall blue and another blend.
Wait for the wall to be dry. Start with the wide upright post: one long rectangle of Warm white from the top edge down to the bottom edge, its right side about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
Add the rest in pieces: a thinner inner post down the window view, a thin crossbar across the leaves near the top, and a broad bottom ledge slanting down toward the left edge.
Keep the edges straight and flat, with no shading yet. Leave the sky and leaves showing in the panes, and the blue wall showing under the ledge.
When you stop, a flat cream frame stands over the window view and the wall. Don't thin the paint too much, or the blue will show through.
Let the frame dry. With the 1/4 inch flat and Lavender gray, start at the top of the wide post and pull a narrow band down its inner side, all the way to the bottom edge.

Add the other pieces: a thin band down the inner post, a strip under the crossbar, and a band along the top of the bottom ledge where it meets the post. Paint a narrow shadow strip down the blue wall, right of the white window frame, too.
Leave cream showing on the faces that catch the light from the window.
When you stop, the frame looks square and solid, cream with cool shadow bands. Keep each band thin; a wide band turns the whole post gray.

Let the frame and wall dry. Start with the sill's top: one long slanted rectangle of Warm wood brown whose top edge is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge, running from the left edge to the right edge.
Let that top edge rise toward the window and fall a little toward the right edge. Then add the front edge as a strip along the bottom, with a slanted line between the two pieces.
Paint right up to the foot of the white window frame and the blue wall, leaving no white gaps.
When you stop, a flat warm-brown sill fills the bottom of the canvas, with no shading. Paint it solid; streaks will show later through the sunny patch.
Wait for the sill to dry. Dip only the tip of the 3/4 inch flat in Warm wood brown and wipe it until it feels dry.
Start where the sill meets the window, and skim long, light strokes along the grain toward the right edge of the canvas, then along the front edge. Build it up in several light passes.
Below the window, leave a lighter slanted patch with two thin bands crossing it, where the sun will fall.
When you stop, the sill looks streaked and grainy, darker along the front and away from the window. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim lighter.

Let the dry brushing dry. With the 1/2 inch flat and Sunny peach, start with the big wedge of sunlight on the sill's top below the window, then add a smaller bar above it and a sliver at the left edge.
Each piece slants the same way, like light coming through the window. Keep the pieces separate.
Leave brown bands between the pieces: they are the shadow of the white window frame on the sill.

When you stop, the sunny patch is about 6 1/2 in wide, crisp-edged peach pieces at the left end of the sill, fading into the brown at their far tip. Don't blend them into the brown, or the sunlight goes muddy.
Let the sill dry. Start with a long, low oval of Golden yellow for the rolled bed, its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge and running out to the right edge.
Add the curved roll and the folded front as rounded pieces at the end near the window, like ( ), so that end looks stacked in two soft lobes.
Paint it flat and solid, right through where the cat will lie. Leave the sill showing in a thin line under its lower edge.
When you stop, a smooth golden-yellow blanket lies on the sill, with no loops yet. Two coats may be needed for yellow to cover the brown.
Wait for the yellow to dry. Load the #8 round fully with Dark ochre. Touch down, press and lift, so each loop is a little comma.
Start in the hollow of the bed and under the roll, then work in rows along the fold and the lower front, out to the right edge. Set the commas close together there.
Keep them sparse on the top of the roll and on the rim of the hollow, where the light hits, leaving the gold showing between them.
When you stop, the blanket looks knitted, darkest in its folds. If a comma turns into a blob, use less paint and lift faster.
Let the dark loops dry. With the #6 round and Pale yellow, press and lift fewer, smaller commas than before.
Start on the end of the roll nearest the window, setting the loops thickly down its rounded face. Then scatter a few along the tops of the roll and the fold.
Leave the dark ochre loops showing in the hollow and along the folds.
When you stop, the knit catches light on its tops and on the end facing the window. Don't cover the whole blanket, or it goes flat again.
Let the blanket dry. With Mid gray, start with a big oval for the curled body lying in the hollow of the blanket, its far end almost at the right edge of the canvas.

Add a circle for the head at the window end of the body, overlapping the roll. Then two triangles for the ears, one at the side of the head and one on top, the top ear's tip about 1 1/4 in from the top edge.
Follow the fur with your strokes, curving over the back. Keep the blanket's roll showing around the cat.
When you stop, a flat gray cat shape sits in the blanket, with no shading. A lumpy edge is fine; aim for one smooth silhouette.
Let the gray dry. With Dark gray, bend each stroke with the body. Start at the deep curve where the head meets the body and pull down along it.
Then shade the round back end of the body, where the belly meets the blanket, and the tail curling along the front, sweeping around the curve. Add a little under the head.
Leave the top of the back and the head mid gray. Paint around the muzzle, the chest patch and the two paws, so their gray shapes stay clean.
When you stop, the cat looks round, with its shadow away from the window. Don't paint straight strokes; they flatten it.
Wait until the gray is dry. With the #8 round and Warm white, start on the muzzle and chin under the head, curving each stroke down the face.
Then paint the two front paws as rounded mounds tucked under the chin, and a white patch on the chest and side, pulled in curves along the fur.
Do two or three thin coats, drying between them, rather than one thick one. Leave a thin dark line between the paws.
When you stop, the cat has a white face patch, a white side patch and two white paws. If gray shows through, wait and add another thin coat.
Let the white dry. Load the 1/4 inch angle with Charcoal. Press the full width, then turn to the edge and lighten up, so each stripe tapers to a point.
Start on the back and pull stripes down around the body, following its curve. Add bands across the tail, then shorter ones on the top of the head and the cheeks.
Leave gray between the stripes, and keep the white patches and the ears clean.
When you stop, curving tabby stripes wrap the body, tail and head. Don't make them straight or even; let them bend and thin out.
Wait for the stripes to dry. With the #4 round and Soft pink, press and lift inside each ear, starting at its base and pulling toward the tip.
Do both ears: the one at the side of the head and the one on top.
Leave a gray rim around each ear's outer edge.
When you stop, both ears are pink inside with gray edges. Too much paint makes a blob: use less and lift quickly.
Let everything on the cat dry. Load the small fan brush lightly with Light gray and flick quick strokes, lifting off so each mark thins at its tip.
Start on the head near the window, then work across the top of the back and down the body and the tail, flicking along the way the fur lies.
Let the flicks break the edges of the stripes, but leave dark gray and stripes showing between them. Keep off the white patches.
When you stop, the coat looks soft and furry. Too much paint makes flat smears; wipe the brush and flick lighter.
Let the fur dry. With the #4 round and Soft pink, press and lift a small triangle nose on the white muzzle, pointing down.
Add a few small touches inside each ear, near the base, to warm the pink.
Leave the white of the muzzle all round the nose.
When you stop, the cat has a small pink nose. Keep it tiny; a big nose takes over the face.
Wait for the nose to dry. Thin Charcoal with water and hold the #1 liner upright.

Start with two curved lines for the closed eyes, smiling downward, on the cheeks above the muzzle. Add a short mouth line under the nose, a thin dark edge along the top of each ear, and a few short lines on the cheek next to the body.
Use light, steady pressure, thicker at the start and thinning out.
When you stop, the cat looks asleep. If the line skips, add water; if it spreads, the paint underneath is still wet.
Let the eye lines dry. Thin Warm white with water and load the #1 liner.
Start at the muzzle beside the nose and pull long, thin lines fanning out on each side: one set across the dark cheek toward the white chest patch, the other over the paws and onto the blanket.
Keep them few and light, tapering to nothing, with a slight curve.
When you stop, the painting is finished. Reload often so the lines don't break.
Start in the top left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, at the very top edge and the very left edge. Stroke side to side, working downward.
Keep this sky small. It is a patch about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall, tucked into the corner. Let its lower edge be soft and uneven, like clouds.
Without rinsing, pick up Warm white for the lowest strokes so the sky gets paler as it comes down. Stroke back over the join while both are wet.

When you stop, the corner is a smooth pale blue, lighter low down, and the rest of the canvas is still bare white. Don't stop with a hard line where the two colours meet: add a little more Warm white there and blend again.
Let the sky dry first. Wipe the old stiff brush nearly dry, then tap Leaf green with its tip into the sky patch, starting at the top edge in the corner.
Tap loose clumps, mostly in the upper part of the sky through the window, and work down its outer edge in a ragged line. Leave pale sky showing in spots, mostly low down where the sky is lightest.
When you stop, the corner is a deeper, dappled patch with a few pale gaps. If the paint goes on as blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it on a paper towel and tap again.
Wait until the Leaf green is dry. Load the old stiff brush lightly with Sunny leaf green and tap over the same corner patch.
Use smaller, fewer taps than before. Put them on the tops of the clumps, the side toward the light, and leave the darker taps showing underneath.

When you stop, the patch looks lit and leafy, with dark green still between the bright taps and pale sky in the gaps. The rest of the canvas is still bare. If one spot goes solid, break it up with a few taps of the darker green.
Let the window view dry. Start with Deep wall blue just beside the window view in the upper left corner, and stroke side to side down that side of the canvas.
Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it across to the right edge. Stroke back over the join several times so the deep blue fades softly into the lighter one.
Cover the whole canvas, out to all four edges, right through where the sill, blanket and cat will go. Paint around the leaves and sky, leaving them showing in the corner.
When you stop, the canvas is one smooth blue wall, deeper near the window, softer to the right. A hard line at the join means more Wall blue and another blend.
Wait for the wall to be dry. Start with the wide upright post: one long rectangle of Warm white from the top edge down to the bottom edge, its right side about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
Add the rest in pieces: a thinner inner post down the window view, a thin crossbar across the leaves near the top, and a broad bottom ledge slanting down toward the left edge.
Keep the edges straight and flat, with no shading yet. Leave the sky and leaves showing in the panes, and the blue wall showing under the ledge.
When you stop, a flat cream frame stands over the window view and the wall. Don't thin the paint too much, or the blue will show through.
Let the frame dry. With the 1/4 inch flat and Lavender gray, start at the top of the wide post and pull a narrow band down its inner side, all the way to the bottom edge.

Add the other pieces: a thin band down the inner post, a strip under the crossbar, and a band along the top of the bottom ledge where it meets the post. Paint a narrow shadow strip down the blue wall, right of the white window frame, too.
Leave cream showing on the faces that catch the light from the window.
When you stop, the frame looks square and solid, cream with cool shadow bands. Keep each band thin; a wide band turns the whole post gray.
Let the frame and wall dry. Start with the sill's top: one long slanted rectangle of Warm wood brown running from the left edge to the right edge of the canvas.
Let that top edge rise toward the window and fall a little toward the right edge. Then add the front edge as a strip along the bottom, with a slanted line between the two pieces.
Paint right up to the foot of the white window frame and the blue wall, leaving no white gaps.
When you stop, a flat warm-brown sill fills the bottom of the canvas, with no shading. Paint it solid; streaks will show later through the sunny patch.
Wait for the sill to dry. Dip only the tip of the 3/4 inch flat in Warm wood brown and wipe it until it feels dry.
Start where the sill meets the window, and skim long, light strokes along the grain toward the right edge of the canvas, then along the front edge. Build it up in several light passes.
Below the window, leave a lighter slanted patch with two thin bands crossing it, where the sun will fall.
When you stop, the sill looks streaked and grainy, darker along the front and away from the window. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded: let it dry and skim lighter.

Let the dry brushing dry. With the 1/2 inch flat and Sunny peach, start with the big wedge of sunlight on the sill's top below the window, then add a smaller bar nearer the window and a sliver at the left edge.
Each piece slants the same way, like light coming through the window. Keep the pieces separate.
Leave brown bands between the pieces: they are the shadow of the white window frame on the sill.

When you stop, the sunny patch is about 6 1/2 in wide, crisp-edged peach pieces at the left end of the sill, fading into the brown at their far tip. Don't blend them into the brown, or the sunlight goes muddy.
Let the sill dry. Start with a long, low oval of Golden yellow for the rolled bed, its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge and running out to the right edge.
Add the curved roll and the folded front as rounded pieces at the end near the window, like ( ), so that end looks stacked in two soft lobes.
Paint it flat and solid, right through where the cat will lie. Leave the sill showing in a thin line under its lower edge.
When you stop, a smooth golden-yellow blanket lies on the sill, with no loops yet. Two coats may be needed for yellow to cover the brown.
Wait for the yellow to dry. Load the #8 round fully with Dark ochre. Touch down, press and lift, so each loop is a little comma.
Start in the hollow of the bed and under the roll, then work in rows along the fold and the lower front, out to the right edge. Set the commas close together there.
Keep them sparse on the top of the roll and on the rim of the hollow, where the light hits, leaving the gold showing between them.

Leave the dark ochre loops showing in the hollow and along the folds.
When you stop, the knit catches light on its tops and on the end facing the window. Don't cover the whole blanket, or it goes flat again.
