words: This sky covers the whole canvas. It reaches all four edges of the canvas, because the mountains, hills and cow all go on top of it later.

Start at the top edge with Sky blue and pull long side-to-side strokes from the left edge to the right edge. Without rinsing, pick up Cream gold and work it in below the blue. Then lay Pale gold lower down, and add a warm glow near the top right corner where the sun sits. Make the bands wavy, letting blue and gold take turns down the canvas.
Stroke back over each join while it is wet so the colours melt into each other. When you stop, no white should show anywhere.
If a hard line forms where two colours meet, add more of the lighter one at the join and blend again.
Let the sky dry completely first. Wet paint underneath turns dry-brush into mud.

Dip only the tip of the brush in Warm peach and wipe it until it feels dry. Start along the top edge and skim long, slightly slanted streaks across the canvas with light pressure. Work your way down in loose rows, almost to the bottom of the sky.
Touch Dusky rose along the underside of some streaks so each cloud has a darker belly. Leave plenty of the blue and gold sky between the streaks and through their broken edges.
When you stop you should see soft, ragged rows of peach and rose, never solid blocks. If a streak goes on solid, your brush was too loaded. Let it dry and skim a little sky colour back over it.
Wait until the peach and rose streaks are dry.

Load just the tip of the brush with Pale gold and wipe it nearly dry. Skim it along the upper edges of the cloud streaks, pulling side to side the way each streak already runs. Start with the top rows of clouds and work down.

Put a little more of it on the right side of the sunset clouds, nearer the sun, because that is where the light is strongest. Keep the gold on the tops only, so the Dusky rose still shows along each cloud's underside.
When you stop, the clouds should look lit from above, with broken gold tops and blue sky still showing between them.
The sky must be dry. The mountains are a band across the canvas: its top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.

Start with Far violet for the farthest range. Pull soft, low peaks with the brush kept level, leaving the gold glow above them. Then use Mountain blue for the nearer ridge, starting at the left edge and pulling long level strokes to the right edge so it overlaps the foot of the violet range.
Keep both ranges flat, with no light on them yet. When you stop, the paler violet peaks should sit behind a darker slate-blue ridge running edge to edge, and the sky should still show below them.
Let the mountains dry. This is only a whisper of colour on the very tops of the peaks, inside a strip whose bottom is about 3 in from the top edge.
Load the tip of the brush with Warm peach and wipe it nearly dry. Skim it lightly along the crests of the far violet peaks, side to side, following each ridge line.
Most of it goes on the right side of the far blue mountains, on the peaks closest to the sun. Leave the slopes below the crests their flat blue.
When you stop you should barely notice it: a few thin, broken warm edges on the peaks. If it looks like a stripe, you used too much paint.

The mountains should be dry. The lake is a small sliver at the foot of the mountains. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge and its right side is at the right edge, and it is about 2 in wide and 1/2 in tall.
Start at the right edge with Cream gold and pull short level strokes toward the left, letting the strip thin to a point at its left end.
Keep the dark ridge just above it untouched so the water reads as lying under the hills. When you stop you should see one thin, pale, shining strip of water.
Let the mountains and lake dry. The green ground starts just under the mountain ridge, with its top about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and runs to the bottom edge and across from edge to edge.

Begin at the top with Yellow green. Pull long strokes along each hill, following the slope as it runs down across the canvas. Lower down, switch to Hill green for the big meadow and keep pulling long strokes all the way to the bottom edge.
Don't cover the mountains or the lake. Bits of sky may peek through between your strokes, and that's fine: the next step fills them.
When you stop, the lower canvas should read as light green slopes over an olive-green meadow.
Let the first greens dry so the dark bands stay crisp.

Start just under the mountains with Deep green, laying a dark ridge of far hill. Then pull long strokes along the slopes in bands, following the roll of each hill and leaving light green between them. Fill any sky that still peeks through.
Most of it goes in the bottom half of the green hills and meadow. Brush the front of the meadow dark all the way to the bottom edge, and keep the sunny middle of the meadow light.
When you stop, the hills should show alternating dark and light stripes, and the meadow should go from light in the middle to dark at the front.
Wait for the green bands to dry. The bushes sit on the hills, in a strip whose top is about 4 in from the top edge.

Load the round brush lightly with Deep green, with no water. Tap clusters of small round bushes along the slopes, in rows that follow the hill bands. Put a group near the left edge, a short row in the middle, and longer rows toward the right edge.
Keep them small and dotted. Tap more in the middle of each clump to make it solid, and less at its edges. Leave the meadow below untouched.
If you get blobs instead of dots, wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
Let the ground dry. The cow is a big shape whose left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge. It is about 7 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall, and its bottom is about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

Start with Rust brown as a big upright oval for the body. Then add curved pieces around it: a rounded head bump at the top right of the oval, and a ragged lower edge where the hair hangs into the grass. Pull each stroke downward, the way the hair falls.
Leave the hills and meadow showing all around it.
When you stop it should be one flat, solid rust-brown blob. It's supposed to look plain at this stage.
The rust shape must be dry first.
With Dark umber, start at the top of the back and pull long curved strokes down the left side of the cow, the side away from the sun. Bend each stroke with the round of the body.

Add darker curves under the fringe and under the chin, a few long dark streaks down the body where the locks will part, and some low on the body near the grass. Keep the face and the top of the head rust.
When you stop, the cow should look round: darkest on the shadow side and at the bottom, with rust still showing where the light hits.
Let the coat dry. The two horns sit inside an area whose top is about 3 in from the top edge, and they stretch about 6 1/2 in across.

With Horn tan, start each horn as a wide piece where it meets the top of the head. Then add curving pieces that taper to a point. The left horn rises high and leans out. The right horn swings out and curves up at its tip.
Keep the edges clean against the sky and the mountains behind them.
When you stop you should have two flat, pale tan horns with sharp tips and no shading yet.
Wait for the Horn tan to dry.

With Dark umber on the small round brush, start at the tip of each horn and pull curved strokes back along the horn's underside toward the head, following its bend. Make it darkest at the tips, then lighten your pressure as you go so it fades out along the curve.
Leave a pale tan stripe along the top edge of each horn, where the light will go.
When you stop, the horns should look round, with dark tips and undersides and a lighter top.
The shadows must be dry. The locks cover the whole coat, from the top of the head down to a bottom about 4 in from the bottom edge.

With Rust brown, start at the top of the head and the fringe. Press the full width of the brush, then turn onto its edge and lift as you pull down, so each lock is wide at the top and ends in a point. Work down over the body, bending each lock with the round of the body.
Let the fringe hang in locks over where the eyes would be. Leave thin gaps of Dark umber between locks so the coat looks layered.
When you stop, the whole cow should read as long hanging locks, not a smooth shape.
Let the ginger locks dry.

With Honey gold on the small flat brush, pull just a few short locks with the same wide-to-pointed stroke. Put some on top of the back and down the shoulder, and one on the edge of the head nearest the sun.
Add a couple of small gold touches in the meadow right of the cow, as hints of sunlit grass.
Keep them few and small, so the ginger and dark brown still show all around them. When you stop, the coat should just catch a little more light.
The meadow and the cow must be dry. This grass covers the meadow from the left edge and the bottom edge, about 11 1/2 in wide and 6 in tall.
Load the fan brush lightly with Deep green. Start near the bottom edge and flick quick strokes upward from the base, lifting off so each blade thins at the top. Slant them all the same way.
Most of them go in the bottom half of the meadow's tall grass, bigger at the front and smaller and fewer toward the hills. Flick some over the cow's lower edge so it stands in the grass.
If you get flat blobs, there's too much paint on the brush.
Let the dark grass dry. This pass reaches up to a top about 6 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Load the fan brush lightly with Yellow green and flick quick upward strokes between the dark ones, slanted the same way. Start at the bottom edge and work up, getting fewer toward the hills.
Flick a few up over the bottom of the cow's coat. Leave the dark blades showing between your marks.
When you stop, the meadow should be a busy mix of dark and light slanted blades.
Wait for the green flicks to dry. The gold spreads across the meadow, about 11 1/2 in wide and 7 1/2 in tall.

Load the fan brush lightly with Honey gold and flick upward strokes, slanted like the others. Put a cluster near the left edge beside the cow, a broad band of gold right of the cow, and a scattered row along the bottom edge.

When you stop, the meadow should glow, with three colours of grass mixed together.
The coat must be dry.

With Pale gold on the small flat brush, start on the top of the head and the fringe. Press, then lift as you pull down, so each stroke is short, thick at the top and pointed at the end. Then run strokes along the top of the back, and down the right side of the cow from the head and chest toward the grass.

When you stop, the cow should look lit from behind, with a glowing edge much thinner than the locks under it.
Let the dark horn tips dry.
With Cream gold on the small round brush, start at the base of each horn and pull a thin curved stroke along its top edge toward the tip, bending with the horn.
Stop before the dark tip and keep the darker underside showing below your line.
When you stop, each horn should have a pale, lit top edge, which makes it look round.
The coat must be dry. The face sits inside an area whose right side is about 4 in from the right edge, about 2 1/2 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.

Wait for the Rosy nose to dry.

The nose must be fully dry, or your lines will spread.

If a line skips, add water and reload. When you stop, the face is finished.

Most of it goes on the right side of the cow, the side facing the sun. Leave the shadow side of the body and its lower half untouched.
When you stop, the cow should look lit from behind, with a glowing edge much thinner than the locks under it.

light-horns.text: Let the dark horn tips dry.
With Cream gold on the small round brush, start at the base of each horn and pull a thin curved stroke along its top edge toward the tip, bending with the horn.
Stop before the dark tip, and keep the darker underside of each horn showing.
When you stop, each horn should have a pale, lit top edge, which makes it look round.

paint-nose.text: The coat must be dry. The face sits inside an area whose right side is about 4 in from the right edge, about 2 1/2 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
With Rosy nose, start just under the fringe and paint a broad rounded nose, curving your strokes around its shape. Then pull a curved line under the muzzle, following the jaw.
Let the fringe stay over the top of the face, and keep the gold rim around it.
When you stop, the nose should be a flat pinkish-brown shape peeking out from the hair.

nose-shine.text: Wait for the Rosy nose to dry.
With Nose pink on the small round brush, lay a short curved stroke across the top of the nose. That area's top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
Keep it on the top only. Leave the Rosy nose showing around the sides and lower down, where the nostrils go.
When you stop, the nose should look rounded and catch the light on top.

nostrils-mouth.text: The nose must be fully dry, or your lines will spread.
Thin the Dark umber with water so it flows. Hold the liner upright and paint two short curved nostrils on either side of the nose, where the pink ends. Then draw a short mouth line under the nose.
Add a few lines down from the chin into the coat for the dark shadow under the jaw, letting them fork and wobble a little.
If a line skips, add water and reload. When you stop, the face is finished.

words: This haze covers the whole canvas, reaching all four edges. Start with Blue-violet mist at the right edge of the canvas and low down, and stroke side to side with the big flat.

Without rinsing, work Misty blue in across the middle. Then bring Pale gold into the sky's upper left corner, letting it drift down the left side of the canvas. Stroke back and forth over each join while it is wet, so gold melts into blue.
Keep it soft and streaky, with a few faint up-and-down streaks in the blue like distant trees. Nothing sharp yet.
If you get a hard line where gold meets blue, add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
Let the sky dry to the touch so the cream stays bright.
The sun sits right against the left edge of the canvas, in the gold glow. Its top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 2 in tall.
With the tip of the round, make small circles, working outward from the brightest spot at the left edge so the rim stays bumpy and soft, like light breaking through mist.
Stop when you have a small glowing disk with a ragged edge. If the edge looks hard, soften it with lighter circles.
Let the sky dry first. This is one small misty trunk in the middle of the haze: its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge and its top about 3 1/2 in from the top edge.

Start at the trunk's foot with the full width of the flat pressed down, so the foot spreads a little, then pull straight up, turning onto the edge and lightening as you go, so it ends in a thin point.
Add one short soft arm reaching off the trunk toward the sun, pressed flat and left blurry.
It should look faint and plain, only a little darker than the haze.
The firs stand in a group reaching the right edge of the canvas. The group's top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and it's about 6 1/2 in wide.

Start each fir with Deep pine green at its tip and tap down in a zigzag with the middle of the fan, pressing harder as it widens toward its base. Make the tallest firs at the right end of the group and smaller ones toward the middle of the canvas.
At the end nearest the middle of the canvas, stamp a few smaller firs in Misty blue so they fade into the mist, and wash a little Misty blue behind the dark ones.
Leave the bases ragged where they fade. If marks look clumpy, thin the paint and spread the fan.
Let the dark firs dry, so the light doesn't turn to mud.
This light is only a few small patches, not whole trees. Tap the fan's tips on the sunny sides of the firs, mostly low down, with most of it on the left side of the fir trees.

The biggest patch goes at the foot of the hazy firs at the end of the group nearest the middle of the canvas. Add a slim strip on the sunny edge of the next dark fir, and a few small taps near the feet of the tall ones.
Keep the dark showing on the shady side of every fir. Stop while the light is still scattered.
Let the firs dry. These four trunks stand in a row in the open middle of the canvas, between the sun and the fir trees.
Start with the tall Smoky brown trunk; its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge. Press the full flat at its foot and pull up, lightening as you go, so it tapers.

Then pull three Blue-violet mist trunks the same way, each shorter, stepping toward the fir trees. Let the crowns of the first two spread a little into soft bushy shapes, and keep the last one a small stub.
They stay plain, with no bark marks, softer than you think.
Let everything dry first. The floor covers the lower part of the canvas: its top is about 7 in from the top edge, and it runs out to the left, right and bottom edges.

Start at the back, where the ground meets the mist, with Golden ochre, and pull long level strokes left and right. Work down toward the bottom edge, bringing in more Leaf brown so the front is darker and rougher.
Let the strokes leave light and dark bands across the ground, like sun and shadow lying on it, and let the back line break a little where trunks stand.
Leave the haze untouched above the floor. Keep the brush level.
Let the floor dry. Mark one dot where the path vanishes into the mist; its far end is about 7 1/4 in from the top edge. Draw three to five faint lines fanning down from it to the bottom edge.

Starting at the bottom edge, pull Path mauve strokes along those lines toward the dot, wide in front and a thin thread at the back. Across its middle it runs from about 7 1/2 in to 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
Leave a patch of the Golden ochre floor showing in the front, so the path splits around it, and let the path's edges stay ragged.
If your strokes run parallel, go back to the dot and the fan of lines.
Let the path dry. Use a dry, lightly loaded stiff brush and tap with its tip; this covers most of the ground and the bushes.

Cover the forest floor in Burnt orange and Leaf brown dabs: big ones at the bottom edge, smaller toward the mist, thinner over the far end of the path. The big leaf mass's top is about 3 in from the top edge.

Build low orange bushes each side of the path, and a darker Moss green bush right of the path, in front of the fir trees. Tap a few loose Burnt orange dabs in the treetops along the top of the canvas.
Leave small gaps of the earlier paint between dabs. If you get blobs, wipe the brush and tap again.
Let the dark leaves dry, or the yellow turns to mud.
Tap Golden yellow with the stiff brush, most of it on the left side of the canvas. Its left side is about 1/2 in from the left edge and its right side about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
Start in the treetops along the top, hanging loose clusters toward the sun. Build the big bush left of the path into a bright golden mass, heaviest on its sunny side.
Then scatter separate dabs over the ground and path and a few on the bushes right of the path. Leave the orange and brown showing between them; stop while the dark still reads.
Let the golden leaves dry. Tap Pale gold lightly, almost all of it in the top half and on the left side of the canvas, near the sun.

Start in the treetops by the sun and tap along the sunny edges of the hanging leaf clusters, then follow them down along the crown of the big golden bush. Add a few taps in the treetops farther along the top, keeping the right side about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
Keep these as edges and sparkles, not solid patches; most of the golden yellow must still show.
Leave the ground leaves alone.
The rock sits on the leaves right of the path. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and it's about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Start with one wide, low oval of Moss green, domed on its crown and flat where it meets the leaves. Then add a smaller rounded piece at each end.
Fill it flat and solid, with no shading yet. Let the leaves overlap its base a little so it sits down into them rather than floating.
Let the Moss green dry first.

Dip just the tip of the flat into Deep pine green, wipe it nearly dry, and skim lightly over the rock. Work heaviest along the bottom of the mossy rock where it sits on the leaves, and on the right side of the mossy rock, away from the sun.
Let it break up over the rest so the rock looks mottled. Leave a little Moss green showing along its crown at the sunny end.
If it goes on solid, let it dry and skim Moss green back over part of it.
Let the shading dry. This light is only a thin streak, about 1 3/4 in wide, on the crown of the rock at its sunny end.
With a nearly dry brush tipped in Moss light, skim along the curve of the rock's crown in one or two light strokes, following its shape. Add one or two small touches nearby.
Keep the Deep pine green everywhere else. The rock should look lit only along its sunny rim.
Let all the leaves and the rock dry. These pale trunks go straight over everything, most of it on the left side of the canvas.

Start each trunk at its foot on the ground with the full width of the 1 inch flat, flaring the foot, and pull up to the top edge, easing off a little as you go. Paint a slim one at the left edge, two big leaning ones left of the path, one big one with its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge, and one at the right edge.
Turn the brush on its edge for a few slim pale trunks farther back among the leaves.
Paint them flat and even, with no marks.
Let the Birch gray dry. Its bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
Skim Birch shadow down each big trunk with a dry brush, starting at the crown and pulling toward the foot, heaviest on the shady side away from the sun.
Let it break up so ragged patches of Birch gray stay showing, small ones high up and big pale patches near the feet.
Touch a little Moss green into the trunk feet. The trunks should look round and lavender, not flat gray.
Let the shading dry. The patches cross every big birch, most of it on the left side of the canvas and low down.

Press the full width of the flat for a short dark bar across the trunk, then lift onto the edge so it tapers. Space these bars up the trunks, small and broken high up, bigger and closer near the feet.
At each big trunk's foot, join the patches into a solid dark base where it meets the leaves.
Leave plenty of pale bark between the patches. If every trunk gets the same pattern, they look striped; vary them.
Only paint these over dry paint, or the lines feather.

Thin the Bark dark with water and hold the liner upright. Draw short, wobbly marks across the trunks between the patches, crowding them up the middle of each trunk so they build into a broken, rough grain.
Keep most of it on the left side of the canvas and in the top half, and go lighter near the feet.
Leave the shady and sunny edges clean. Reload often; if the line skips, add water.
Let the bark lines dry. Its top is at the top edge.
Dip the tip of the flat in Birch white, wipe it nearly dry, and skim down the sunny side of each birch, from the crown toward the ground, most of it on the left side of the canvas.
Let it catch the canvas texture and break over the dark marks in places. Stop well short of the trunk feet.
Leave the shady side lavender. If it goes on solid, let it dry and skim Birch shadow back over part of it.
Let the trunks dry. With a dry #12 round, tap Pale gold leaves across the ground; its top is about 8 in from the top edge, and it stops about 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

Start along the path, tapping a stream of light leaves up its middle toward the mist, then add clusters around the trunk feet and near the base of the mossy rock, with more of it on the right side of the canvas.
Keep them as separate leaf shapes with orange and brown showing between. Stop before the front fills in; the painting is finished.

Then scatter separate dabs over the ground and path and a few on the bushes in front of the fir trees. Leave the orange and brown showing between them; stop while the dark still reads.

dab-sunlit-canopy.text: Let the golden leaves dry. Tap Pale gold lightly, almost all of it in the top half and on the left side of the canvas, near the sun.

Start in the treetops by the sun and tap along the sunny edges of the hanging leaf clusters, then follow them down along the crown of the big golden bush. Add a few taps in the treetops farther along the top, keeping the right side about 2 1/2 in from the right edge.
Keep these as edges and sparkles, not solid patches; most of the golden yellow must still show.
Leave the ground leaves alone.

block-in-rock.text: The rock sits on the leaves right of the path. Its bottom is about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and it's about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Start with one wide, low oval of Moss green, domed on its crown and flat where it meets the leaves. Then add a smaller rounded piece at each end.
Fill it flat and solid, with no shading yet. Let the leaves overlap its base a little so it sits down into them rather than floating.

shade-rock.text: Let the Moss green dry first.

Dip just the tip of the flat into Deep pine green, wipe it nearly dry, and skim lightly over the rock. Work heaviest along the bottom of the mossy rock where it sits on the leaves, and on the right side of the mossy rock, away from the sun.
Let it break up over the rest so the rock looks mottled. Leave a little Moss green showing along its crown at the sunny end.
If it goes on solid, let it dry and skim Moss green back over part of it.

light-rock.text: Let the shading dry. This light is only a thin streak, about 1 3/4 in wide, on the crown of the rock at its sunny end.
With a nearly dry brush tipped in Moss light, skim along the curve of the rock's crown in one or two light strokes, following its shape. Add one or two small touches nearby.
Keep the Deep pine green everywhere else. The rock should look lit only along its sunny rim.

pull-birches.text: Let all the leaves and the rock dry. These pale trunks go straight over everything, most of it on the left side of the canvas.

Start each trunk at its foot on the ground with the full width of the 1 inch flat, flaring the foot, and pull up to the top edge, easing off a little as you go. Paint a slim one at the left edge, two big leaning ones left of the path, one big one with its left side about 13 1/2 in from the left edge, and one at the right edge.
Turn the brush on its edge for a few slim pale trunks farther back among the leaves.
Paint them flat and even, with no marks.

shade-birches.text: Let the Birch gray dry. Its bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
Skim Birch shadow down each big trunk with a dry brush, starting at the crown and pulling toward the foot, heaviest on the shady side away from the sun.
Let it break up so ragged patches of Birch gray stay showing, small ones high up and big pale patches near the feet.
Touch a little Moss green into the trunk feet. The trunks should look round and lavender, not flat gray.

mark-bark.text: Let the shading dry. The patches cross every big birch, most of it on the left side of the canvas and low down.

Press the full width of the flat for a short dark bar across the trunk, then lift onto the edge so it tapers. Space these bars up the trunks, small and broken high up, bigger and closer near the feet.
At each big trunk's foot, join the patches into a solid dark base where it meets the leaves.
Leave plenty of pale bark between the patches. If every trunk gets the same pattern, they look striped; vary them.

line-bark.text: Only paint these over dry paint, or the lines feather.

Thin the Bark dark with water and hold the liner upright. Draw short, wobbly marks across the trunks between the patches, crowding them up the middle of each trunk so they build into a broken, rough grain.
Keep most of it on the left side of the canvas and in the top half, and go lighter near the feet.
Leave the shady and sunny edges clean. Reload often; if the line skips, add water.

light-bark.text: Let the bark lines dry. Its top is at the top edge.
Dip the tip of the flat in Birch white, wipe it nearly dry, and skim down the sunny side of each birch, from the crown toward the ground, most of it on the left side of the canvas.
Let it catch the canvas texture and break over the dark marks in places. Stop well short of the trunk feet.
Leave the shady side lavender. If it goes on solid, let it dry and skim Birch shadow back over part of it.

tap-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the trunks dry. With a dry #12 round, tap Pale gold leaves across the middle of the ground, leaving the leaves along the front edge alone.

Start along the path, tapping a stream of light leaves up its middle toward the mist, then add clusters around the trunk feet and near the base of the mossy rock, with more of it on the right side of the canvas.
Keep them as separate leaf shapes with orange and brown showing between. Stop before the front fills in; the painting is finished.

blend-sky.start: Start in the sky's upper left corner with Pale gold, where the sun's glow will be. Lay Misty blue across the middle of the canvas, then Blue-violet mist down the right side and along the bottom.
blend-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side with the full width of the brush. Without rinsing, pick up the next colour and paint beside the last one. Then stroke back over each join while it's still wet.
blend-sky.inside: The gold stays in the upper left, because the low sun is there. The colours cool to blue and blue-violet as they move away from it, so the right side and the lower part of the canvas read as cool, shaded haze.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas shows anywhere. The haze reaches all four edges.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze: warm gold in the upper left melting into blue and blue-violet, with soft joins and no hard lines.

glow-sun.start: Put the brush tip in the gold glow at the left edge. The sun's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
glow-sun.strokes: Make small circles with the tip, working outward from the brightest middle, so the edge stays bumpy and soft.
glow-sun.inside: Sun cream sits only in this small disk against the left edge, inside the gold, where the light comes from.
glow-sun.leave: Leave all the gold and blue haze around it untouched.
glow-sun.stop: Stop at a small, soft cream glow cut off by the left edge, with a bumpy rim. A beginner often makes the edge hard and round: soften it with lighter circles.

pull-far-trunks.start: This far trunk stands near the middle of the canvas. Its top is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and the whole shape starts about 6 1/2 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Begin at the trunk's foot, pressing the full brush width, then turn onto the edge and lighten the pressure as you pull up to a thin tip. Add one soft, short branch shape to the side of the trunk.
pull-far-trunks.inside: It is all one pale Blue-violet mist, with no light side. At that distance it melts into the haze.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the haze all around it, and keep the edges soft.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Stop when there is one pale violet trunk, about 1 1/2 in across with its branch, flaring a little at the foot. It should read as faint and plain.

stamp-pines.first: Let the sky and far trunk dry.
stamp-pines.start: The firs fill the right side of the canvas. Their tallest top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and the group runs from about 9 1/4 in from the left edge all the way to the right edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Work each fir from its tip down in a zigzag, stamping with the middle of the fan and pressing harder as you go down so it widens.
stamp-pines.inside: Use Deep pine green for the big near firs. Use Misty blue for the smaller hazy firs between and behind them. Each one is flat, with no lighter side yet.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the haze showing in the gaps between the firs and all over the left side of the canvas.
stamp-pines.stop: Stop when there is a row of dark firs with a misty blue band behind them, and ragged bottoms fading into the mist. Clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick.

light-pines.start: Start low on the left side of the fir trees. The biggest patch starts about 8 in from the left edge, with its top about 5 in from the top edge.
light-pines.strokes: Tap with the middle of the fan in short strokes in different directions. Fill the pale gaps where the haze still shows between the firs.
light-pines.inside: Most of this Pine light green goes on the left side and in the bottom half of the fir trees. It thickens the lower fir mass, plus a few small taps among the firs.
light-pines.leave: Leave the fir tips and the dark firs on the right untouched.
light-pines.stop: Stop when the gaps at the base of the firs are closed into a fuller, rougher mass. Only a few patches change.

pull-middle-trunks.start: Start with the tallest trunk. Its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, its top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in tall.
pull-middle-trunks.strokes: Pull each trunk thick to thin: press the full width at the foot, then turn to the edge and lighten as you rise.
pull-middle-trunks.inside: Use Smoky brown for the tall trunk. Use Blue-violet mist for the three shorter, softer trunks beside it, each with a blurry crown, reaching toward the firs. The farther ones are paler.
pull-middle-trunks.leave: Leave the haze between the trunks, and the firs, untouched.
pull-middle-trunks.stop: Stop when there are four plain trunks in a loose row across the left half of the woods, the tall one the darkest, with no bark marks.

lay-floor.first: Let the trunks and firs dry.
lay-floor.start: Start along the back of the ground, about 7 in from the top edge, just where the firs and trunks meet the mist.
lay-floor.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Lay band after band down to the bottom edge, from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-floor.inside: Use Golden ochre for the sunny bands and Leaf brown for the shadow bands between them. The shadow bands get darker and wider toward the bottom, where the ground is nearest.
lay-floor.leave: Leave the trunks' feet and the bases of the firs sitting on the ground line. Don't paint up into the mist.
lay-floor.stop: Stop when the whole lower part of the canvas is striped ground, lighter and smoother at the back and darker in front.

pull-path.start: Mark one dot at the path's far end, about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. The path's middle is about 9 3/4 in from the left edge. Fan a few faint lines from the dot down to the bottom edge.
pull-path.strokes: Pull each stroke along its line, wide at the bottom edge and thin as it nears the dot. The path bends gently as it narrows.
pull-path.inside: Path mauve sits only on the track, widest where it is nearest.
pull-path.leave: Leave the ground's gold bands showing on both sides of the path, and a little at its front edges.
pull-path.stop: Stop when there is a mauve-brown track running from the bottom edge up into the mist. Avoid parallel edges: mark the dot first.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the path and floor dry.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start on the ground at the bottom edge, where the leaves are biggest. Most of this step is in the bottom half of the canvas.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of a dry stiff brush. Use bigger dabs in front and smaller ones toward the mist.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Use Burnt orange and Leaf brown to carpet the ground and the path. Use Burnt orange for the bushes along the path, and Moss green for the big dark bush right of the path. Up top, tap a few loose Burnt orange clusters, one at the top edge starting about 10 3/4 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the path's line showing through the leaves, and leave the firs' tips and the mist uncovered.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the ground and bushes are thick with dark leaves and the treetops have only a sprinkle. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-mid-leaves.start: Start in the treetops at the top edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
dab-mid-leaves.strokes: Tap the same way, light and dry, building clusters that hang down from the top edge.
dab-mid-leaves.inside: Golden yellow fills the treetop leaves across the top and the big bush on the left side of the canvas. That bush patch is about 7 in wide, and its top is about 2 in from the top edge. Scatter separate dabs over the ground and path, with a few on the bushes right of the path.
dab-mid-leaves.leave: Leave the orange and brown dabs showing between the gold ones on the ground, and the firs clear.
dab-mid-leaves.stop: Stop when the canopy and the left bush glow gold and the ground has gold leaves dotted through the darker ones.

dab-sunlit-canopy.start: Start next to the sun at the left edge. Nearly all of this step sits in the top half and on the left side of the canvas.
dab-sunlit-canopy.strokes: Tap lightly with a nearly dry brush on top of the gold clusters.
dab-sunlit-canopy.inside: Pale gold goes only on the treetop leaves nearest the sun. The biggest spread starts about 1 in from the left edge and is about 6 1/2 in wide, because those leaves face the light.
dab-sunlit-canopy.leave: Leave the Golden yellow and Burnt orange showing under and around each tap, and leave the ground leaves alone.
dab-sunlit-canopy.stop: Stop when the upper left canopy shimmers pale and sunlit while the right treetops stay deeper gold.

block-in-rock.start: The rock sits right of the path. Its left side is about 10 3/4 in from the left edge and its top is about 7 in from the top edge. It is about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
block-in-rock.strokes: Paint one wide low oval first, then add smaller curved pieces at each end, like ( ).
block-in-rock.inside: Fill the whole boulder flat with Moss green, including a small lump at its back end.
block-in-rock.leave: Leave the leaves around its base. Don't paint them over.
block-in-rock.stop: Stop when there is one flat moss-green boulder lying on the leaves, with no shading yet.

shade-rock.start: Start where the rock meets the leaves. This shading is about 2 1/2 in wide, and its left side is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
shade-rock.strokes: Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim lightly along the rock's length in several passes.
shade-rock.inside: Deep pine green covers most of the boulder: its underside, its right end and much of its body. That side faces away from the sun at the upper left.
shade-rock.leave: Leave the Moss green showing along the rock's upper left edge, and let it show through in places.
shade-rock.stop: Stop when the rock reads dark, broken and mottled, with green only along its upper left rim. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

light-rock.start: Start at the rock's upper left edge. This light is about 1 3/4 in wide, and its top is about 7 in from the top edge.
light-rock.strokes: With a dry brush, skim one light stroke along the top of the rock, then add a tiny touch further along.
light-rock.inside: Moss light sits only on the rock's upper left rim, where the sun from the upper left catches it.
light-rock.leave: Leave the whole dark body of the rock showing.
light-rock.stop: Stop at one thin pale rim of light along the top of the rock. It should be a line, not a patch.

pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of each big trunk, low on the leaves. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas: one trunk at the left edge, and two big ones leaning toward the path left of the path.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full brush width at the flared foot and pull straight up to the top edge, tapering slightly.
pull-birches.inside: Use Birch gray, flat and solid. Add two trunks on the right side of the canvas; the first starts about 13 1/2 in from the left edge, and the other runs along the right edge. Pull a few slim trunks among the woods too.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves around each trunk's foot. Paint straight over the sky and the canopy.
pull-birches.stop: Stop when there are five flat gray trunks from the leaves to the top edge, with no shading.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top edge on the big trunks left of the path. The shading's bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
shade-birches.strokes: With a dry brush, skim down each trunk in long, light strokes, building in passes.
shade-birches.inside: Birch shadow covers most of each trunk, in a streaky lavender gray. Touch Moss green into the feet of the front birch trunks.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged Birch gray patches showing through, scattered up each trunk and broad at the foot.
shade-birches.stop: Stop when every trunk is lavender gray with irregular pale patches. It should never be a solid coat.

mark-bark.start: Start at the foot of the big left trunk. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the bottom half.
mark-bark.strokes: Press the brush's full width to set each patch, then lift onto the edge so it tapers off across the trunk.
mark-bark.inside: Bark dark goes in short bands across the front birch trunks. The bands are scattered up high and heavier near the base, where they merge into dark trunk feet. Do the trunks at the right edge too.
mark-bark.leave: Leave plenty of pale trunk showing between the patches.
mark-bark.stop: Stop when every birch has broken black-brown bands and dark feet, the left trunks the heaviest.

line-bark.first: Let the bark patches dry, or the lines will spread.
line-bark.start: Start high on the big trunk nearest the left edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the top half.
line-bark.strokes: Hold the liner upright, with thin inky paint, and pull many short lines down the trunk with light, steady pressure. Wobble them and let them overlap.
line-bark.inside: Bark dark lines gather down the darker middle of each trunk, between the patches, building a streaky texture. Add some on the trunks at the right edge too.
line-bark.leave: Leave the pale edges of each trunk and its feet clear.
line-bark.stop: Stop when the trunks' shadowed middles look streaked and rough. Reload often.

light-bark.start: Start at the top edge on the big trunks left of the path. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
light-bark.strokes: Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim long, light strokes down each trunk.
light-bark.inside: Birch white catches on the sunny side and middle of the front birch trunks, broken over the patches in places, because the sun is at the upper left. Do the trunks at the right edge too.
light-bark.leave: Leave the dark patches peeking through, and leave the trunk feet darker.
light-bark.stop: Stop when the birches gleam near-white in broken streaks down their lengths, with shadow and bark still showing.

tap-sunlit-leaves.start: Start on the path where it meets the ground. The band of leaves runs with its top about 8 in from the top edge and its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
tap-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap with the round's tip, light and dry, in separate leaf-sized dabs.
tap-sunlit-leaves.inside: Pale gold sits in a band along the path and across the ground, around the feet of the front birch trunks. Most of it goes on the right side of the canvas, where the sunlit path opens.
tap-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the darker leaves showing between every dab, and leave the very front clear.
tap-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when gold leaves glint along the path and around the trunk feet. The painting is finished.

blend-sky.start: Start in the sky's upper left corner with Pale gold, where the sun's glow will be. Lay Misty blue across the middle of the canvas, then Blue-violet mist down the right side and along the bottom.
blend-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side with the full width of the brush. Without rinsing, pick up the next colour and lay it so it touches the band before. Then stroke back over each join while it's still wet.
blend-sky.inside: The gold stays in the upper left, because the low sun is there. The colours cool to blue and blue-violet as they move away from it, so the right side and the lower part of the canvas read as cool, shaded haze.
blend-sky.leave: No white canvas shows anywhere. The haze reaches all four edges.
blend-sky.stop: Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze: warm gold in the upper left melting into blue and blue-violet, with soft joins and no hard lines.

glow-sun.start: Put the brush tip in the gold glow at the left edge. The sun's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
glow-sun.strokes: Make small circles with the tip, working outward from the brightest middle, so the edge stays bumpy and soft.
glow-sun.inside: Sun cream sits only in this small disk against the left edge, where the light comes from.
glow-sun.leave: Leave all the gold and blue haze around it untouched.
glow-sun.stop: Stop at a small, soft cream glow cut off by the left edge, with a bumpy rim. A beginner often makes the edge hard and round: soften it with lighter circles.

pull-far-trunks.start: This far trunk stands near the middle of the canvas. Its top is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and the whole shape starts about 6 1/2 in from the left edge.
pull-far-trunks.strokes: Begin at the trunk's foot, pressing the full brush width, then turn onto the edge and lighten the pressure as you pull up to a thin tip. Add one soft, short branch shape to the side of the trunk.
pull-far-trunks.inside: It is all one pale Blue-violet mist, with no light side. At that distance it melts into the haze.
pull-far-trunks.leave: Leave the haze all around it, and keep the edges soft.
pull-far-trunks.stop: Stop when there is one pale violet trunk, about 1 1/2 in across with its branch, flaring a little at the foot. It should read as faint and plain.

stamp-pines.first: Let the sky and far trunk dry.
stamp-pines.start: The firs fill the right side of the canvas. Their tallest top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and the group runs from about 9 1/4 in from the left edge all the way to the right edge.
stamp-pines.strokes: Work each fir from its tip down in a zigzag, stamping with the middle of the fan and pressing harder as you go down so it widens.
stamp-pines.inside: Use Deep pine green for the big near firs. Use Misty blue for the smaller hazy firs between and behind them. Each one is flat, with no lighter side yet.
stamp-pines.leave: Leave the haze showing in the gaps between the firs and all over the left side of the canvas.
stamp-pines.stop: Stop when there is a row of dark firs with a misty blue band behind them, and ragged bottoms fading into the mist. Clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick.

light-pines.start: Start low on the left side of the fir trees. The biggest patch starts about 8 in from the left edge, with its top about 5 in from the top edge.
light-pines.strokes: Tap with the middle of the fan in short strokes in different directions. Fill the pale gaps where the haze still shows between the firs.
light-pines.inside: Most of this Pine light green goes on the left side and in the bottom half of the fir trees. It thickens the lower fir mass, plus a few small taps among the firs.
light-pines.leave: Leave the fir tips and the dark firs on the right untouched.
light-pines.stop: Stop when the gaps at the base of the firs are closed into a fuller, rougher mass. Only a few patches change.

pull-middle-trunks.start: Start with the tallest trunk. Its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, its top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in tall.
pull-middle-trunks.strokes: Pull each trunk thick to thin: press the full width at the foot, then turn to the edge and lighten as you rise.
pull-middle-trunks.inside: Use Smoky brown for the tall trunk. Use Blue-violet mist for the three shorter, softer trunks, each with a blurry crown, reaching toward the firs. The farther ones are paler.
pull-middle-trunks.leave: Leave the haze between the trunks, and the firs, untouched.
pull-middle-trunks.stop: Stop when there are four plain trunks in a loose row across the left half of the woods, the tall one the darkest, with no bark marks.

lay-floor.first: Let the trunks and firs dry.
lay-floor.start: Start along the back of the ground, about 7 in from the top edge, just where the firs and trunks meet the mist.
lay-floor.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Lay band after band down to the bottom edge, from the left edge to the right edge.
lay-floor.inside: Use Golden ochre for the sunny bands and Leaf brown for the shadow bands between them. The shadow bands get darker and wider toward the bottom, where the ground is nearest.
lay-floor.leave: Leave the trunks' feet and the bases of the firs sitting on the ground line. Don't paint up into the mist.
lay-floor.stop: Stop when the whole lower part of the canvas is striped ground, lighter and smoother at the back and darker in front.

pull-path.start: Mark one dot at the path's far end, about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. The path's middle is about 9 3/4 in from the left edge. Fan a few faint lines from the dot toward the front of the ground.
pull-path.strokes: Pull each stroke along its line, wide in front and thin as it nears the dot. The path bends gently as it narrows.
pull-path.inside: Path mauve sits only on the track, widest where it is nearest.
pull-path.leave: Leave the ground's gold bands showing on both sides of the path, and a little at its front edges.
pull-path.stop: Stop when there is a mauve-brown track running from the front of the ground up into the mist. Avoid parallel edges: mark the dot first.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the path and floor dry.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start on the ground at the bottom edge, where the leaves are biggest. Most of this step is in the bottom half of the canvas.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Tap with the tip of a dry stiff brush. Use bigger dabs in front and smaller ones toward the mist.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Use Burnt orange and Leaf brown to carpet the ground and the path. Use Burnt orange for the bushes along the path, and Moss green for the big dark bush in front of the firs. Up top, tap a few loose Burnt orange clusters, one at the top edge starting about 10 3/4 in from the left edge.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the path's line showing through the leaves, and leave the firs' tips and the mist uncovered.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the ground and bushes are thick with dark leaves and the treetops have only a sprinkle. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-mid-leaves.start: Start in the treetops at the top edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
dab-mid-leaves.strokes: Tap the same way, light and dry, building leafy clusters through the treetops.
dab-mid-leaves.inside: Golden yellow fills the treetop leaves across the top and the big bush on the left side of the canvas. That bush patch is about 7 in wide, and its top is about 2 in from the top edge. Scatter separate dabs over the ground and path, with a few on the bushes in front of the firs.
dab-mid-leaves.leave: Leave the orange and brown dabs showing between the gold ones on the ground, and the firs clear.
dab-mid-leaves.stop: Stop when the canopy and the left bush glow gold and the ground has gold leaves dotted through the darker ones.

dab-sunlit-canopy.start: Start next to the sun at the left edge. Nearly all of this step sits in the top half and on the left side of the canvas.
dab-sunlit-canopy.strokes: Tap lightly with a nearly dry brush on top of the gold clusters.
dab-sunlit-canopy.inside: Pale gold goes only on the treetop leaves nearest the sun. The biggest spread starts about 1 in from the left edge and is about 6 1/2 in wide, because those leaves face the light.
dab-sunlit-canopy.leave: Leave the Golden yellow and Burnt orange showing under and around each tap, and leave the ground leaves alone.
dab-sunlit-canopy.stop: Stop when the upper left canopy shimmers pale and sunlit while the right treetops stay deeper gold.

block-in-rock.start: The rock sits right of the path. Its left side is about 10 3/4 in from the left edge and its top is about 7 in from the top edge. It is about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
block-in-rock.strokes: Paint one wide low oval first, then add smaller curved pieces at each end, like ( ).
block-in-rock.inside: Fill the whole boulder flat with Moss green, including a small lump at its back end.
block-in-rock.leave: Leave the leaves around its base. Don't paint them over.
block-in-rock.stop: Stop when there is one flat moss-green boulder lying on the leaves, with no shading yet.

shade-rock.start: Start where the rock meets the leaves. The rock's shadow and light is about 2 1/2 in wide, and its left side is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
shade-rock.strokes: Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim lightly along the rock's length in several passes.
shade-rock.inside: Deep pine green covers most of the boulder: its underside, its far end and much of its body. That side faces away from the low sun.
shade-rock.leave: Leave the Moss green showing along the rock's upper left edge, and let it show through in places.
shade-rock.stop: Stop when the rock reads dark, broken and mottled, with green only along its upper left rim. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

light-rock.start: Start at the rock's upper left edge. This light is about 1 3/4 in wide, and its top is about 7 in from the top edge.
light-rock.strokes: With a dry brush, skim one light stroke along the top of the rock, then add a tiny touch further along.
light-rock.inside: Moss light sits only on the rock's upper left rim, where the sun from the upper left catches it.
light-rock.leave: Leave the whole dark body of the rock showing.
light-rock.stop: Stop at one thin pale rim of light along the top of the rock. It should be a line, not a patch.

pull-birches.start: Start at the foot of each big trunk, low on the leaves. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas: one trunk at the left edge, and two big ones leaning toward the path left of the path.
pull-birches.strokes: Press the full brush width at the flared foot and pull straight up to the top edge, tapering slightly.
pull-birches.inside: Use Birch gray, flat and solid. Add two more front birch trunks at the right edge of the canvas. Pull a few slim trunks among the woods too.
pull-birches.leave: Leave the leaves around each trunk's foot. Paint straight over the sky and the canopy.
pull-birches.stop: Stop when there are five flat gray front birch trunks from the leaves to the top edge, with no shading.

shade-birches.start: Start at the top edge on the big trunks left of the path. The shading's bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
shade-birches.strokes: With a dry brush, skim down each trunk in long, light strokes, building in passes.
shade-birches.inside: Birch shadow covers most of each trunk, in a streaky lavender gray. Touch Moss green into the feet of the front birch trunks.
shade-birches.leave: Leave ragged Birch gray patches showing through, scattered up each trunk and broad at the foot.
shade-birches.stop: Stop when every trunk is lavender gray with irregular pale patches. It should never be a solid coat.

mark-bark.start: Start at the foot of the big left trunk. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the bottom half.
mark-bark.strokes: Press the brush's full width to set each patch, then lift onto the edge so it tapers off across the trunk.
mark-bark.inside: Bark dark goes in short bands across the front birch trunks. The bands are scattered up high and heavier near the base, where they merge into dark trunk feet. Do the front birch trunks at the right edge too.
mark-bark.leave: Leave plenty of pale trunk showing between the patches.
mark-bark.stop: Stop when every birch has broken black-brown bands and dark feet, the left trunks the heaviest.

line-bark.first: Let the bark patches dry, or the lines will spread.
line-bark.start: Start high on the big trunk nearest the left edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the top half.
line-bark.strokes: Hold the liner upright, with thin inky paint, and pull many short lines down the trunk with light, steady pressure. Wobble them and let them overlap.
line-bark.inside: Bark dark lines gather down the darker middle of each trunk, between the patches, building a streaky texture. Add some on the trunks at the right edge too.
line-bark.leave: Leave the pale edges of each trunk and its feet clear.
line-bark.stop: Stop when the trunks' shadowed middles look streaked and rough. Reload often.

light-bark.start: Start at the top edge on the two big front birch trunks that lean toward the path. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
light-bark.strokes: Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim long, light strokes down each trunk.
light-bark.inside: Birch white catches on the sunny side and middle of the front birch trunks, broken over the patches in places, because the sun is at the upper left. Do the front birch trunks at the right edge too.
light-bark.leave: Leave the dark patches peeking through, and leave the trunk feet darker.
light-bark.stop: Stop when the birches gleam near-white in broken streaks down their lengths, with shadow and bark still showing.

tap-sunlit-leaves.start: Start on the path where it meets the ground. The band of leaves runs with its top about 8 in from the top edge and its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
tap-sunlit-leaves.strokes: Tap with the round's tip, light and dry, in separate leaf-sized dabs.
tap-sunlit-leaves.inside: Pale gold sits in a band along the path and across the ground, around the feet of the front birch trunks. Most of it goes on the right side of the canvas, where the sunlit path opens.
tap-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave the darker leaves showing between every dab, and leave the very front clear.
tap-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop when gold leaves glint along the path and around the trunk feet. The painting is finished.

blend-sky.text: Start in the sky's upper left corner with Pale gold, where the sun's glow will be. Lay Misty blue across the middle of the canvas, then Blue-violet mist down the right side and along the bottom.
Stroke side to side with the full width of the brush. Without rinsing, pick up the next colour and lay it so it touches the band before. Then stroke back over each join while it's still wet.

The gold stays in the upper left, because the low sun is there. The colours cool to blue and blue-violet as they move away from it, so the right side and the lower part of the canvas read as cool, shaded haze.
No white canvas shows anywhere. The haze reaches all four edges.
Stop when the whole canvas is one soft haze: warm gold in the upper left melting into blue and blue-violet, with soft joins and no hard lines.

glow-sun.text: Let the misty sky dry.
Put the brush tip in the gold glow at the left edge. The sun's top is about 1 1/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 1 1/4 in wide.
Make small circles with the tip, working outward from the brightest middle, so the edge stays bumpy and soft.
Sun cream sits only in this small disk against the left edge, where the light comes from.
Leave all the gold and blue haze around it untouched.
Stop at a small, soft cream glow cut off by the left edge, with a bumpy rim. A beginner often makes the edge hard and round: soften it with lighter circles.

pull-far-trunks.text: Let the sky dry.
This far trunk stands near the middle of the canvas. Its top is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge, and the whole shape starts about 6 1/2 in from the left edge.
Begin at the trunk's foot, pressing the full brush width, then turn onto the edge and lighten the pressure as you pull up to a thin tip. Add one soft, short branch shape to the side of the trunk.
It is all one pale Blue-violet mist, with no light side. At that distance it melts into the haze.
Leave the haze all around it, and keep the edges soft.
Stop when there is one pale violet trunk, about 1 1/2 in across with its branch, flaring a little at the foot. It should read as faint and plain.

stamp-pines.text: Let the sky and far trunk dry.
The firs fill the right side of the canvas. Their tallest top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and the group runs from about 9 1/4 in from the left edge all the way to the right edge.
Work each fir from its tip down in a zigzag, stamping with the middle of the fan and pressing harder as you go down so it widens.
Use Deep pine green for the big near firs. Use Misty blue for the smaller hazy firs between and behind them. Each one is flat, with no lighter side yet.
Leave the haze showing in the gaps between the firs and all over the left side of the canvas.
Stop when there is a row of dark firs with a misty blue band behind them, and ragged bottoms fading into the mist. Clumpy marks mean the paint is too thick.

light-pines.text: Let the firs dry.
Start low on the left side of the fir trees. The biggest patch starts about 8 in from the left edge, with its top about 5 in from the top edge.
Tap with the middle of the fan in short strokes in different directions. Fill the pale gaps where the haze still shows between the firs.
Most of this Pine light green goes on the left side and in the bottom half of the fir trees. It thickens the lower fir mass, plus a few small taps among the firs.
Leave the fir tips and the dark firs on the right untouched.
Stop when the gaps at the base of the firs are closed into a fuller, rougher mass. Only a few patches change.

pull-middle-trunks.text: Let the firs dry.
Start with the tallest trunk. Its left side is about 2 3/4 in from the left edge, its top is about 3/4 in from the top edge, and it is about 8 in tall.
Pull each trunk thick to thin: press the full width at the foot, then turn to the edge and lighten as you rise.
Use Smoky brown for the tall trunk. Use Blue-violet mist for the three shorter, softer trunks, each with a blurry crown, reaching toward the firs. The farther ones are paler.
Leave the haze between the trunks, and the firs, untouched.
Stop when there are four plain trunks in a loose row across the left half of the woods, the tall one the darkest, with no bark marks.

lay-floor.text: Let the trunks and firs dry.
Start along the back of the ground, about 7 in from the top edge, just where the firs and trunks meet the mist.
Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Lay band after band down to the bottom edge, from the left edge to the right edge.
Use Golden ochre for the sunny bands and Leaf brown for the shadow bands between them. The shadow bands get darker and wider toward the bottom, where the ground is nearest.
Leave the trunks' feet and the bases of the firs sitting on the ground line. Don't paint up into the mist.
Stop when the whole lower part of the canvas is striped ground, lighter and smoother at the back and darker in front.

pull-path.text: Let the floor dry.
Mark one dot at the path's far end, about 7 1/2 in from the top edge. The path's middle is about 9 3/4 in from the left edge. Fan a few faint lines from the dot toward the front of the ground.
Pull each stroke along its line, wide in front and thin as it nears the dot. The path bends gently as it narrows.
Path mauve sits only on the track, widest where it is nearest.
Leave the ground's gold bands showing on both sides of the path, and a little at its front edges.
Stop when there is a mauve-brown track running from the front of the ground up into the mist. Avoid parallel edges: mark the dot first.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the path and floor dry.
Start on the ground at the bottom edge, where the leaves are biggest. Most of this step is in the bottom half of the canvas.
Tap with the tip of a dry stiff brush. Use bigger dabs in front and smaller ones toward the mist.

Use Burnt orange and Leaf brown to carpet the ground and the path. Use Burnt orange for the bushes along the path, and Moss green for the big dark bush in front of the firs. Up top, tap a few loose Burnt orange clusters, one at the top edge starting about 10 3/4 in from the left edge.
Leave the path's line showing through the leaves, and leave the firs' tips and the mist uncovered.
Stop when the ground and bushes are thick with dark leaves and the treetops have only a sprinkle. Blobs mean the brush is too wet.

dab-mid-leaves.text: Let the dark leaves dry.
Start in the treetops at the top edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
Tap the same way, light and dry, building leafy clusters through the treetops.

Golden yellow fills the treetop leaves across the top and the big bush on the left side of the canvas. That bush patch is about 7 in wide, and its top is about 2 in from the top edge. Scatter separate dabs over the ground and path, with a few on the bushes in front of the firs.
Leave the orange and brown dabs showing between the gold ones on the ground, and the firs clear.
Stop when the canopy and the left bush glow gold and the ground has gold leaves dotted through the darker ones.

dab-sunlit-canopy.text: Let the golden leaves dry.
Start next to the sun at the left edge. Nearly all of this step sits in the top half and on the left side of the canvas.
Tap lightly with a nearly dry brush on top of the gold clusters.
Pale gold goes only on the treetop leaves nearest the sun. The biggest spread starts about 1 in from the left edge and is about 6 1/2 in wide, because those leaves face the light.
Leave the Golden yellow and Burnt orange showing under and around each tap, and leave the ground leaves alone.
Stop when the upper left canopy shimmers pale and sunlit while the right treetops stay deeper gold.

block-in-rock.text: The rock sits right of the path. Its left side is about 10 3/4 in from the left edge and its top is about 7 in from the top edge. It is about 3 in wide and 1 1/2 in tall.
Paint one wide low oval first, then add smaller curved pieces at each end, like ( ).
Fill the whole boulder flat with Moss green, including a small lump at its back end.
Leave the leaves around its base. Don't paint them over.
Stop when there is one flat moss-green boulder lying on the leaves, with no shading yet.

shade-rock.text: Let the rock dry.
Start where the rock meets the leaves. The rock's shadow and light is about 2 1/2 in wide, and its left side is about 11 1/4 in from the left edge.
Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim lightly along the rock's length in several passes.
Deep pine green covers most of the boulder: its underside, its far end and much of its body. That side faces away from the low sun.
Leave the Moss green showing along the rock's upper left edge, and let it show through in places.
Stop when the rock reads dark, broken and mottled, with green only along its upper left rim. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

light-rock.text: Start at the rock's upper left edge. This light is about 1 3/4 in wide, and its top is about 7 in from the top edge.
With a dry brush, skim one light stroke along the top of the rock, then add a tiny touch further along.
Moss light sits only on the rock's upper left rim, where the sun from the upper left catches it.
Leave the whole dark body of the rock showing.
Stop at one thin pale rim of light along the top of the rock. It should be a line, not a patch.

pull-birches.text: Let everything dry.
Start at the foot of each big trunk, low on the leaves. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas: one trunk at the left edge, and two big ones leaning toward the path left of the path.
Press the full brush width at the flared foot and pull straight up to the top edge, tapering slightly.
Use Birch gray, flat and solid. Add two more front birch trunks at the right edge of the canvas. Pull a few slim trunks among the woods too.
Leave the leaves around each trunk's foot. Paint straight over the sky and the canopy.
Stop when there are five flat gray front birch trunks from the leaves to the top edge, with no shading.

shade-birches.text: Let the trunks dry completely.
Start at the top edge on the big trunks left of the path. The shading's bottom is about 1 1/4 in from the bottom edge.
With a dry brush, skim down each trunk in long, light strokes, building in passes.
Birch shadow covers most of each trunk, in a streaky lavender gray. Touch Moss green into the feet of the front birch trunks.
Leave ragged Birch gray patches showing through, scattered up each trunk and broad at the foot.
Stop when every trunk is lavender gray with irregular pale patches. It should never be a solid coat.

mark-bark.text: Let the shading dry.
Start at the foot of the big left trunk. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the bottom half.
Press the brush's full width to set each patch, then lift onto the edge so it tapers off across the trunk.

Bark dark goes in short bands across the front birch trunks. The bands are scattered up high and heavier near the base, where they merge into dark trunk feet. Do the front birch trunks at the right edge too.
Leave plenty of pale trunk showing between the patches.
Stop when every birch has broken black-brown bands and dark feet, the left trunks the heaviest.

line-bark.text: Let the bark patches dry, or the lines will spread.
Start high on the big trunk nearest the left edge. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas and in the top half.
Hold the liner upright, with thin inky paint, and pull many short lines down the trunk with light, steady pressure. Wobble them and let them overlap.
Bark dark lines gather down the darker middle of each trunk, between the patches, building a streaky texture. Add some on the trunks at the right edge too.
Leave the pale edges of each trunk and its feet clear.
Stop when the trunks' shadowed middles look streaked and rough. Reload often.

light-bark.text: Let the bark marks dry.
Start at the top edge on the two big front birch trunks that lean toward the path. Most of this step is on the left side of the canvas.
Dip only the tip, wipe it, and skim long, light strokes down each trunk.
Birch white catches on the sunny side and middle of the front birch trunks, broken over the patches in places, because the sun is at the upper left. Do the front birch trunks at the right edge too.
Leave the dark patches peeking through, and leave the trunk feet darker.
Stop when the birches gleam near-white in broken streaks down their lengths, with shadow and bark still showing.

tap-sunlit-leaves.text: Start on the path where it meets the ground. The band of leaves runs with its top about 8 in from the top edge and its bottom about 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
Tap with the round's tip, light and dry, in separate leaf-sized dabs.
Pale gold sits in a band along the path and across the ground, around the feet of the front birch trunks. Most of it goes on the right side of the canvas, where the sunlit path opens.
Leave the darker leaves showing between every dab, and leave the very front clear.
Stop when gold leaves glint along the path and around the trunk feet. The painting is finished.
