blend-sky.start: Lay Sky blue in a broad band across the middle of the canvas, from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, work Cream gold into the blue's upper and lower edges. Then add Pale gold near the top edge and across the lower part of the canvas, stroking back over each join while it's wet.
blend-sky.inside: Keep the gold brightest at the right edge near the top, where the sun sets. Bring a thin strip of blue back along the bottom edge.
blend-sky.leave: Leave no bare canvas. The sky covers everything, and later paint goes over it.
blend-sky.stop: The whole canvas, 12 in wide and 16 in tall, is soft bands of gold, blue and gold. If a hard line shows where two colors meet, add more of the lighter color there and blend again.

dry-brush-clouds.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will smear it.
dry-brush-clouds.start: Start at the top edge with thin Warm peach streaks that run all the way across the sunset clouds.
dry-brush-clouds.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush in paint. Skim long, slightly slanted strokes side to side with light pressure, so the marks break up on the canvas texture.
dry-brush-clouds.inside: Put Warm peach on the tops of the streaks and Dusky rose along their undersides, in groups down the canvas. The biggest group is about 10 in wide, and its top is about 6 1/2 in from the top edge.
dry-brush-clouds.leave: Leave the sky's blue and gold showing between the streaks and through their broken edges.
dry-brush-clouds.stop: Soft, broken bands of peach and rose cross the canvas from the top edge downward. None of them is solid.

light-cloud-tops.first: The cloud streaks must be dry.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start on the upper edge of a peach streak near the top edge.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Use the dry brush with only its tip in Pale gold and no water. Skim short side-to-side strokes along the upper edge of each streak.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Gold goes only on the upper edges of the streaks. Put a little more on the right side of the sunset clouds, where the sun sets.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the Dusky rose undersides and the blue between the streaks untouched.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Small, broken gold caps sit on the streaks all down the canvas, with the rose still showing underneath.

lay-mountains.first: Let the sky and clouds dry.
lay-mountains.start: Begin with Far violet for the far peaks. Their top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and they run across the canvas.
lay-mountains.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Let the upper edge rise and dip into a few soft peaks, then fill in downward.
lay-mountains.inside: Lay Mountain blue over the foot of the violet as a nearer, wider ridge that reaches the left and right edges. Make it darkest along its lower edge, where the hills will start.
lay-mountains.leave: Keep the gold sky showing over the violet peaks, and keep the violet tops showing over the Mountain blue.
lay-mountains.stop: Two flat mountain bands cross the canvas, pale violet behind and slate blue in front, with no texture. The sky still shows lower down.

light-ridges.start: Start at the Far violet peak nearest the right edge, where the sun sets.
light-ridges.strokes: Use the dry brush with only its tip in Warm peach. Skim a few short strokes along the very top of the ridge with feather-light pressure.
light-ridges.inside: Only the ridge tops facing the sun get peach. Put most of it on the right side of the far blue mountains, plus one small touch on a middle peak.
light-ridges.leave: Leave the rest of both ranges in their flat violet and blue.
light-ridges.stop: A few faint warm edges catch the peaks. If it reads as a stripe, there was too much paint on the brush.

lay-lake.first: Let the Mountain blue ridge dry.
lay-lake.start: Start at the right edge, at the foot of the Mountain blue ridge.
lay-lake.strokes: Pull short level strokes in from the right edge, keeping the brush flat and the strip thin.
lay-lake.inside: The lake is a thin wedge about 2 in wide. It is thickest at the right edge and tapers to a point where it meets the mountains.
lay-lake.leave: Keep the dark blue ridge line crisp where it meets the lake.
lay-lake.stop: A short, pale cream sliver of water shines at the right edge, at the foot of the mountains.

lay-hills-meadow.first: Let the mountains and lake dry.
lay-hills-meadow.start: Start with Yellow green at the left edge, at the foot of the mountains. The top of the hills is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-hills-meadow.strokes: Pull long level strokes across, tilting them down toward the right so the slopes roll. Build the hill bands one after another, then lay a wide band of Hill green across the meadow.
lay-hills-meadow.inside: The far slopes are the lighter Yellow green, and the meadow is Hill green. Lower down, lay the strokes more loosely and let them stay broken.
lay-hills-meadow.leave: Let the sky show in streaks between the hill bands and in gaps across the lower meadow. The next step fills them.
lay-hills-meadow.stop: Green covers most of the canvas below the far blue mountains, down to the bottom edge, still broken with sky. The lake stays clear.

darken-bands.first: The first greens must be dry.
darken-bands.start: Start just below the far blue mountains with a dark ridge that runs from the left edge to the lake.
darken-bands.strokes: Use long, level strokes left and right, following each hill band down toward the right.
darken-bands.inside: Fill the sky gaps between the hill bands. Then lay dark green down the lower meadow to the bottom edge. Most of it goes in the bottom half, where the meadow is nearest.
darken-bands.leave: Leave the light green tops of the hill bands, the wide sunlit band across the middle of the meadow, and the lake.
darken-bands.stop: No sky shows below the far blue mountains. The hills have dark and light bands, with a bright meadow band and darker grass toward the bottom edge.

dab-bushes.first: Let the hill bands dry so the dabs stay crisp.
dab-bushes.start: Start near the left edge on the top hill band, about 4 in from the top edge.
dab-bushes.strokes: Wipe the brush nearly dry and tap with the tip. Make round clumps in short rows that follow each band down toward the right.
dab-bushes.inside: Set the clumps along the dark edge of each band, making them smaller toward the far slopes. None go in the meadow.
dab-bushes.leave: Keep the light green band tops showing around the clumps, and leave the meadow plain.
dab-bushes.stop: Rows of dark round bushes run across the hills from edge to edge. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

block-in-cow.first: The hills and meadow must be dry.
block-in-cow.start: Start with a big upright oval for the body, its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-cow.strokes: Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), pulling every stroke downward the way the hair hangs. Add a rounded cap for the head and fringe at the top, on the side toward the lake.
block-in-cow.inside: It is one flat Rust brown shape, about 7 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall. Give the head a small bump for the chin, and end the bottom in pointed strands in the meadow.
block-in-cow.leave: Let the grass show between the pointed strands, and keep the edges shaggy, not smooth.
block-in-cow.stop: A flat rust silhouette of a shaggy cow stands in the meadow, head high toward the lake. A blob is right for now.

shade-cow.start: Start where the head meets the top of the back, then pull down the left side of the Highland cow.
shade-cow.strokes: Curve each stroke down the coat the way the hair falls, starting at the top of each bulge.
shade-cow.inside: Go darkest on the side away from the sun, where the fringe meets the face, in a long gap down the middle of the coat, and where the chin meets the chest. Most of it is in the left half of the cow's shadows. Light strokes over the rest give texture.
shade-cow.leave: Leave a strip of plain Rust brown down the sunlit edge of the chest.
shade-cow.stop: The cow is shaggy rust with deep brown shade. The sunlit chest edge stays plain.

block-in-horns.start: Start with the wide base of the tall horn, where the head meets the top of the back.
block-in-horns.strokes: Lay the wide base piece, then add curving pieces that taper to a point. The tall horn rises almost straight up, its top about 2 1/2 in from the top edge. The short horn sweeps out toward the lake and turns up.
block-in-horns.inside: Fill each horn flat with Horn tan, wide at the head and narrow at the tip.
block-in-horns.leave: Keep the sky and mountains crisp around both horns.
block-in-horns.stop: Two flat, pale tan horns stand on the head, with no shading.

shade-horns.start: Start at the point of the tall horn.
shade-horns.strokes: Pull curved strokes from the tip back along the horn's underside, following its bend and pressing lighter as you near the head.
shade-horns.inside: Put dark brown on both tips and along the undersides, the edges away from the sun, fading it out along the curve.
shade-horns.leave: Leave pale tan along the top of each horn and at its base.
shade-horns.stop: Both horns look round, with dark tips and undersides and pale tan tops.

pull-orange-locks.first: The shadows and horns must be dry.
pull-orange-locks.start: Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns, and pull locks down over the head.
pull-orange-locks.strokes: Press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down, so it tapers to a point.
pull-orange-locks.inside: Hang locks down the fringe, the head and the whole coat, curving with its roundness. Put fewer on the shade side, and let the fringe locks fall over the horn bases.
pull-orange-locks.leave: Leave dark brown gaps between the locks, and leave a few spots of the earlier coat on the chest.
pull-orange-locks.stop: The coat reads as long ginger locks over dark, with the fringe hanging over the eyes and no gold yet.

pull-gold-locks.start: Start with a small lock about 3/4 in wide on the top of the back, its top about 6 in from the top edge.
pull-gold-locks.strokes: Use short thick-to-thin strokes: full width at the top, then onto the edge and lighter as you pull down.
pull-gold-locks.inside: Add only a handful: a few down the shade side of the coat, one on the ear beside the fringe, and a couple of small touches in the grass past the chest.
pull-gold-locks.leave: Leave nearly all the ginger locks and dark gaps as they are.
pull-gold-locks.stop: A few honey-gold locks catch the light, and the coat still reads mostly ginger.

flick-dark-grass.first: The meadow and the bottom of the coat must be dry.
flick-dark-grass.start: Start with the biggest marks at the bottom edge, near the left edge.
flick-dark-grass.strokes: Load lightly and flick quickly upward from the base, lifting off so each mark thins at the top. Slant the marks the same way as the grass already there.
flick-dark-grass.inside: Scatter marks across the meadow below and beside the Highland cow, with more toward the bottom edge. A few touch the coat's pointed strands, and they thin out as you go up.
flick-dark-grass.leave: Leave plenty of the green meadow showing between the marks.
flick-dark-grass.stop: Dark slanted grass marks dot the lower meadow. Flat blobs mean too much paint on the brush.

flick-green-grass.start: Start at the bottom edge and work up between the dark marks.
flick-green-grass.strokes: Flick quickly upward from the base and lift off, slanting the marks the same way as the dark ones.
flick-green-grass.inside: Pack the marks densest toward the bottom of the meadow and thin them out as you go up. Let a few cross the pointed strands at the bottom of the coat.
flick-green-grass.leave: Leave the dark marks showing between them.
flick-green-grass.stop: The lower meadow is a weave of dark and yellow-green slanted marks.

flick-gold-grass.start: Start at the left edge beside the cow, at the top of the meadow's tall grass, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
flick-gold-grass.strokes: Flick quickly upward from the base and lift off, slanting the marks with the other grass.
flick-gold-grass.inside: Put clumps along the top of the meadow beside the cow, most on the right side of the meadow's tall grass, and more along the bottom edge.
flick-gold-grass.leave: Leave dark and yellow-green marks showing between them, and keep the gold off the cow.
flick-gold-grass.stop: Golden grass catches the low sun across the meadow.

rim-light-cow.first: The coat and grass must be dry.
rim-light-cow.start: Start on the top of the fringe, between the horns, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
rim-light-cow.strokes: Use short thick-to-thin strokes: press, then turn onto the edge and lift, so each touch of light tapers to a point down the hair.
rim-light-cow.inside: Light the edges facing the sun: the top of the fringe and head, the top of the back, the outer edge of the head and chest, and down the sunlit front. Most of it is in the right half of the sunlit rim, with a few small touches on the shade side.
rim-light-cow.leave: Leave the shade side, the face where the fringe meets it, and the dark gaps alone.
rim-light-cow.stop: The cow glows along its sunlit edges, with ginger and brown inside the rim.

light-horns.start: Start at the base of the tall horn, on its upper edge.
light-horns.strokes: Pull one curved stroke along the top of the horn toward the tip, following its bend. Do the same on the short horn, whose middle is about 8 3/4 in from the left edge.
light-horns.inside: Cream gold goes only along the upper, sunlit edge of each horn.
light-horns.leave: Leave the dark tips and undersides showing.
light-horns.stop: Each horn has a thin pale line of light along its top and looks round.

paint-nose.first: The rim light must be dry.
paint-nose.start: Start with the rounded muzzle at the end of the head, where the fringe ends, on the side toward the lake. Its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Curve strokes around the roundness of the muzzle, then pull one curved line back along the jaw and add a small dab further down the jaw.
paint-nose.inside: Rosy nose fills the muzzle, plus a small patch on the face where the fringe ends.
paint-nose.leave: Keep the fringe locks over the face.
paint-nose.stop: A flat, pinkish-brown nose ends the face, with no shine or nostrils.

nose-shine.start: Start on the top of the nose, whose top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
nose-shine.strokes: Make one or two short curved strokes across the top of the nose, following its roundness.
nose-shine.inside: Nose pink sits only on the top of the nose, between where the nostrils will go, in a patch about 1 1/4 in wide.
nose-shine.leave: Leave the Rosy nose showing all around it.
nose-shine.stop: The nose has a soft pale top and reads round.

nostrils-mouth.first: The nose must be dry, or the lines will spread.
nostrils-mouth.start: Start with a nostril at each lower corner of the nose.
nostrils-mouth.strokes: Thin the Dark umber with water, hold the brush upright and pull short curved lines with light, steady pressure. Reload often, and add water if a line skips.
nostrils-mouth.inside: Paint two dark nostrils, a short mouth line just past the nose, and a few lines darkening the jaw where it meets the chest.
nostrils-mouth.leave: Leave the pale top of the nose and the pinkish brown between the nostrils.
nostrils-mouth.stop: The face is finished, with dark nostrils and a mouth line on the pink nose.

blend-sky.start: Lay Sky blue in a broad band across the middle of the canvas, from the left edge to the right edge.
blend-sky.strokes: Pull long side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, work Cream gold into the blue's upper and lower edges. Then add Pale gold near the top edge and across the lower part of the canvas, stroking back over each join while it's wet.
blend-sky.inside: Keep the gold brightest at the right edge near the top, where the sun sets. Bring a thin strip of blue back along the bottom edge.
blend-sky.leave: Leave no bare canvas. The sky covers everything, and later paint goes over it.
blend-sky.stop: The whole canvas, 12 in wide and 16 in tall, is soft bands of gold, blue and gold. If a hard line shows where two colors meet, add more of the lighter color there and blend again.

dry-brush-clouds.first: Let the sky dry completely, or the dry brush will smear it.

dry-brush-clouds.strokes: Dip only the tip of the dry brush in paint. Skim long, slightly slanted strokes side to side with light pressure, so the marks break up on the canvas texture.
dry-brush-clouds.inside: Put Warm peach on the tops of the streaks and Dusky rose along their undersides, in groups down the canvas. The biggest group is about 10 in wide, and its top is about 6 1/2 in from the top edge.
dry-brush-clouds.leave: Leave the sky's blue and gold showing between the streaks and through their broken edges.
dry-brush-clouds.stop: Soft, broken bands of peach and rose cross the canvas from the top edge downward. None of them is solid.

light-cloud-tops.first: The cloud streaks must be dry.
light-cloud-tops.start: Start on the upper edge of a peach streak near the top edge.
light-cloud-tops.strokes: Use the dry brush with only its tip in Pale gold and no water. Skim short side-to-side strokes along the upper edge of each streak.
light-cloud-tops.inside: Gold goes only on the upper edges of the streaks. Put a little more on the right side of the sunset clouds, where the sun sets.
light-cloud-tops.leave: Leave the Dusky rose undersides and the blue between the streaks untouched.
light-cloud-tops.stop: Small, broken gold caps sit on the streaks all down the canvas, with the rose still showing underneath.

lay-mountains.first: Let the sky and clouds dry.
lay-mountains.start: Begin with Far violet for the far peaks. Their top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and they run across the canvas.
lay-mountains.strokes: Keep the brush level and pull long strokes left and right. Let the upper edge rise and dip into a few soft peaks, then fill in downward.
lay-mountains.inside: Lay Mountain blue over the foot of the violet as a nearer, wider ridge that reaches the left and right edges. Make it darkest along its lower edge, where the hills will start.
lay-mountains.leave: Keep the gold sky showing over the violet peaks, and keep the violet tops showing over the Mountain blue.
lay-mountains.stop: Two flat mountain bands cross the canvas, pale violet behind and slate blue in front, with no texture. The sky still shows lower down.

light-ridges.start: Start at the Far violet peak nearest the right edge, where the sun sets.
light-ridges.strokes: Use the dry brush with only its tip in Warm peach. Skim a few short strokes along the very top of the ridge with feather-light pressure.
light-ridges.inside: Only the ridge tops facing the sun get peach. Put most of it on the right side of the far blue mountains, plus one small touch on a middle peak.
light-ridges.leave: Leave the rest of both ranges in their flat violet and blue.
light-ridges.stop: A few faint warm edges catch the peaks. If it reads as a stripe, there was too much paint on the brush.

lay-lake.first: Let the Mountain blue ridge dry.
lay-lake.start: Start at the right edge, at the foot of the Mountain blue ridge.
lay-lake.strokes: Pull short level strokes in from the right edge, keeping the brush flat and the strip thin.
lay-lake.inside: The lake is a thin wedge about 2 in wide. It is thickest at the right edge and tapers to a point where it meets the mountains.
lay-lake.leave: Keep the dark blue ridge line crisp where it meets the lake.
lay-lake.stop: A short, pale cream sliver of water shines at the right edge, at the foot of the mountains.

lay-hills-meadow.first: Let the mountains and lake dry.
lay-hills-meadow.start: Start with Yellow green at the left edge, at the foot of the mountains. The top of the hills is about 3 1/2 in from the top edge.
lay-hills-meadow.strokes: Pull long level strokes across, tilting them down toward the right so the slopes roll. Build the hill bands one after another, then lay a wide band of Hill green across the meadow.
lay-hills-meadow.inside: The far slopes are the lighter Yellow green, and the meadow is Hill green. Lower down, lay the strokes more loosely and let them stay broken.
lay-hills-meadow.leave: Let the sky show in streaks between the hill bands and in gaps across the lower meadow. The next step fills them.
lay-hills-meadow.stop: Green covers most of the canvas below the far blue mountains, down to the bottom edge, still broken with sky. The lake stays clear.

darken-bands.first: The first greens must be dry.
darken-bands.start: Start just below the far blue mountains with a dark ridge that runs from the left edge to the lake.
darken-bands.strokes: Use long, level strokes left and right, following each hill band down toward the right.
darken-bands.inside: Fill the sky gaps between the hill bands. Then lay dark green down the lower meadow to the bottom edge. Most of it goes in the bottom half, where the meadow is nearest.
darken-bands.leave: Leave the light green tops of the hill bands, the wide sunlit band across the middle of the meadow, and the lake.
darken-bands.stop: No sky shows below the far blue mountains. The hills have dark and light bands, with a bright meadow band and darker grass toward the bottom edge.

dab-bushes.first: Let the hill bands dry so the dabs stay crisp.
dab-bushes.start: Start near the left edge on the top hill band, about 4 in from the top edge.
dab-bushes.strokes: Wipe the brush nearly dry and tap with the tip. Make round clumps in short rows that follow each band down toward the right.
dab-bushes.inside: Set the clumps along the dark edge of each band, making them smaller toward the far slopes. None go in the meadow.
dab-bushes.leave: Keep the light green band tops showing around the clumps, and leave the meadow plain.
dab-bushes.stop: Rows of dark round bushes run across the hills from edge to edge. If you get blobs, wipe the brush on a paper towel and tap again.

block-in-cow.strokes: Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), pulling every stroke downward the way the hair hangs. Add a rounded cap for the head and fringe at the top, on the side toward the lake.
block-in-cow.inside: It is one flat Rust brown shape, about 7 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall. Give the head a small bump for the chin, and end the bottom in pointed strands in the meadow.
block-in-cow.leave: Let the grass show between the pointed strands, and keep the edges shaggy, not smooth.
block-in-cow.stop: A flat rust silhouette of a shaggy cow stands in the meadow, head high toward the lake. A blob is right for now.

Start with a big upright oval for the body, its left side about 1 1/4 in from the left edge.
Add curved pieces around the oval, like ( ), pulling every stroke downward the way the hair hangs. Add a rounded cap for the head and fringe at the top, on the side toward the lake.
It is one flat Rust brown shape, about 7 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall. Give the head a small bump for the chin, and end the bottom in pointed strands in the meadow.
Let the grass show between the pointed strands, and keep the edges shaggy, not smooth.
A flat rust silhouette of a shaggy cow stands in the meadow, head high toward the lake. A blob is right for now.

shade-cow.text: Let the Rust brown dry.
Start where the head meets the top of the back, then pull down the left side of the Highland cow.
Curve each stroke down the coat the way the hair falls, starting at the top of each bulge.

Go darkest on the side away from the sun, where the fringe meets the face, in a long gap down the middle of the coat, and where the chin meets the chest. Most of it is in the left half of the cow's shadows. Light strokes over the rest give texture.
Leave a strip of plain Rust brown down the sunlit edge of the chest.
The cow is shaggy rust with deep brown shade. The sunlit chest edge stays plain.

block-in-horns.text: The coat must be dry.
Start with the wide base of the tall horn, where the head meets the top of the back.

Lay the wide base piece, then add curving pieces that taper to a point. The tall horn rises almost straight up, its top about 2 1/2 in from the top edge. The short horn sweeps out toward the lake and turns up.
Fill each horn flat with Horn tan, wide at the head and narrow at the tip.
Keep the sky and mountains crisp around both horns.
Two flat, pale tan horns stand on the head, with no shading.

shade-horns.text: Let the Horn tan dry.
Start at the point of the tall horn.
Pull curved strokes from the tip back along the horn's underside, following its bend and pressing lighter as you near the head.
Put dark brown on both tips and along the undersides, the edges away from the sun, fading it out along the curve.
Leave pale tan along the top of each horn and at its base.
Both horns look round, with dark tips and undersides and pale tan tops.

pull-orange-locks.text: The shadows and horns must be dry.
Start at the top of the fringe, between the horns, and pull locks down over the head.
Press the full brush width at the top of each lock, then turn onto the edge and lighten as you pull down, so it tapers to a point.
Hang locks down the fringe, the head and the whole coat, curving with its roundness. Put fewer on the shade side, and let the fringe locks fall over the horn bases.
Leave dark brown gaps between the locks, and leave a few spots of the earlier coat on the chest.
The coat reads as long ginger locks over dark, with the fringe hanging over the eyes and no gold yet.

pull-gold-locks.text: Let the ginger locks dry.
Start with a small lock about 3/4 in wide on the top of the back, its top about 6 in from the top edge.
Use short thick-to-thin strokes: full width at the top, then onto the edge and lighter as you pull down.
Add only a handful: a few down the shade side of the coat, one on the ear at the end of the fringe, and a couple of small touches in the grass past the chest.
Leave nearly all the ginger locks and dark gaps as they are.
A few honey-gold locks catch the light, and the coat still reads mostly ginger.

flick-dark-grass.text: The meadow and the bottom of the coat must be dry.
Start with the biggest marks at the bottom edge, near the left edge.
Load lightly and flick quickly upward from the base, lifting off so each mark thins at the top. Slant the marks the same way as the grass already there.
Scatter marks across the meadow below and beside the Highland cow, with more toward the bottom edge. A few touch the coat's pointed strands, and they thin out as you go up.
Leave plenty of the green meadow showing between the marks.
Dark slanted grass marks dot the lower meadow. Flat blobs mean too much paint on the brush.

flick-green-grass.text: Let the dark grass dry.
Start at the bottom edge and work up between the dark marks.
Flick quickly upward from the base and lift off, slanting the marks the same way as the dark ones.
Pack the marks densest toward the bottom of the meadow and thin them out as you go up. Let a few cross the pointed strands at the bottom of the coat.
Leave the dark marks showing between them.
The lower meadow is a weave of dark and yellow-green slanted marks.

flick-gold-grass.text: Let the green grass dry.
Start at the left edge beside the cow, at the top of the meadow's tall grass, about 7 1/4 in from the top edge.
Flick quickly upward from the base and lift off, slanting the marks with the other grass.
Put clumps along the top of the meadow beside the cow, most on the right side of the meadow's tall grass, and more along the bottom edge.
Leave dark and yellow-green marks showing between them, and keep the gold off the cow.
Golden grass catches the low sun across the meadow.

rim-light-cow.text: The coat and grass must be dry.
Start on the top of the fringe, between the horns, about 4 1/2 in from the top edge.
Use short thick-to-thin strokes: press, then turn onto the edge and lift, so each touch of light tapers to a point down the hair.

Light the edges facing the sun: the top of the fringe and head, the top of the back, the outer edge of the head and chest, and down the sunlit front. Most of it is in the right half of the sunlit rim, with a few small touches on the shade side.
Leave the shade side, the face where the fringe meets it, and the dark gaps alone.
The cow glows along its sunlit edges, with ginger and brown inside the rim.

light-horns.text: Let the horn shading dry.
Start at the base of the tall horn, on its upper edge.
Pull one curved stroke along the top of the horn toward the tip, following its bend. Do the same on the short horn, whose middle is about 8 3/4 in from the left edge.
Cream gold goes only along the upper, sunlit edge of each horn.
Leave the dark tips and undersides showing.
Each horn has a thin pale line of light along its top and looks round.

paint-nose.text: The rim light must be dry.
Start with the rounded muzzle at the end of the head, where the fringe ends, on the side toward the lake. Its right side is about 4 in from the right edge.
Curve strokes around the roundness of the muzzle, then pull one curved line back along the jaw and add a small dab further down the jaw.
Rosy nose fills the muzzle, plus a small patch on the face where the fringe ends.
Keep the fringe locks over the face.
A flat, pinkish-brown nose ends the face, with no shine or nostrils.

nose-shine.text: Start on the top of the nose, whose top is about 7 1/2 in from the top edge.
Make one or two short curved strokes across the top of the nose, following its roundness.
Nose pink sits only on the top of the nose, between where the nostrils will go, in a patch about 1 1/4 in wide.
Leave the Rosy nose showing all around it.
The nose has a soft pale top and reads round.

nostrils-mouth.text: The nose must be dry, or the lines will spread.
Start with a nostril at each lower corner of the nose.
Thin the Dark umber with water, hold the brush upright and pull short curved lines with light, steady pressure. Reload often, and add water if a line skips.
Paint two dark nostrils, a short mouth line just past the nose, and a few lines darkening the jaw where it meets the chest.
Leave the pale top of the nose and the pinkish brown between the nostrils.
The face is finished, with dark nostrils and a mouth line on the pink nose.

failed_first.why: step 15 (pull-gold-locks), line 4 (inside): "beside the fringe" can't find 'the fringe' on the sheet; sheet: nothing on the sheet

blend-window-sky.start: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, right at the top edge and the left edge.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the corner. Then, without rinsing, pick up Warm white, paint it in just below the blue, and stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The blue stays at the top of the patch and the Warm white goes in low down, so the sky gets lighter toward its bottom, the way a sky does near the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave the rest of the canvas bare white. The patch is only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall, with a soft, bumpy lower edge.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the corner is a smooth pale blue with no hard line where the two colors meet. If a hard line shows, add a little more Warm white at the join and blend again.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky patch dry to the touch.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start at the top of the sky patch, in the upper left corner of the canvas.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Wipe most of the Leaf green off on a paper towel, then tap straight down with the tip of the stiff brush. Work down the patch's ragged outer edge, and let a short tail of taps drop to about 2 in from the top edge.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Tap the upper part of the patch more often so it goes nearly solid. Tap less toward its bottom, so small gaps of pale sky still peek through.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the palest bit of sky showing low in the patch, and keep the rest of the canvas bare.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the corner reads as a darker clump over pale sky, with soft dappled edges. If you get blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it and tap again.

dab-sunlit-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green taps dry.
dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start on the top of the dark clump, about 1/2 in from the top edge and about 1 in from the left edge.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: With almost no Sunny leaf green on the stiff brush, tap just a few times with its tip, and keep each tap small.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Put it only on the tops of the clump, where daylight catches the leaves. It is a tiny touch, about 1/4 in wide.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave almost all of the Leaf green and the pale sky showing. Don't cover the clump.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop after a handful of taps. The corner should look nearly the same as before, just a hint brighter on top.

blend-wall.first: Let the window corner dry completely so the blue doesn't drag into it.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top edge, just right of the sky through the window, with Deep wall blue.
blend-wall.strokes: Stroke side to side in long, wide rows down the canvas. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it toward the right edge, stroking back over each join while it's wet. Let some strokes slant so the wall looks brushed.
blend-wall.inside: The deeper blue stays near the window and Wall blue spreads over the rest. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go, down to the bottom edge.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the window view in the upper left corner of the canvas showing, and paint carefully around its edge.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when everything except the window view is blue, out to every edge of the canvas, with no hard lines between the two blues.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall dry fully. White over damp blue goes streaky.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide upright post, a tall rectangle of Warm white from the top edge down to the bottom edge. Its right side is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-frame.strokes: Pull each stroke straight down the post with the flat, keeping its edge crisp against the wall. Then add the other pieces: a narrower post in the upper part of the window, a thin crossbar across the view, and lower down a thicker slanted ledge that runs out to the left edge of the canvas.
block-in-frame.inside: Keep every piece one flat Warm white, with no shading yet.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave sky and leaves showing in the two panes the crossbar makes. Leave blue wall in the corner where the ledge and the post meet, down at the bottom edge.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when a flat cream frame stands crisp over the view and the wall, reaching the top and bottom edges.

shade-frame.start: Start at the top edge, on the half of the wide post that faces the wall.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay each band in pieces with the small flat. Pull straight down the posts and straight along the crossbar and the ledge, keeping to their edges.
shade-frame.inside: The bands go on the faces turned away from the daylight: the wall-facing half of the wide post, the edge of the narrow post, the underside of the crossbar and the front of the slanted ledge. Then pull one long band down the wall just right of the white window frame, from the top edge to the bottom edge, for the frame's shadow.
shade-frame.leave: Leave cream showing on the window-facing half of each post, and leave a slim cream wedge where the ledge meets the post.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when the frame looks solid and squared, cream on one face and lavender on the other, with a dark band down the wall beside it.

block-in-sill.first: Let the frame and wall dry.
block-in-sill.start: Start with the long slanted top of the sill. Its top line begins about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, at the foot of the window frame, and slopes gently down toward the right edge.
block-in-sill.strokes: Fill that slanted rectangle with long side-to-side strokes of Warm wood brown, running along the length of the sill like wood grain. Then add the front edge as a strip across the bottom of the canvas, and a small raised lip at the left edge where the sill meets the ledge.
block-in-sill.inside: It is all one flat brown for now, covering the wall and the foot of the frame down to the bottom edge.
block-in-sill.leave: Leave the wall and the frame untouched above the sill's top line, and keep that line straight.
block-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat brown sill runs across the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, with its front edge still readable as a separate strip.

shade-sill.first: Let the brown sill dry completely, or the dry brush will lift it.
shade-sill.start: Start on the sill top at the foot of the window frame, where the sill meets the wall.
shade-sill.strokes: Put only the tip of the dry brush in Warm wood brown and wipe it. Skim long, light strokes along the grain, the length of the sill, out to the right edge of the canvas. Build it up in several light passes.
shade-sill.inside: Lay the streaks thickest along the back of the sill, across the far stretch of its top and along the front edge, so those parts read as shade. Near the window, skim around the slanted shapes where the sunlight will fall: two long slanted pieces split by a thin diagonal bar.
shade-sill.leave: Leave those sunny shapes plain, and leave a few bits of the front edge broken, where the paint skips.
shade-sill.stop: Stop when the sill looks streaky and grained, with the sun shapes still clear near the window. If a patch goes solid, let it dry and dry-brush back over part of it.

light-sill.start: Start with the biggest sunny shape, the long slanted wedge on the sill top near the window. Its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.
light-sill.strokes: Lay Sunny peach in flat pieces with the small flat. Block in the wedge first, then a narrow slanted bar nearer the wall, then a small piece at the left edge of the canvas. Run each stroke along the slant of the window light.
light-sill.inside: The peach goes where daylight through the panes lands on the sill. It slants away from the window and breaks into ragged bits at the far tip of the wedge.
light-sill.leave: Leave the brown bands between the pieces showing. They are the shadows of the frame's posts and crossbar.
light-sill.stop: Stop when the sill shows three bright peach patches split by brown bands, reading as window light on wood.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long, low oval of Golden yellow across the lower middle of the canvas. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and it runs all the way to the right edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Fill the oval with big flat strokes. Then, at the end nearest the window, add the curved roll and the folded front edge as two rounded pieces, like ( ). Carry the yellow across where the cat will lie.
block-in-blanket.inside: Keep it one flat yellow with no shading. The two bumps at the window end show the roll sitting on the fold.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave the sunny peach patches showing on the sill near the window, and a thin line of dark sill showing along the blanket's bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when a smooth, solid golden shape lies on the sill, its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge.

shade-blanket.first: Let the Golden yellow dry fully.
shade-blanket.start: Start along the back rim of the blanket, at the end nearest the window.
shade-blanket.strokes: Load the round full of Dark ochre and make short commas: touch the tip down, press, then pull and lift. Run them in rows along the roll's length, and on the front fold set them in little V pairs, like knit stitches.
shade-blanket.inside: Pack them thickest in the hollow inside the roll, along the inner side of the back rim, and in the creases of the front fold, where the knit turns away from the light.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave gold showing on the top of the roll, on the flat bed in the middle, and between every loop.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the whole blanket reads as chunky knit, gold on the tops and ochre in the dips, out to the right edge. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.start: Start on the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, on the top of the roll.
light-blanket.strokes: Load the smaller round with Pale yellow and make short press-and-lift commas, the same way as the dark loops but smaller.
light-blanket.inside: Crowd them on the rounded end facing the window, where daylight hits the knit. Then scatter just a few dots and commas over the flat bed and along the front fold.
light-blanket.leave: Leave most of the dark ochre loops and the gold showing. This is a light sprinkle, not a coat.
light-blanket.stop: Stop when the window end of the blanket glows and the rest just sparkles here and there.

block-in-cat.start: Start with a big oval of Mid gray for the curled body, sitting in the hollow of the blanket and reaching the right edge of the canvas. Then add a circle for the head at the end nearest the window.
block-in-cat.strokes: Build the rest from pieces: two triangles for the ears, one on the top of the head with its tip about 1 1/4 in from the top edge and one pointing toward the window, then curved pieces for the tail and the paws. Let your strokes follow the curl of the fur.
block-in-cat.inside: Keep it all one flat gray. The shading comes next.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket's front roll and fold showing in front of the cat, with a thin rim of gold where the body meets the blanket.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when a flat gray curled-cat shape lies on the blanket, its bottom about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

shade-cat.start: Start with Dark gray in the deep curve behind the head, where the head tucks against the body.
shade-cat.strokes: Pull curved strokes down that crescent, from the top of the body toward the blanket. Then sweep around the round end of the body and along the tail, bending every stroke with the shape.
shade-cat.inside: Dark gray goes on the far round end of the body, along the tail lying in front, where the chin meets the blanket, and in the crescent behind the head. These are the parts turned away from the window light.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the head, the ears and the top of the body Mid gray. Also leave the muzzle, the paws and a patch on the side plain gray, ready for the white.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the cat looks round: light on its head and top, dark around its back end and tail, with a few soft gray flecks where the two meet.

paint-white-patches.start: Start on the muzzle and chin, the patch between the face and the paws. Its left side is about 3 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: Curve each Warm white stroke with the round of the shape: around the muzzle, over each front paw from its top down, and down the side patch along the fur.
paint-white-patches.inside: White goes on the muzzle and chin, on the two front paws tucked at the chin, and on a pointed patch on the side, its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge, where the chest fur shows.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave a thin gray line between the two paws, and another between the paws and the chin, so they stay separate.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop after 2 or 3 thin coats, when the patches are bright and solid with soft, furry points along their edges. One thick coat goes streaky.

paint-stripes.start: Start with short Charcoal stripes on the top of the head, between the ears.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush to start each stripe, then turn it onto its edge and lighten up so the stripe tapers. On the body, curve each stripe around the round, from the spine down toward the blanket. On the tail, pull short bands across it.
paint-stripes.inside: Stripes go on the forehead, the cheeks, all over the body and in bands along the tail. Make them broadest on the shadowed end of the body. Darken the rims of the ears too.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave the white muzzle, paws and side patch clean, and leave plenty of gray between the stripes.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when the cat clearly reads as a tabby, its stripes wrapping around the curl.

paint-ears.start: Start in the ear that points toward the window. Its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ears.strokes: Touch the round's tip down near the ear's base, press, then pull toward the tip and lift, so each mark points into the corner of the ear.
paint-ears.inside: Fill the inside of both triangles: this ear and the ear on the top of the head, whose middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ears.leave: Leave a gray rim showing all around each ear.
paint-ears.stop: Stop when both ears are soft pink inside and come to a point at the tips.

flick-fur.first: Let the pink and the stripes dry.
flick-fur.start: Start on the top of the head and the top of the curled back, where the window light hits.
flick-fur.strokes: With very little Light gray on the fan brush, flick short, quick strokes, lifting off each one so it thins at the end. Follow the way the fur lies around the curl.
flick-fur.inside: Flick over the head, the back, the round of the body and the tail, so the gray between the stripes turns into lighter, softer fur. Let some flicks cross the stripe edges to break them up.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the stripes mostly dark, the white patches and pink ears untouched, and the face blank.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the coat looks soft and furry and the stripes are still clear. Flat blobs mean too much paint, so wipe the brush.

paint-nose.start: Start on the white muzzle, just over the paws, with a small triangle nose. Its middle is about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Touch the round's tip down at the nose's point, press so the mark widens, then lift. Two or three tiny strokes make the triangle, wide end up.
paint-nose.inside: Then add a few small touches of Soft pink along the tips and inner edges of both ears to deepen them.
paint-nose.leave: Leave white all around the nose.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a small, neat pink nose sits on the muzzle.

line-eyes.first: Let the nose and the fur dry. Liner lines spread on wet paint.
line-eyes.start: Start with the eye nearest the window, a gentle curved line where the gray cheek meets the white muzzle.
line-eyes.strokes: Thin the Charcoal with water and hold the liner upright. Pull each line with light, steady pressure, starting a little thicker and easing off to a thin end.
line-eyes.inside: Line both closed eyes, then a tiny mouth line just beneath the nose and a few short lines on the cheek past the second eye. Add a dark shadow where the chin tucks into the paws, and a thin dark edge along the outer rims of both ears.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the pink nose and the white muzzle clean.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the face looks peacefully asleep. Add water if a line skips.

line-whiskers.start: Start at the edge of the white muzzle, near the nose.
line-whiskers.strokes: Thin the Warm white and hold the liner upright. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one steady stroke, lightening as you go so it tapers, and reload often.
line-whiskers.inside: Fan three or four whiskers across the cheek and over the paws toward the window, reaching to about 2 3/4 in from the left edge. Fan three or four more out the other side of the muzzle, across the cheek.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave the eye lines and the nose untouched, and let a few whiskers cross the stripes.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop when thin, light whiskers fan out from both sides of the muzzle, and the painting is finished.

blend-window-sky.start: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, right at the top edge and the left edge.
blend-window-sky.strokes: Stroke side to side across the corner. Then, without rinsing, pick up Warm white, paint it in at the foot of the patch, and stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
blend-window-sky.inside: The blue stays at the top of the patch and the Warm white goes in low down, so the sky gets lighter toward its bottom, the way a sky does near the horizon.
blend-window-sky.leave: Leave the rest of the canvas bare white. The patch is only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall, with a soft, bumpy lower edge.
blend-window-sky.stop: Stop when the corner is a smooth pale blue with no hard line where the two colors meet. If a hard line shows, add a little more Warm white at the join and blend again.

dab-dark-leaves.first: Let the sky patch dry to the touch.
dab-dark-leaves.start: Start at the top of the sky patch, in the upper left corner of the canvas.
dab-dark-leaves.strokes: Wipe most of the Leaf green off on a paper towel, then tap straight down with the tip of the stiff brush. Work down the patch's ragged outer edge, and let a short tail of taps trail down from it.
dab-dark-leaves.inside: Tap the upper part of the patch more often so it goes nearly solid. Tap less toward its bottom, so small gaps of pale sky still peek through.
dab-dark-leaves.leave: Leave the palest bit of sky showing low in the patch, and keep the rest of the canvas bare.
dab-dark-leaves.stop: Stop when the corner reads as a darker clump over pale sky, with soft dappled edges. If you get blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it and tap again.

dab-sunlit-leaves.first: Let the Leaf green taps dry.
dab-sunlit-leaves.start: Start on the top of the dark clump, about 1/2 in from the top edge and about 1 in from the left edge.
dab-sunlit-leaves.strokes: With almost no Sunny leaf green on the stiff brush, tap just a few times with its tip, and keep each tap small.
dab-sunlit-leaves.inside: Put it only on the tops of the clump, where daylight catches the leaves. It is a tiny touch, about 1/4 in wide.
dab-sunlit-leaves.leave: Leave almost all of the Leaf green and the pale sky showing. Don't cover the clump.
dab-sunlit-leaves.stop: Stop after a handful of taps. The corner should look nearly the same as before, just a hint brighter on top.

blend-wall.first: Let the window corner dry completely so the blue doesn't drag into it.
blend-wall.start: Start at the top edge, next to the window view, with Deep wall blue.
blend-wall.strokes: Stroke side to side in long, wide rows down the canvas. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it toward the right edge, stroking back over each join while it's wet. Let some strokes slant so the wall looks brushed.
blend-wall.inside: The deeper blue stays near the window and Wall blue spreads over the rest. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go, down to the bottom edge.
blend-wall.leave: Leave the window view in the upper left corner of the canvas showing, and paint carefully around its edge.
blend-wall.stop: Stop when everything except the window view is blue, out to every edge of the canvas, with no hard lines between the two blues.

block-in-frame.first: Let the wall dry fully. White over damp blue goes streaky.
block-in-frame.start: Start with the wide upright post, a tall rectangle of Warm white from the top edge down to the bottom edge. Its right side is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.
block-in-frame.strokes: Pull each stroke straight down the post with the flat, keeping its edge crisp against the wall. Then add the other pieces: a narrower post in the upper part of the window, a thin crossbar across the view, and lower down a thicker slanted ledge that runs out to the left edge of the canvas.
block-in-frame.inside: Keep every piece one flat Warm white, with no shading yet.
block-in-frame.leave: Leave sky and leaves showing in the two panes the crossbar makes. Leave blue wall in the corner where the ledge and the post meet, down at the bottom edge.
block-in-frame.stop: Stop when a flat cream frame stands crisp over the view and the wall, reaching the top and bottom edges.

shade-frame.start: Start at the top edge, on the half of the wide post that faces the wall.
shade-frame.strokes: Lay each band in pieces with the small flat. Pull straight down the posts and straight along the crossbar and the ledge, keeping to their edges.
shade-frame.inside: The bands go on the faces turned away from the daylight: the wall-facing half of the wide post, the edge of the narrow post, the underside of the crossbar and the front of the slanted ledge. Then pull one long band down the wall where it meets the wide post, from the top edge to the bottom edge, for the frame's shadow.
shade-frame.leave: Leave cream showing on the window-facing half of each post, and leave a slim cream wedge where the ledge meets the post.
shade-frame.stop: Stop when the frame looks solid and squared, cream on one face and lavender on the other, with a dark band down the wall along the wide post.

block-in-sill.first: Let the frame and wall dry.
block-in-sill.start: Start with the long slanted top of the sill. Its top line begins about 7 1/4 in from the top edge, at the foot of the window frame, and slopes gently down toward the right edge.
block-in-sill.strokes: Fill that slanted rectangle with long side-to-side strokes of Warm wood brown, running along the length of the sill like wood grain. Then add the front edge as a strip across the bottom of the canvas, and a small raised lip at the left edge where the sill meets the ledge.
block-in-sill.inside: It is all one flat brown for now, covering the wall and the foot of the frame down to the bottom edge.
block-in-sill.leave: Leave the wall and the frame untouched above the sill's top line, and keep that line straight.
block-in-sill.stop: Stop when a flat brown sill runs across the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, with its front edge still readable as a separate strip.

shade-sill.first: Let the brown sill dry completely, or the dry brush will lift it.
shade-sill.start: Start on the sill top at the foot of the window frame, where the sill meets the wall.
shade-sill.strokes: Put only the tip of the dry brush in Warm wood brown and wipe it. Skim long, light strokes along the grain, the length of the sill, out to the right edge of the canvas. Build it up in several light passes.
shade-sill.inside: Lay the streaks thickest along the back of the sill, across the far stretch of its top and along the front edge, so those parts read as shade. Near the window, skim around the slanted shapes where the sunlight will fall: two long slanted pieces split by a thin diagonal bar.
shade-sill.leave: Leave those sunny shapes plain, and leave a few bits of the front edge broken, where the paint skips.
shade-sill.stop: Stop when the sill looks streaky and grained, with the sun shapes still clear near the window. If a patch goes solid, let it dry and dry-brush back over part of it.

light-sill.start: Start with the biggest sunny shape, the long slanted wedge on the sill top near the window. Its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge.
light-sill.strokes: Lay Sunny peach in flat pieces with the small flat. Block in the wedge first, then a narrow slanted bar nearer the wall, then a small piece at the left edge of the canvas. Run each stroke along the slant of the window light.
light-sill.inside: The peach goes where daylight through the panes lands on the sill. It slants away from the window and breaks into ragged bits at the far tip of the wedge.
light-sill.leave: Leave the brown bands between the pieces showing. They are the shadows of the frame's posts and crossbar.
light-sill.stop: Stop when the sill shows three bright peach patches split by brown bands, reading as window light on wood.

block-in-blanket.start: Start with a long, low oval of Golden yellow across the lower middle of the canvas. Its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge, and it runs all the way to the right edge.
block-in-blanket.strokes: Fill the oval with big flat strokes. Then, at the end nearest the window, add the curved roll and the folded front edge as two rounded pieces, like ( ). Carry the yellow across where the cat will lie.
block-in-blanket.inside: Keep it one flat yellow with no shading. The two bumps at the window end show the roll sitting on the fold.
block-in-blanket.leave: Leave the sunny peach patches showing on the sill near the window, and a thin line of dark sill showing along the blanket's bottom edge.
block-in-blanket.stop: Stop when a smooth, solid golden shape lies on the sill, its bottom about 1 in from the bottom edge.

shade-blanket.first: Let the Golden yellow dry fully.
shade-blanket.start: Start along the back rim of the blanket, at the end nearest the window.
shade-blanket.strokes: Load the round full of Dark ochre and make short commas: touch the tip down, press, then pull and lift. Run them in rows along the roll's length, and on the front fold set them in little V pairs, like knit stitches.
shade-blanket.inside: Pack them thickest in the blanket's hollow middle, along the inner side of the back rim, and in the creases of the front fold, where the knit turns away from the light.
shade-blanket.leave: Leave gold showing on the top of the roll, on the flat bed in the middle, and between every loop.
shade-blanket.stop: Stop when the whole blanket reads as chunky knit, gold on the tops and ochre in the dips, out to the right edge. If you get blobs, use less paint and lift faster.

light-blanket.start: Start on the rounded end of the blanket nearest the window, on the top of the roll.
light-blanket.strokes: Load the smaller round with Pale yellow and make short press-and-lift commas, the same way as the dark loops but smaller.
light-blanket.inside: Crowd them on the rounded end facing the window, where daylight hits the knit. Then scatter just a few dots and commas over the flat bed and along the front fold.
light-blanket.leave: Leave most of the dark ochre loops and the gold showing. This is a light sprinkle, not a coat.
light-blanket.stop: Stop when the window end of the blanket glows and the rest just sparkles here and there.

block-in-cat.start: Start with a big oval of Mid gray for the curled body, sitting in the hollow of the blanket and reaching the right edge of the canvas. Then add a circle for the head at the end nearest the window.
block-in-cat.strokes: Build the rest from pieces: two triangles for the ears, one standing up from the top of the head and one pointing toward the window, then curved pieces for the tail and the paws. Let your strokes follow the curl of the fur.
block-in-cat.inside: Keep it all one flat gray. The shading comes next.
block-in-cat.leave: Leave the blanket's front roll and fold showing in front of the cat, with a thin rim of gold where the body meets the blanket.
block-in-cat.stop: Stop when a flat gray curled-cat shape lies on the blanket, its bottom about 3 1/2 in from the bottom edge.

shade-cat.start: Start with Dark gray in the deep curve behind the head, where the head tucks against the body.
shade-cat.strokes: Pull curved strokes down that crescent, from the top of the body toward the blanket. Then sweep around the round end of the body and along the tail, bending every stroke with the shape.
shade-cat.inside: Dark gray goes on the far round end of the body, along the tail lying in front, where the chin meets the blanket, and in the crescent behind the head. These are the parts turned away from the window light.
shade-cat.leave: Leave the head, the ears and the top of the body Mid gray. Also leave the muzzle, the paws and a patch on the side plain gray, ready for the white.
shade-cat.stop: Stop when the cat looks round: light on its head and top, dark around its back end and tail, with a few soft gray flecks where the two meet.

paint-white-patches.start: Start on the muzzle and chin, the patch between the face and the paws. Its left side is about 3 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-white-patches.strokes: Curve each Warm white stroke with the round of the shape: around the muzzle, over each front paw from its top down, and down the side patch along the fur.
paint-white-patches.inside: White goes on the muzzle and chin, on the two front paws tucked at the chin, and on a pointed patch on the side, its middle about 9 1/4 in from the left edge, where the chest fur shows.
paint-white-patches.leave: Leave a thin gray line between the two paws, and another between the paws and the chin, so they stay separate.
paint-white-patches.stop: Stop after 2 or 3 thin coats, when the patches are bright and solid with soft, furry points along their edges. One thick coat goes streaky.

paint-stripes.start: Start with short Charcoal stripes on the top of the head, between the ears.
paint-stripes.strokes: Press the full width of the angle brush to start each stripe, then turn it onto its edge and lighten up so the stripe tapers. On the body, curve each stripe around the round, from the spine down toward the blanket. On the tail, pull short bands across it.
paint-stripes.inside: Stripes go on the forehead, the cheeks, all over the body and in bands along the tail. Make them broadest on the shadowed end of the body. Darken the rims of the ears too.
paint-stripes.leave: Leave the white muzzle, paws and side patch clean, and leave plenty of gray between the stripes.
paint-stripes.stop: Stop when the cat clearly reads as a tabby, its stripes wrapping around the curl.

paint-ears.start: Start in the ear that points toward the window. Its middle is about 2 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ears.strokes: Touch the round's tip down near the ear's base, press, then pull toward the tip and lift, so each mark points into the corner of the ear.
paint-ears.inside: Fill that ear with Soft pink, then the ear on the top of the head, whose middle is about 6 1/4 in from the left edge.
paint-ears.leave: Leave a gray rim showing all around each ear.
paint-ears.stop: Stop when both ears are soft pink with a gray rim and come to a point at the tips.

flick-fur.first: Let the pink and the stripes dry.
flick-fur.start: Start on the top of the head and the top of the curled back, where the window light hits.
flick-fur.strokes: With very little Light gray on the fan brush, flick short, quick strokes, lifting off each one so it thins at the end. Follow the way the fur lies around the curl.
flick-fur.inside: Flick over the head, the back, the round of the body and the tail, so the gray between the stripes turns into lighter, softer fur. Let some flicks cross the stripe edges to break them up.
flick-fur.leave: Leave the stripes mostly dark, the white patches and pink ears untouched, and the face blank.
flick-fur.stop: Stop when the coat looks soft and furry and the stripes are still clear. Flat blobs mean too much paint, so wipe the brush.

paint-nose.start: Start on the white muzzle, just over the paws, with a small triangle nose. Its middle is about 5 3/4 in from the left edge.
paint-nose.strokes: Touch the round's tip down at the nose's point, press so the mark widens, then lift. Two or three tiny strokes make the triangle, wide end up.
paint-nose.inside: Then add a few small touches of Soft pink along the tips and inner edges of both ears to deepen them.
paint-nose.leave: Leave white all around the nose.
paint-nose.stop: Stop when a small, neat pink nose sits on the muzzle.

line-eyes.first: Let the nose and the fur dry. Liner lines spread on wet paint.
line-eyes.start: Start with the eye nearest the window, a gentle curved line where the gray cheek meets the white muzzle.
line-eyes.strokes: Thin the Charcoal with water and hold the liner upright. Pull each line with light, steady pressure, starting a little thicker and easing off to a thin end.
line-eyes.inside: Line both closed eyes, then a tiny mouth line from the point of the pink nose and a few short lines on the cheek past the second eye. Add a dark shadow where the chin tucks into the paws, and a thin dark edge along the outer rims of both ears.
line-eyes.leave: Leave the pink nose and the white muzzle clean.
line-eyes.stop: Stop when the face looks peacefully asleep. Add water if a line skips.

line-whiskers.start: Start at the edge of the white muzzle, near the nose.
line-whiskers.strokes: Thin the Warm white and hold the liner upright. Pull each whisker out from the muzzle in one steady stroke, lightening as you go so it tapers, and reload often.
line-whiskers.inside: Fan three or four whiskers across the cheek and over the paws toward the window, reaching to about 2 3/4 in from the left edge. Fan three or four more out the other side of the muzzle, across the cheek.
line-whiskers.leave: Leave the eye lines and the nose untouched, and let a few whiskers cross the stripes.
line-whiskers.stop: Stop when thin, light whiskers fan out from both sides of the muzzle, and the painting is finished.

blend-window-sky.text: Start in the upper left corner of the canvas with Pale sky blue, right at the top edge and the left edge.
Stroke side to side across the corner. Then, without rinsing, pick up Warm white, paint it in at the foot of the patch, and stroke back up over the join while both are wet.
The blue stays at the top of the patch and the Warm white goes in low down, so the sky gets lighter toward its bottom, the way a sky does near the horizon.
Leave the rest of the canvas bare white. The patch is only about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall, with a soft, bumpy lower edge.
Stop when the corner is a smooth pale blue with no hard line where the two colors meet. If a hard line shows, add a little more Warm white at the join and blend again.

dab-dark-leaves.text: Let the sky patch dry to the touch.
Start at the top of the sky patch, in the upper left corner of the canvas.
Wipe most of the Leaf green off on a paper towel, then tap straight down with the tip of the stiff brush. Work down the patch's ragged outer edge, and let a short tail of taps trail down from it.
Tap the upper part of the patch more often so it goes nearly solid. Tap less toward its bottom, so small gaps of pale sky still peek through.
Leave the palest bit of sky showing low in the patch, and keep the rest of the canvas bare.
Stop when the corner reads as a darker clump over pale sky, with soft dappled edges. If you get blobs, the brush is too wet: wipe it and tap again.

dab-sunlit-leaves.text: Let the Leaf green taps dry.
Start on the top of the dark clump, about 1/2 in from the top edge and about 1 in from the left edge.
With almost no Sunny leaf green on the stiff brush, tap just a few times with its tip, and keep each tap small.
Put it only on the tops of the clump, where daylight catches the leaves. It is a tiny touch, about 1/4 in wide.
Leave almost all of the Leaf green and the pale sky showing. Don't cover the clump.
Stop after a handful of taps. The corner should look nearly the same as before, just a hint brighter on top.

blend-wall.text: Let the window corner dry completely so the blue doesn't drag into it.
Start at the top edge, next to the window view, with Deep wall blue.

Stroke side to side in long, wide rows down the canvas. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and carry it toward the right edge, stroking back over each join while it's wet. Let some strokes slant so the wall looks brushed.
The deeper blue stays near the window and Wall blue spreads over the rest. Paint straight through where the frame, sill, blanket and cat will go, down to the bottom edge.
Leave the window view in the upper left corner of the canvas showing, and paint carefully around its edge.
Stop when everything except the window view is blue, out to every edge of the canvas, with no hard lines between the two blues.

block-in-frame.text: Let the wall dry fully. White over damp blue goes streaky.
Start with the wide upright post, a tall rectangle of Warm white from the top edge down to the bottom edge. Its right side is about 3 3/4 in from the left edge.

Pull each stroke straight down the post with the flat, keeping its edge crisp against the wall. Then add the other pieces: a narrower post in the upper part of the window, a thin crossbar across the view, and lower down a thicker slanted ledge that runs out to the left edge of the canvas.
Keep every piece one flat Warm white, with no shading yet.
Leave sky and leaves showing in the two panes the crossbar makes. Leave blue wall in the corner where the ledge and the post meet, down at the bottom edge.
Stop when a flat cream frame stands crisp over the view and the wall, reaching the top and bottom edges.

shade-frame.text: Start at the top edge, on the half of the wide post that faces the wall.
Lay each band in pieces with the small flat. Pull straight down the posts and straight along the crossbar and the ledge, keeping to their edges.

The bands go on the faces turned away from the daylight: the wall-facing half of the wide post, the edge of the narrow post, the underside of the crossbar and the front of the slanted ledge. Then pull one long band down the wall where it meets the wide post, from the top edge to the bottom edge, for the frame's shadow.
Leave cream showing on the window-facing half of each post, and leave a slim cream wedge where the ledge meets the post.
Stop when the frame looks solid and squared, cream on one face and lavender on the other, with a dark band down the wall along the wide post.

It is all one flat brown for now, covering the wall and the foot of the frame down to the bottom edge.
Leave the wall and the frame untouched above the sill's top line, and keep that line straight.
Stop when a flat brown sill runs across the canvas from the left edge to the right edge, with its front edge still readable as a separate strip.

stage-free.note: The pictures are shared and carry the same faults on both sides. Step 7's green has odd cut-out patches no brush makes. Step 8 jumps from those patches to fully rendered hills and a textured meadow. Step 21 brings in eye shading and the chin along with the nose. A's words describe what to paint in plain terms (bands, streaks, locks, where each sits), so a beginner can follow most steps. Agreement still slips at 8, where the meadow texture appears unasked, and at 22, where 'Nose pink' mixes to a grey-green but paints on near-white.

v3.note: Same pictures and same faults as A. B's words are templated: 'inside the outlined area', 'the paint map shows', and outline boxes that don't fit the picture. Step 20 says the area is 1/4 in by 1/4 in, and step 2 says its bottom is 2 in from the top while the streaks run down the whole canvas. Step 8 promises 'flat, level bands' over a picture of grass texture, and step 12's '( )' shape advice doesn't describe a horn. It does catch two things A misses: the gold dab in the meadow at 15 and the greyer nose at 23.

ab.note: The pictures are identical, so the choice rests on the words. A tells a beginner what to paint and where, while B leans on outlines and paint maps the painter doesn't have and gives sizes that contradict the picture. I'm clear on this, though both share the step 8 jump and the face suddenly coming together at step 21.

stage-free.note: The pictures are the same on both sides and carry the main faults. Steps 2 and 3 paint leaves that never show, then step 4 makes leaves and a bigger sky appear while its words only ask for a wall. Step 8's same-brown dry-brush somehow lays pale streaks, and step 11 turns a flat gold block into a rimmed, knitted bed in one go. A's words are plain and paintable, but they describe things the pictures don't show: leaves in steps 2-3, and in step 14 it leaves the head mid gray when the picture darkens almost the whole cat.
